nodes.rationale: DISTINCT ON expressions must be the leading ORDER BY expressions (42P10 otherwise). Omitting ORDER BY is legal and returns an arbitrary row per group.

nodes.label: DISTINCT ON vs row_number vs LATERAL
nodes.rationale: DISTINCT ON for top-1 over a whole table; row_number() for top-N or the rank; LATERAL when the outer set is small and indexed, and to keep groups with no rows.

nodes.label: Plain DISTINCT
nodes.rationale: Deduplicates the entire computed select list. A unique column in the list makes every row distinct. Treats NULLs as equal. Do not use it to mask join fan-out.

nodes.label: COALESCE
nodes.rationale: First non-null argument; short-circuits. NULLIF(a,b) returns NULL when equal — x / NULLIF(y,0) avoids 22012.

nodes.label: GREATEST/LEAST skip nulls
nodes.rationale: Opposite of most SQL: GREATEST(NULL, 2) is 2. NULL only if every argument is null. Row-wise, not aggregates.

nodes.label: CASE expression
nodes.rationale: First matching WHEN wins. Implicit ELSE NULL if none match. Short form uses = and cannot express IS NULL. Useful for custom ORDER BY.

nodes.label: || vs concat vs concat_ws
nodes.rationale: || propagates null ('x' || NULL is NULL). concat treats null as empty. concat_ws skips null values but a null separator voids the result.

nodes.label: generate_series
nodes.rationale: Set-returning function that invents rows. Both endpoints inclusive (hourly over one day → 25). Descending needs a negative step; default +1 silently returns no rows. Step 0 → 22023.

nodes.label: Gap filling with generate_series
nodes.rationale: LEFT JOIN from the series so missing days survive. count(e.id) not count(*) — count(*) is 1 even with no match. Series must be the left side.

nodes.label: WITH ORDINALITY
nodes.rationale: Adds a position column to any SRF so client-supplied order survives a join. unnest(ARRAY['c','a','b']) WITH ORDINALITY → positions 1,2,3.

nodes.label: SRF planner assumes 1000 rows
nodes.rationale: No statistics for a generated set; unbounded series is a memory problem. Materialise and ANALYZE a huge series if join order goes wrong.

nodes.label: Always name INSERT columns
nodes.rationale: INSERT INTO t VALUES binds to current column order; adding a column silently rewires statements. Omit columns that have defaults. Explicit NULL overrides DEFAULT.

nodes.label: INSERT RETURNING
nodes.rationale: Only correct way to learn a generated id. A follow-up SELECT can see another transaction's row under concurrency.

nodes.label: INSERT speed ladder
nodes.rationale: 10k rows: per-row autocommit 19551 ms; one tx 2262 ms (8.6×); multi-row VALUES 148 ms; unnest 81 ms; COPY 243 ms. WAL flush per statement plus round trips dominate.

nodes.label: 65535 bind-parameter ceiling
nodes.rationale: Protocol stores parameter count in 16 bits. 21845×3 ok; 21846 → 08P01 about parameter formats, not the limit. Chunk or unnest one array per column.

nodes.label: OFFSET cost grows with depth
nodes.rationale: OFFSET is produce-then-discard. 500k rows LIMIT 20: 1.22 ms at 0 vs 105.85 ms at 499980; EXPLAIN shows rows=500000 feeding Limit 20. Index cannot skip counting.

nodes.label: Keyset pagination
nodes.rationale: WHERE id > $1 ORDER BY id LIMIT 20 seeks the index. Same depth: 0.93 ms and 4 buffers vs 105.85 ms and 5045. Loses random access to page N.

nodes.label: OFFSET pages drift under writes
nodes.rationale: An insert between requests shifts later pages; item 16 served twice. A delete hides a row. Keyset uses a value, not a count.

nodes.label: Unique ORDER BY tiebreaker
nodes.rationale: Non-unique sort: paging 100 rows by 5 gave 54 distinct ids and 46 repeats on a static table. ORDER BY grp, id is a total order.

nodes.label: LIMIT without ORDER BY
nodes.rationale: No default order. An UPDATE rewrote a tuple at heap end and changed which five rows came back. Only correct when identity of rows does not matter.

nodes.label: count(*) vs reltuples vs LIMIT n+1
nodes.rationale: Exact count 25.69 ms on 500k; reltuples 0.49 ms. LIMIT n+1 answers 'is there a next page?' for free. Clamp user-supplied limit.

nodes.label: Logical query processing order
nodes.rationale: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT. Aliases are created at SELECT (seventh). Defines semantics, not execution.

nodes.label: Select-list alias visibility
nodes.rationale: WHERE total > 10 → 42703 because WHERE runs before SELECT. Same alias works in ORDER BY. Repeat the expression or wrap in a subquery/CTE.

nodes.label: WHERE vs HAVING
nodes.rationale: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups. Aggregates in WHERE → 42803. Non-aggregate filters belong in WHERE to reduce grouping work.

nodes.label: Logical order is not execution order
nodes.rationale: Planner pushes predicates, uses top-N heapsort, reorders joins. 'Most selective WHERE first' has no effect. Use EXPLAIN for performance.

nodes.label: MERGE
nodes.rationale: SQL-standard insert/update/delete in one pass from a source. Not a drop-in ON CONFLICT replacement; wrong tool for concurrent upsert. Does support RETURNING and merge_action().

nodes.label: MERGE is not concurrency-safe for upsert
nodes.rationale: MERGE can still raise a unique violation under concurrent inserts because it does not use the unique index as an arbiter the same way ON CONFLICT does.

nodes.label: INSERT … ON CONFLICT
nodes.rationale: Atomic upsert. Only correct insert-if-absent. Check-then-insert raced: 20 workers, 20 duplicates, 0 errors. Conflict target needs a unique index (42P10 otherwise).

nodes.label: EXCLUDED row
nodes.rationale: The row that would have been inserted. SET qty = stock.qty + EXCLUDED.qty accumulates; SET qty = EXCLUDED.qty overwrites. WHERE on DO UPDATE skips no-op writes.

nodes.label: xmax = 0 as was_insert
nodes.rationale: RETURNING (xmax = 0) is true for insert, false for update. Implementation detail; prefer created_at vs updated_at if the distinction is load-bearing.

nodes.label: DO NOTHING returns no row
nodes.rationale: rowCount 0 and empty RETURNING on skip. Workarounds: no-op DO UPDATE (a real write) or follow-up SELECT.

nodes.label: Identity consumed before conflict
nodes.rationale: Identity is generated before conflict detection. Three idempotent two-row seeds left last_value at 6. Harmless because sequences are not gapless.

nodes.label: ORDER BY
nodes.rationale: Without ORDER BY there is no row order. Sorting is free only when an index supplies the order; otherwise it spills past work_mem.

nodes.label: No default SELECT order
nodes.rationale: A SELECT with no ORDER BY may return any order and can change after VACUUM, a plan switch, or an UPDATE that relocates a heap row.

nodes.label: Unique ORDER BY tiebreaker
nodes.rationale: ORDER BY plus LIMIT on a non-unique column is not a total order. Measured 46 duplicate page rows of 100; append the primary key.

nodes.label: NULLS FIRST and NULLS LAST
nodes.rationale: Default is NULLS LAST for ASC and NULLS FIRST for DESC. Indexes record null placement; a mismatch forces an in-memory sort.

nodes.label: Collation and libc vs ICU
nodes.rationale: musl Alpine sorts en_US.utf8 by byte value; glibc applies dictionary order. libc upgrades can silently corrupt text btrees.

nodes.label: Pin an ICU or builtin collation
nodes.rationale: Do not inherit collation from the container image. ICU is versioned by PostgreSQL; builtin C.UTF-8 is stable byte order.

nodes.label: Sort in SQL not JavaScript
nodes.rationale: LIMIT must sort server-side; sorting a page in JS reorders the wrong twenty rows.

nodes.label: Parameterized queries
nodes.rationale: Values go in as $1, never into the SQL string. Safety is the wire protocol, not escaping.

nodes.label: Extended query protocol
nodes.rationale: Parse then bind. Multi-statement text fails with 42601. An empty params array stays on the simple protocol.

nodes.label: Simple query protocol
nodes.rationale: The SQL string is a script and may contain several statements. Concatenated ORDER BY dropped a table in one request.

nodes.label: Parameters cannot be identifiers
nodes.rationale: ORDER BY $1 sorts by a constant string with no error. Table, column, and ASC/DESC slots are structure, not values.

nodes.label: Identifier allowlist
nodes.rationale: Map user input to a hard-coded identifier and reject the rest. Interpolate only your own object values.

nodes.label: format %I identifier quoting
nodes.rationale: For genuinely unknown names, format('%I') quotes the payload as one identifier. %s quotes nothing.

nodes.label: LIKE wildcard abuse
nodes.rationale: A parameter keeps % as data, but LIKE still matches everything. Escape % and _ when the user means them literally.

nodes.label: 65535 parameter ceiling
nodes.rationale: The protocol stores the count in 16 bits. 21845 three-column rows succeed; one more fails with 08P01.

nodes.label: RETURNING
nodes.rationale: The only way to read what a write did without a second query that can see a different transaction's data.

nodes.label: RETURNING vs later SELECT
nodes.rationale: Under READ COMMITTED a follow-up SELECT takes a fresh snapshot and can race. RETURNING is the same statement.

nodes.label: RETURNING old. and new.
nodes.rationale: PostgreSQL 18 can return both versions of an updated row. On 17 and below this is a syntax error.

nodes.label: ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING trap
nodes.rationale: A skipped conflict returns no row. DO UPDATE of a harmless column plus xmax = 0 always returns a row.

nodes.label: RETURNING into a CTE
nodes.rationale: DELETE … RETURNING can feed an INSERT in one atomic statement. Sibling CTEs share a snapshot and see only RETURNING output.

nodes.label: Multi-row RETURNING has no order
nodes.rationale: RETURNING takes no ORDER BY. Wrap in a CTE and sort the outer SELECT.

nodes.label: SELECT clause skeleton
nodes.rationale: Written order is SELECT FROM WHERE GROUP BY HAVING ORDER BY LIMIT. Evaluation order differs.

nodes.label: SELECT alias invisible in WHERE
nodes.rationale: WHERE runs before the select list. WHERE total > 10 raises 42703; ORDER BY total works.

nodes.label: SELECT * is for psql
nodes.rationale: Star silently widens payloads, defeats index-only scans, and collapses duplicate join column names.

nodes.label: bigint and numeric as JS strings
nodes.rationale: pg returns bigint and numeric as text to preserve precision. id === 5 is false for id '5'.

nodes.label: Optional filter $1 IS NULL OR col = $1
nodes.rationale: One statement serves filtered and unfiltered lists so the plan cache stays warm. Cast $1 so the type can be inferred.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL string functions
nodes.rationale: Everyday set is case, trim, substring, split, pad, replace, and format. SQL strings are 1-indexed.

nodes.label: SQL strings are 1-indexed
nodes.rationale: substring('abcdef' FROM 2 FOR 3) is 'bcd'. FOR is a length, not an end position.

nodes.label: length vs octet_length
nodes.rationale: 'héllo' is 5 characters and 6 bytes. varchar(n) counts characters; btree entries have a byte limit.

nodes.label: format %I %L %s
nodes.rationale: %I quotes identifiers, %L quotes literals, %s does nothing. Application values still belong in $1 parameters.

nodes.label: Case-insensitive matching
nodes.rationale: lower() needs an expression index; ILIKE needs pg_trgm for leading wildcards; citext or a CI collation compare directly.

nodes.label: TRUNCATE vs DELETE
nodes.rationale: DELETE is O(rows) and fires triggers. TRUNCATE is near O(1), reclaims space immediately, and has different semantics.

nodes.label: TRUNCATE is transactional
nodes.rationale: Unlike MySQL and Oracle, PostgreSQL TRUNCATE rolls back. It takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE until commit.

nodes.label: TRUNCATE RESTART IDENTITY
nodes.rationale: Plain TRUNCATE leaves sequences alone. After 10000 rows the next id was 10001.

nodes.label: TRUNCATE skips row triggers
nodes.rationale: AFTER DELETE FOR EACH ROW never fires. Audit and counter side effects silently vanish. Use AFTER TRUNCATE FOR EACH STATEMENT.

nodes.label: TRUNCATE CASCADE vs named tables
nodes.rationale: Inbound FKs raise 0A000. CASCADE empties referencing tables transitively, unlike DROP CASCADE which removes objects not data.

nodes.label: Row constructors and tuple comparison
nodes.rationale: (a, b) > ($1, $2) is lexicographic. It replaces an OR chain the planner handles worse.

nodes.label: Keyset pagination
nodes.rationale: Seek to the last row's sort key. Tuple, ORDER BY, and index must match; the last column must be unique.

nodes.label: NULL in a row constructor
nodes.rationale: (1,NULL) < (1,2) is unknown. WHERE discards it, so pagination silently stops. Only paginate NOT NULL columns.

nodes.label: Opaque keyset cursor
nodes.rationale: Round-trip both values as one server-issued token. Base64 is not encryption; validate types before binding.

nodes.label: UPDATE
nodes.rationale: SET can reference current values. Forget WHERE and every row changes; read-modify-write loses concurrent increments.

nodes.label: UPDATE ... FROM
nodes.rationale: Inner-join a source of new values. Duplicate source keys pick one winner arbitrarily; MERGE raises 21000 instead.

nodes.label: Lost updates from read-modify-write
nodes.rationale: 20 concurrent SELECT-then-UPDATE increments produced 2. SET qty = qty + 1 serialises under a row lock and produced 20.

nodes.label: PATCH via COALESCE
nodes.rationale: SET col = COALESCE($n, col) leaves unsent fields alone. It cannot set a column to NULL; then build SET from present keys.

nodes.label: UPDATE writes a new tuple version
nodes.rationale: PostgreSQL never updates in place. Dead versions wait for VACUUM; non-HOT updates also write new index entries.

nodes.label: VALUES as a table
nodes.rationale: SELECT FROM (VALUES …) AS t(cols) joins a client list without a temp table. Types are inferred from the first row.

nodes.label: unnest
nodes.rationale: Several arrays unnest in parallel, not as a cross join. Shorter arrays pad with NULL.

nodes.label: unnest bulk-parameter bridge
nodes.rationale: 5000 rows through exactly 3 parameters. One statement shape forever, so the plan cache does not fragment.

nodes.label: col = ANY($1::type[])
nodes.rationale: One array parameter replaces a generated IN list and avoids the NOT IN NULL trap.

nodes.label: Three-valued WHERE logic
nodes.rationale: WHERE keeps only true. Unknown is discarded like false, silently.

nodes.label: IS DISTINCT FROM
nodes.rationale: Null-safe comparison. qty != 5 dropped the NULL row; IS DISTINCT FROM 5 kept it.

nodes.label: NOT IN with NULL
nodes.rationale: One NULL in the list makes every row unknown. Prefer NOT EXISTS for subqueries.

nodes.label: Sargable predicates
nodes.rationale: An index on col serves bare col. date(created_at) or lower(email) needs a matching expression index.

nodes.label: Half-open time ranges
nodes.rationale: BETWEEN is inclusive on both ends and double-counts midnight boundaries. Use >= start AND < end.

nodes.label: MERGE RETURNING
nodes.rationale: Supported since PostgreSQL 17. Widely-repeated advice that MERGE has no RETURNING is obsolete.

nodes.label: merge_action()
nodes.rationale: Returns INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE per row. Legal only in a MERGE RETURNING list; elsewhere 42601. rowCount is the total only.

nodes.label: MERGE
nodes.rationale: One statement can insert, update, and delete. First matching WHEN branch wins, so specific conditions must precede bare MATCHED.

nodes.label: WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE
nodes.rationale: PostgreSQL 17 delete-half of a reconcile: target rows the source no longer has.

nodes.label: MERGE is not index-arbitrated
nodes.rationale: ON CONFLICT uses a unique index as arbiter. Concurrent MERGE can both take NOT MATCHED and raise 23505 or insert duplicates.

nodes.label: MERGE 21000 source duplicate
nodes.rationale: Two source rows matching one target raise 21000. Deduplicate with DISTINCT ON before merging.

nodes.label: Join alias discipline
nodes.rationale: Alias every table and qualify every column. An unqualified unique name silently rebinds after a same-named column is added.

nodes.label: 42702 ambiguous column
nodes.rationale: PostgreSQL will not pick a side. The dangerous case is the unambiguous one that later becomes wrong.

nodes.label: Alias replaces the table name
nodes.rationale: After FROM t AS c, t.id is 42P01. That replacement is what makes a self join possible.

nodes.label: CROSS JOIN
nodes.rationale: Every left row pairs with every right row. Deliberate for spines and grids; accidental via comma FROM with no error.

nodes.label: Comma FROM accidental product
nodes.rationale: FROM a, b with a missing WHERE produced 20 rows from 4×5 with no error. JOIN … ON makes the same omission a syntax error.

nodes.label: Calendar spine
nodes.rationale: CROSS JOIN generate_series then LEFT JOIN facts with the date filter in ON. count(*) reports 1 on empty days; count(o.id) reports 0.

nodes.label: INNER JOIN
nodes.rationale: One row per matching pair, not per left row. Unmatched rows disappear; multiple matches duplicate and inflate sum().

nodes.label: Join row-count rule
nodes.rationale: Dee has no orders and vanishes; Ann has two and duplicates. The fixture is shared across the joins phase.

nodes.label: Joining on expressions
nodes.rationale: ON accepts any boolean. Non-equality leaves only nested loops; hash and merge joins need equality.

nodes.label: Range join with @>
nodes.rationale: Price-at-sale via tstzrange @> sold_at. Guard overlaps with EXCLUDE USING gist; index the range with GiST.

nodes.label: Expression indexes need selectivity
nodes.rationale: A 200k×200k join on lower() was 211 ms with or without the index. The same index made a 50-row driving side 59× faster.

nodes.label: LATERAL
nodes.rationale: A FROM subquery may reference tables to its left and run once per driving row. Without LATERAL that reference is 42P01.

nodes.label: LEFT JOIN LATERAL … ON true
nodes.rationale: CROSS JOIN LATERAL drops empty driving rows. LEFT JOIN LATERAL requires ON true because matching already happened in WHERE.

nodes.label: LATERAL top-N per group
nodes.rationale: With a real 500-row group table and an index, LATERAL was 9.3 ms vs 51.8 ms for row_number(). Drive from a dimension table.

nodes.label: LEFT JOIN
nodes.rationale: Keeps every left row and NULL-extends the right. A right-table predicate in WHERE turns it back into an INNER JOIN.

nodes.label: ON vs WHERE on outer joins
nodes.rationale: The single most common SQL bug in application code. count(*) and count(o.id) disagree by the unmatched left rows.

nodes.label: Multi-table joins
nodes.rationale: Joins chain left to right. Inner joins may be reordered; an outer join is not, so a later INNER JOIN cancels a LEFT JOIN.

nodes.label: join_collapse_limit
nodes.rationale: Default 8. Past that the planner stops enumerating orders and written join order starts to matter.

nodes.label: Compounding join fan-out
nodes.rationale: Two independent one-to-many branches multiply: 2 tags × 3 comments = 6 rows. Pre-aggregate each child first.

nodes.label: Junction table
nodes.rationale: Composite PK (a_id, b_id) enforces pair uniqueness and indexes the first column. Index the second FK for the reverse lookup.

nodes.label: array_agg FILTER and coalesce
nodes.rationale: FILTER drops the manufactured NULL row; coalesce turns an empty aggregate into {}. They are not interchangeable.

nodes.label: Has-all-tags relational division
nodes.rationale: IN is has-any. Restrict, GROUP BY parent, HAVING count(DISTINCT tag_id) = cardinality($1).

nodes.label: JOIN ON
nodes.rationale: Any boolean condition. The only form that works when FK and PK names differ, the normal customer_id = id case.

nodes.label: JOIN USING
nodes.rationale: Equality on identically named columns, merged into one output column. On FULL OUTER JOIN that column is coalesced.

nodes.label: NATURAL JOIN
nodes.rationale: Infers equality on every same-named column. A shared created_at silently cut two rows to one. Do not write it.

nodes.label: SELECT * join column collapse
nodes.rationale: The server returns both id columns; pg keys objects by name and keeps the last. Six columns became four keys.

nodes.label: RIGHT JOIN
nodes.rationale: RIGHT JOIN is LEFT JOIN with the operands swapped. Prefer LEFT so the preserved table is read first. RIGHT earns its keep only when FROM order is fixed by a generated query, view, or join chain.

nodes.label: FULL OUTER JOIN
nodes.rationale: Keeps unmatched rows from both sides. The only join with no substitute for reconciliation, migration verification, and snapshot diffs. Requires merge- or hash-joinable equality conditions.

nodes.label: Symmetric difference filter
nodes.rationale: WHERE a.pk IS NULL OR b.pk IS NULL after FULL OUTER JOIN returns only unmatched rows from both sides in one pass.

nodes.label: IS DISTINCT FROM for diffs
nodes.rationale: a.col <> b.col is NULL when either side is NULL, so changed rows drop silently. IS DISTINCT FROM treats NULL as a value and keeps them.

nodes.label: FULL JOIN merge/hash restriction
nodes.rationale: A full join must track unmatched rows on both sides. Hash marks hits then sweeps unhit entries; merge sees both sorted streams. Nested loop has no cheap bookkeeping, so PostgreSQL rejects non-equijoin FULL JOIN.

nodes.label: Emulate FULL OUTER with LEFT plus anti-join
nodes.rationale: LEFT JOIN UNION ALL the reverse NOT EXISTS branch. Use UNION ALL because the branches are disjoint; UNION only pays the 3.5× dedup cost. Fallback when the condition is not hash- or merge-joinable.

nodes.label: USING coalesce on FULL JOIN
nodes.rationale: USING merges the join column as coalesce(left.col, right.col), so the key is never NULL for a row present on either side — the one place USING is clearly better than ON.

nodes.label: Self join
nodes.rationale: An ordinary join where both sides are the same table. Aliases are mandatory (42712 without them). One self join walks one hierarchy level.

nodes.label: Adjacency-list hierarchy
nodes.rationale: FK pointing at the same table. Cheapest hierarchy to write (one UPDATE moves a subtree) and most expensive to read. Use LEFT JOIN so a NULL parent id does not drop the root.

nodes.label: WITH RECURSIVE
nodes.rationale: Anchor plus recursive term joined to the previous iteration until none. UNION ALL is almost always correct. A cycle loops forever; CYCLE (PG 14+) or a path array is the defence.

nodes.label: Recursive CTE cycle detection
nodes.rationale: CYCLE id SET is_cycle USING path_arr on PostgreSQL 14+, or WHERE NOT e.id = ANY(c.path_arr). A depth cap plus statement_timeout limits damage but does not detect the cycle.

nodes.label: Recursive term restrictions
nodes.rationale: May reference the CTE once only; may not appear on the right of a LEFT JOIN, in a subquery, or under EXCEPT/INTERSECT; no aggregates or ORDER BY/LIMIT inside the recursive term.

nodes.label: lag over self-join on id-1
nodes.rationale: lag() scans once and defines previous by ORDER BY. A self join on b.id = a.id - 1 breaks as soon as ids have gaps.

nodes.label: Semi and anti joins
nodes.rationale: A semi join answers whether a match exists without emitting the matched row, so it cannot fan out. Its negation, the anti join, has a quietly broken spelling: NOT IN.

nodes.label: UNION
nodes.rationale: Deduplicates via HashAggregate and blocks until both branches are consumed. Measured 491 ms vs 142 ms for UNION ALL over 600000 rows (3.5×).

nodes.label: UNION ALL
nodes.rationale: Streaming Append that can stop under LIMIT. Default when branches are disjoint. Also the joining operator of a recursive CTE.

nodes.label: INTERSECT
nodes.rationale: Whole-row intersection; same customers-with-orders answer as a semi join but compares entire rows and deduplicates. INTERSECT ALL keeps min(count_left, count_right).

nodes.label: EXCEPT
nodes.rationale: Whole-row set difference. Answers which rows differ, not which entities are missing. EXCEPT ALL keeps count_left − count_right.

nodes.label: Set-op column and type rules
nodes.rationale: Column counts must match (42601). Types resolve like CASE. Names come from the first branch only. INTERSECT binds tighter than UNION and EXCEPT.

nodes.label: Join fan-out
nodes.rationale: A joined parent row is repeated once per child. sum(o.total) after joining items returned 450 against a true 350. The join does not corrupt data; it changes grain.

nodes.label: Result grain
nodes.rationale: What one row represents. A join sets grain to the finest side. An aggregate is only correct on columns at that grain. Detect fan-out with count(*) versus count(DISTINCT parent.id).

nodes.label: Pre-aggregate then join
nodes.rationale: Reduce the child to one row per parent before joining so the grain stays one row per parent. LEFT JOIN plus coalesce so parents with no children survive as 0.

nodes.label: count(DISTINCT) after fan-out
nodes.rationale: Rescues counts only. sum(DISTINCT o.total) collapses two orders that happen to share a total. There is no useful sum(DISTINCT) for money.

nodes.label: INNER JOIN matching pairs
nodes.rationale: Output is the set of pairs that satisfy ON. Simultaneously a filter (no match → dropped) and a multiplier (N matches → N copies). JOIN is INNER JOIN; INNER is optional.

nodes.label: Join cardinality from FK
nodes.rationale: Child to parent via a NOT NULL FK yields exactly one row per child. Parent to child yields the children and silently drops unmatched parents. A nullable FK removes the guarantee both ways.

nodes.label: Nested Loop Hash Merge join strategies
nodes.rationale: Equijoin unlocks all three. Non-equality leaves only nested loop. Planner reorders inner joins freely; outer-join order is semantic.

nodes.label: Comma join silent CROSS JOIN
nodes.rationale: FROM a, b WHERE … is an inner join, but omitting the condition is a silent cross join. Explicit JOIN … ON makes the same omission a syntax error.

nodes.label: LEFT JOIN guarantee
nodes.rationale: Every left row appears at least once, not exactly once. Unmatched left rows are emitted with manufactured right-side NULLs. Fan-out still applies.

nodes.label: Manufactured NULLs
nodes.rationale: Join-created NULLs are indistinguishable from stored ones. Test a NOT NULL column, normally the right table's primary key, to detect unmatched rows.

nodes.label: LEFT JOIN count(*) trap
nodes.rationale: count(*) counts the NULL-extended row (5 vs 4). Per group it turns no-orders into 1. Use count(child.pk) and coalesce(sum(...), 0).

nodes.label: LEFT JOIN IS NULL anti-join idiom
nodes.rationale: WHERE right.pk IS NULL keeps unmatched left rows. Correct if the tested column is NOT NULL; still materialises matching pairs. Prefer NOT EXISTS in new code.

nodes.label: ON vs WHERE on outer joins
nodes.rationale: For inner joins interchangeable. For outer joins, a right-table predicate in WHERE silently converts the join back to inner. Measured 2 rows vs 4.

nodes.label: FROM ON then WHERE pipeline
nodes.rationale: FROM (including JOIN … ON) → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY. ON participates in matching; WHERE runs on finished join output. NULL = 'paid' is unknown and WHERE drops it.

nodes.label: Outer-join predicate classification
nodes.rationale: Right-table filters belong in ON; left-table filters belong in WHERE (in ON they do not filter); the join key belongs in ON. A later INNER JOIN or HAVING on the right side also cancels the outer join.

nodes.label: Planner rewrites LEFT to Hash Join
nodes.rationale: EXPLAIN showing Hash Join where the query says LEFT JOIN means a WHERE predicate made NULL-extended rows unreachable. The node name is the diagnosis.

nodes.label: NOT EXISTS anti join
nodes.rationale: Keeps left rows with no match. Plans as Hash Anti Join. Correct with NULLs because a NULL row simply fails to match.

nodes.label: NOT IN NULL trap
nodes.rationale: x NOT IN (a,b,NULL) expands to x <> a AND x <> b AND x <> NULL. The last conjunct is NULL for any x, so WHERE keeps nothing. One NULL customer_id turned Dee into [].

nodes.label: Four anti-join spellings
nodes.rationale: NOT EXISTS (default), LEFT JOIN … WHERE pk IS NULL (older, fragile), EXCEPT (different whole-row semantics), NOT IN (avoid for subqueries).

nodes.label: EXISTS semi join
nodes.rationale: Filters the left side by whether a match exists, short-circuits, emits the left row at most once, exposes no right-hand columns. Must be correlated.

nodes.label: IN as semi join
nodes.rationale: Positive IN and EXISTS both plan as Parallel Hash Semi Join. Prefer EXISTS when correlated, IN or = ANY($1::int[]) for an independent list.

nodes.label: JOIN plus DISTINCT costs 2.5×
nodes.rationale: HashAggregate at 189.98 ms versus Hash Semi Join at 73–91 ms. The join materialises duplicates then hashes them away; a semi join never produces them.

nodes.label: count variants
nodes.rationale: count(*) counts rows, count(col) counts non-NULL, count(DISTINCT col) counts distinct non-NULL. On the fixture 6, 5 and 2 over the same six rows. The wrong one is never a syntax error.

nodes.label: count(DISTINCT) cost
nodes.rationale: Measured 3.6× slower than an equivalent rewrite and cannot go parallel. An index can flip which form is faster.

nodes.label: WITH CTE
nodes.rationale: Binds a name to a subquery for one statement. Since PostgreSQL 12 a qualifying CTE is inlined rather than fenced; MATERIALIZED restores the boundary and cost 6× here.

nodes.label: CTE inlining rule
nodes.rationale: Inlined when referenced once, not MATERIALIZED, not recursive, does not write, and contains no volatile function. Otherwise materialized into a tuplestore. Referenced twice runs once.

nodes.label: FILTER (WHERE)
nodes.rationale: Restricts the rows one aggregate sees without restricting the query. One scan can answer paid/open/cancelled counts. Not pure CASE sugar: they disagree about the empty set.

nodes.label: FILTER vs CASE empty set
nodes.rationale: sum(x) FILTER (…) returns NULL when nothing matches; sum(CASE … ELSE 0) returns 0. The empty-set NULL is inherited from ordinary aggregates.

nodes.label: Window frame
nodes.rationale: A slice of the partition a window aggregate sees. Default is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, which merges peers. Write ROWS when you mean rows.

nodes.label: ROWS vs RANGE vs GROUPS
nodes.rationale: ROWS counts physical rows, GROUPS counts distinct ordering values present, RANGE with an offset counts units on the ordering scale whether present or not.

nodes.label: GROUP BY
nodes.rationale: Splits rows into groups and emits one row per group. Every select-list column must be a grouping key or an aggregate. HashAggregate vs GroupAggregate can flip 59 ms to 118 ms.

nodes.label: Aggregates skip NULL inputs
nodes.rationale: sum/avg/min/max skip NULL rows while count(*) counts them. An all-NULL group returns NULL, not 0. 0 and NULL are deliberately different on cancelled vs unfinished orders.

nodes.label: agg_orders fixture
nodes.rationale: Six orders and five customers for topics 01–08; ex37 then adds a NULL-FK order and a no-country customer so later topics see 8 orders. Same growing-fixture pattern as phase 5.

nodes.label: GROUPING SETS
nodes.rationale: Several grouping levels in one statement. Not parallelised: three sets took 293.67 ms in one scan versus 170.22 ms as three parallel GROUP BYs.

nodes.label: ROLLUP and CUBE
nodes.rationale: ROLLUP (a,b) expands to ((a,b),(a),()) — n+1 sets. CUBE expands to every subset — 2^n. () is the grand total.

nodes.label: GROUPING()
nodes.rationale: Subtotal rows mark rolled-up columns with NULL, indistinguishable from a data NULL. GROUPING(col) returns 1 for the former and 0 for the latter.

nodes.label: HAVING
nodes.rationale: Filters groups after aggregation. WHERE filters rows into groups. When the same predicate is legal in both, prefer WHERE; the planner can move some HAVING predicates and not others.

nodes.label: HAVING vs WHERE one-line test
nodes.rationale: If a single row can decide the predicate, it belongs in WHERE; if it needs the whole group, it belongs in HAVING. HAVING count(*) > 0 after a LEFT JOIN matches everything.

nodes.label: json_agg and jsonb_agg
nodes.rationale: Nest children into a parent row for a one-query API payload. Do not skip NULL inputs, so LEFT JOIN NULLs become [null] instead of [].

nodes.label: array_agg and string_agg
nodes.rationale: string_agg skips NULL inputs; array_agg keeps them as elements. That inconsistency is the source of most surprises in this family.

nodes.label: Empty-array [null] trap
nodes.rationale: A parent with no children yields NULL or [null], not []. FILTER alone is not the fix; the two-level payload needs coalesce around an inner aggregate that already excluded the NULL row.

nodes.label: lag and lead
nodes.rationale: Return expr from a row offset rows before or after this one. Ignore the frame entirely. First row of each partition is NULL unless a default is supplied.

nodes.label: last_value default-frame trap
nodes.rationale: first_value, last_value and nth_value index the frame. The default frame ends at CURRENT ROW, so last_value famously returns the current row unless the frame is written out to UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING.

nodes.label: Data-modifying CTE
nodes.rationale: A CTE can INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/MERGE. WITH moved AS (DELETE … RETURNING *) INSERT INTO archive SELECT * FROM moved archives in one atomic statement. Always a fence.

nodes.label: Write-CTE snapshot rule
nodes.rationale: A write CTE always runs, referenced or not. Its effect is visible only through its own RETURNING; a sibling SELECT sees the pre-statement snapshot. Two writes touching the same row can lose one silently.

nodes.label: Ordered-set aggregates
nodes.rationale: Need input in order first, via WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY …). Percentiles are the usual meeting point. Cost 3.1× an avg() because sorting is unavoidable.

nodes.label: percentile_cont and percentile_disc
nodes.rationale: cont interpolates at fraction f; disc returns the first actual value at or past f. Several percentiles can share one sort.

nodes.label: mode and bool_and empty-set surprises
nodes.rationale: mode() hides ties by the WITHIN GROUP ordering. bool_and returns NULL for all-of-nothing, the same empty-set NULL rule as other aggregates.

nodes.label: Exact pagination count
nodes.rationale: Twenty rows cost 2.11 ms; exact total: 125000 cost 48.83 ms. count(*) OVER () cost 152.77 ms because the window must see every row and defeats LIMIT.

nodes.label: limit + 1 Next button
nodes.rationale: Fetch page_size + 1. A leftover row means there is a next page. Exact, nearly free, and usually what a list endpoint is actually asked.

nodes.label: Planner estimate and capped count
nodes.rationale: Planner estimate is free at ~0.7% error here with no guarantee. A capped count saved 23× when matches are plentiful and nothing when they are not.

nodes.label: row_number()
nodes.rationale: Always unique within the partition; ties still get consecutive numbers in ORDER BY order.

nodes.label: rank()
nodes.rationale: Tied peers share a rank; the next rank skips so the sequence has gaps.

nodes.label: dense_rank()
nodes.rationale: Tied peers share a rank; the next rank does not skip.

nodes.label: ntile()
nodes.rationale: Splits the partition into N buckets as evenly as possible; remainder buckets get one extra row.

nodes.label: Ranking ties
nodes.rationale: rank and dense_rank treat equal ORDER BY values as peers; row_number never ties.

nodes.label: WITH RECURSIVE
nodes.rationale: Anchor term seeds the working table; the recursive term is evaluated until it returns no rows.

nodes.label: CYCLE clause
nodes.rationale: Detects cycles so a graph walk cannot loop forever.

nodes.label: SEARCH clause
nodes.rationale: Declares breadth-first or depth-first walk order without hand-rolled path bookkeeping.

nodes.label: Scalar subquery
nodes.rationale: Must return at most one row and one column; more than one row is an error.

nodes.label: Correlated subquery
nodes.rationale: Refers to the outer row and is conceptually re-evaluated per outer row.

nodes.label: NOT IN vs NOT EXISTS
nodes.rationale: NOT IN is UNKNOWN when the set contains NULL, so the anti-join silently returns no rows; NOT EXISTS does not have that trap.

nodes.label: OVER without collapse
nodes.rationale: A window function computes over a partition but keeps every input row; GROUP BY collapses.

nodes.label: ERROR 42P20
nodes.rationale: Window functions are illegal in WHERE; they run after grouping.

nodes.label: WindowAgg
nodes.rationale: The plan node that evaluates OVER; it is not free even when the function looks cheap.

nodes.label: LEFT JOIN count(*) trap
nodes.rationale: count(*) after a one-to-many LEFT JOIN counts joined rows, not left-side parents.

nodes.label: Join fan-out
nodes.rationale: Each matching child duplicates the parent; aggregates on the parent then inflate.

nodes.label: LATERAL pre-aggregation
nodes.rationale: Aggregate the many-side first, then join one row back, so the parent is never duplicated.

nodes.label: sum(DISTINCT) is not a fix
nodes.rationale: Distinct values can still collide across parents; it hides the fan-out instead of removing it.

nodes.label: count(*)
nodes.rationale: Counts rows, including rows whose columns are NULL.

nodes.label: count(column)
nodes.rationale: Skips NULL in that column; not a faster count(*).

nodes.label: count(DISTINCT)
nodes.rationale: Counts unique non-NULL values; a different question, not a faster count.

nodes.label: count(1) folklore
nodes.rationale: count(1) is not cheaper than count(*); both count rows.

nodes.label: count(DISTINCT) is not parallel
nodes.rationale: The distinct aggregate cannot be parallelized the way a plain count can.

nodes.label: DISTINCT subquery rewrite
nodes.rationale: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT DISTINCT col …) can unlock a cheaper plan than count(DISTINCT col).

nodes.label: Index-only scan flip
nodes.rationale: A covering index can turn a heap scan count into an index-only scan.

nodes.label: CTE as named subquery
nodes.rationale: WITH names a query so the outer statement can read it like a table.

nodes.label: No forward references
nodes.rationale: A CTE cannot refer to a later sibling unless the WITH is RECURSIVE.

nodes.label: CTE name shadowing
nodes.rationale: A CTE name hides a same-named table in that statement.

nodes.label: WITH on DML
nodes.rationale: WITH can wrap INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE and RETURNING, not only SELECT.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL 12+ CTE inlining
nodes.rationale: A CTE is inlined unless it is referenced more than once, marked MATERIALIZED, recursive, volatile, or a data-modifying statement.

nodes.label: MATERIALIZED fence
nodes.rationale: MATERIALIZED forces the CTE to be computed once and stored; measured about 6.1× the inlined cost when that fence is unnecessary.

nodes.label: Two references compute once
nodes.rationale: Two reads of the same CTE compute the body once and reuse the result.

nodes.label: NOT MATERIALIZED
nodes.rationale: Forces inlining even with multiple references, which can double the work; ignored for volatile CTEs.

nodes.label: OFFSET 0 optimization fence
nodes.rationale: OFFSET 0 is an older fence that blocks pull-up when MATERIALIZED is not available.

nodes.label: FILTER clause
nodes.rationale: Restricts which rows enter one aggregate without a second scan or a CASE wrapper.

nodes.label: FILTER vs CASE
nodes.rationale: FILTER and CASE express the same pivot; FILTER is clearer and does not invent zeros the way COALESCE(sum(CASE…),0) can.

nodes.label: Empty sum is NULL
nodes.rationale: sum FILTER that matches no rows is NULL, not 0; wrap with COALESCE when a pivot needs zeros.

nodes.label: FILTER equals CASE speed
nodes.rationale: FILTER is not faster than the equivalent CASE aggregate; both are one scan.

nodes.label: FILTER vs N subqueries
nodes.rationale: One scan with several FILTER aggregates is about 4× cheaper than N correlated subqueries.

nodes.label: FILTER is not a scan filter
nodes.rationale: FILTER does not reduce the scan; WHERE does. FILTER only chooses which already-read rows enter the aggregate.

nodes.label: Default RANGE peer frame
nodes.rationale: The default frame is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, so peers share the current row's frame.

nodes.label: ROWS vs RANGE
nodes.rationale: ROWS counts physical offsets; RANGE groups by ORDER BY value so ties expand the frame.

nodes.label: Ranking ignores the frame
nodes.rationale: row_number, rank, dense_rank, and ntile use the partition and ORDER BY, not the frame clause.

nodes.label: RANGE offset calendar windows
nodes.rationale: RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '7 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW is a value window, not a row count.

nodes.label: GROUPS frame
nodes.rationale: GROUPS counts peer groups, not rows and not ORDER BY values.

nodes.label: EXCLUDE CURRENT ROW GROUP TIES
nodes.rationale: EXCLUDE CURRENT ROW, GROUP, or TIES drops the current row and/or its peers from the frame.

nodes.label: GROUP BY collapse
nodes.rationale: GROUP BY reduces the input to one row per key; selected expressions must be keys or aggregates.

nodes.label: Aggregates skip NULL
nodes.rationale: Most aggregates skip NULL; count(*) is the exception that still counts the row.

nodes.label: avg is sum over count
nodes.rationale: avg(x) is sum(x)/count(x), so NULLs in x do not enter either side.

nodes.label: bigint numeric as JS strings
nodes.rationale: node-postgres returns bigint and numeric as strings so they are not rounded in JS Number.

nodes.label: No GROUP BY is one row
nodes.rationale: An aggregate query with no GROUP BY always returns exactly one row, even on an empty table.

nodes.label: sum of empty set is NULL
nodes.rationale: sum over no rows is NULL, not 0.

nodes.label: NULL keys group together
nodes.rationale: GROUP BY treats all NULLs as one key even though NULL = NULL is unknown.

nodes.label: ERROR 42803
nodes.rationale: A selected column that is neither grouped nor aggregated raises 42803.

nodes.label: Functional dependency on PK
nodes.rationale: Grouping by a primary key lets other columns of that table be selected without aggregating.

nodes.label: DISTINCT ON
nodes.rationale: DISTINCT ON keeps one row per key using ORDER BY, without requiring the rest of the SELECT to be aggregated.

nodes.label: GROUP BY evaluation order
nodes.rationale: GROUP BY ordinals refer to SELECT-list positions; aliases are visible there after the SELECT is parsed.

nodes.label: GROUP BY equals DISTINCT
nodes.rationale: GROUP BY on every selected column is the same uniqueness as SELECT DISTINCT.

nodes.label: GROUP BY does not order
nodes.rationale: HashAggregate returns groups in hash order; only ORDER BY is a contract.

nodes.label: HashAggregate
nodes.rationale: Builds a hash table of groups in work_mem; preferred when no ordered input is required.

nodes.label: GroupAggregate
nodes.rationale: Aggregates already-sorted input; used when an index or Sort already matches the grouping keys.

nodes.label: work_mem Batches spill
nodes.rationale: When the hash table exceeds work_mem, HashAggregate spills Batches to disk.

nodes.label: Partial and Finalize Aggregate
nodes.rationale: Parallel plans compute Partial aggregates per worker and Finalize them in the leader.

nodes.label: GROUPING SETS
nodes.rationale: One scan produces several GROUP BY combinations listed explicitly.

nodes.label: ROLLUP
nodes.rationale: Hierarchical subtotals from the full key list down to the grand total.

nodes.label: CUBE
nodes.rationale: Every subset of the key list — 2^n grouping sets.

nodes.label: MixedAggregate is not parallel
nodes.rationale: Grouping-sets plans use MixedAggregate and do not parallelize the way a single HashAggregate can.

nodes.label: GROUPING()
nodes.rationale: GROUPING(col) is 1 when that column is aggregated away, so a super-aggregate NULL is not confused with a data NULL.

nodes.label: WHERE vs HAVING
nodes.rationale: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregates exist.

nodes.label: HAVING without GROUP BY
nodes.rationale: HAVING on a no-GROUP-BY aggregate can drop the single result row and return zero rows.

nodes.label: HAVING on grouping columns rewritten to WHERE
nodes.rationale: A HAVING that references only grouping columns is constant per group, so the planner drops the extra grouping key and evaluates the predicate as a scan Filter. Measured plans were identical (55.08 ms vs 57.21 ms). The rewrite needs a non-volatile predicate.

nodes.label: HAVING on an aggregate
nodes.rationale: Filter sits on Finalize HashAggregate because the value does not exist until every group row is read. Selectivity cannot reduce work: HAVING count(*) > 100 keeping 0 of 5000 groups was not cheaper than keeping all. Tune the input, not the HAVING.

nodes.label: HAVING count > 0 rewritten as EXISTS
nodes.rationale: count(...) > 0 forces a full count of every group. EXISTS stops at the first match and can use an index. Does not apply when the threshold is a real count (> 5).

nodes.label: Window functions forbidden in HAVING
nodes.rationale: 42P20: windows run after HAVING so the value does not exist yet. Compute the window in a subquery and filter outside. rank() OVER (ORDER BY count(*) DESC) is legal because windows run after grouping.

nodes.label: string_agg
nodes.rationale: Drops NULLs and emits no delimiter for them. Empty group is NULL not ''. text-only: 42883 on integer without ::text. coalesce(string_agg(...), '') before concatenation.

nodes.label: array_agg
nodes.rationale: Keeps NULLs as elements — opposite of string_agg. FILTER (WHERE x IS NOT NULL) preferred over array_remove; if every value is NULL, FILTER yields NULL and array_remove yields {}.

nodes.label: ORDER BY inside collection aggregates
nodes.rationale: The query's outer ORDER BY orders result rows, not aggregate input. Put ORDER BY inside the parentheses of every collection whose order a consumer can see.

nodes.label: Unordered aggregate inherits sibling ORDER BY
nodes.rationale: When one aggregate has an internal ORDER BY, the executor may sort the shared input once. An unordered sibling silently inherits that order — output can change when an unrelated column is added.

nodes.label: DISTINCT aggregate ORDER BY 42P10
nodes.rationale: array_agg(DISTINCT a ORDER BY b) is rejected: after de-duplicating by a there is no single b. ORDER BY must use the DISTINCT expressions.

nodes.label: jsonb_build_object
nodes.rationale: Alternating key, value. The API contract is written in the query so adding a table column cannot change the response shape.

nodes.label: to_jsonb of a row
nodes.rationale: Emits every column named by column name. Never point it at a table whose columns you do not control — later migrations leak into the API. Safe form: to_jsonb over a subquery that names columns.

nodes.label: jsonb_object_agg
nodes.rationale: NULL key raises 22023 field name must not be null. Duplicate keys silently keep the last value. Aggregate over a pre-grouped subquery.

nodes.label: json versus jsonb
nodes.rationale: json stores source text (duplicates, whitespace, key order). jsonb parses to binary, collapses duplicates, reorders keys. Difference is invisible from Node because JSON.parse also collapses duplicates. jsonb is 2.6× larger here (60 vs 23 bytes) but indexable with GIN.

nodes.label: jsonb_agg
nodes.rationale: Arrives as a real JavaScript array; pg already JSON.parsed it. JSON.parse on the result throws. Same internal ORDER BY rule as array_agg.

nodes.label: The empty-array trap
nodes.rationale: Naked array_agg/jsonb_agg over LEFT JOIN yields [null] because the invented NULL child is a real group member. FILTER removes it and then the empty group is NULL. Both FILTER and coalesce(..., '[]'::jsonb) are required to reach []. '{}'' is an empty JSON object, not an array.

nodes.label: Canonical child-collection expression
nodes.rationale: coalesce(jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object(...) ORDER BY ...) FILTER (WHERE child.id IS NOT NULL), '[]'::jsonb). Four parts: name fields, stable order, drop [null], empty group to [].

nodes.label: Two-level LATERAL JSON payload
nodes.rationale: LEFT JOIN LATERAL … ON true so the inner query can see c.id and childless parents stay. Inner GROUP BY o.id stops fan-out compounding. Measured 292 shaped bytes vs 580 flat.

nodes.label: last_value default frame trap
nodes.rationale: ORDER BY implies RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, so last_value is the current row. first_value looks correct by accident because the frame starts at UNBOUNDED PRECEDING. Fix: full ROWS frame, or first_value over reversed ORDER BY.

nodes.label: first_value
nodes.rationale: Frame-relative start of the window. Default frame makes it the partition first row. first_value OVER (ORDER BY x DESC) is the preferred last-value spelling — no frame reasoning.

nodes.label: nth_value
nodes.rationale: 1-based, frame-relative. With the default frame, nth_value(x, 2) is NULL on the first row of each partition. No negative form — reverse the ordering. Named windows cannot override ORDER BY.

nodes.label: lag
nodes.rationale: Value n rows back (default 1), optional default when the offset falls outside the partition. Frame-independent. Never crosses PARTITION BY. ORDER BY is optional in syntax and always a bug without it. Non-constant offset is accepted and can yield an all-NULL column.

nodes.label: lead
nodes.rationale: Value n rows forward. Same offset/default/partition/ORDER BY rules as lag. First row has no predecessor and last has no successor — both NULL unless a default is supplied.

nodes.label: generate_series date spine for lag
nodes.rationale: lag counts rows, not days. Missing days make day-over-day skip the gap silently. Generate a dense spine and LEFT JOIN; use count(o.id) not count(*) or empty days report 1.

nodes.label: Data-modifying CTE
nodes.rationale: INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/MERGE inside WITH, chained by RETURNING. One statement is already atomic — no BEGIN needed. Always MATERIALIZED; NOT MATERIALIZED cannot inline a write.

nodes.label: Archive with DELETE RETURNING then INSERT
nodes.rationale: WITH moved AS (DELETE … RETURNING *) INSERT INTO archive SELECT * FROM moved. No window where the row is in neither table or both. Measured: 6 orders → 5, 1 archived.

nodes.label: Unreferenced write CTE still runs
nodes.rationale: A SELECT CTE nobody references can be discarded; a write is a promised side effect and executes once regardless. Deleting the reference but not the CTE leaves a write running.

nodes.label: The snapshot rule
nodes.rationale: Every part of one statement shares one snapshot taken before it began. Sibling SELECT on the table cannot see a CTE write (visible_to_sibling: 0, visible_via_returning: 1). CTE execution order is unspecified; one snapshot makes the result deterministic.

nodes.label: Two write CTEs on the same row
nodes.rationale: One update is silently lost — a: 1, b: 0, no error. SERIALIZABLE does not help: there is only one transaction. Merge into one UPDATE, make sets disjoint, or use separate statements.

nodes.label: mode()
nodes.rationale: On a tie, returns the first value in the WITHIN GROUP sort order with no indication of the tie. Four kinds tied at 125000; reversing ORDER BY changed click to view. Ignores NULLs; empty input is NULL.

nodes.label: bool_and / every()
nodes.rationale: every() is a standard-SQL alias. Empty set is NULL not true — vacuous truth is not what SQL returns. coalesce(bool_and(...), true) or a customer with no orders is reported unpaid because NULL is falsy.

nodes.label: Hypothetical-set aggregates
nodes.rationale: rank/dense_rank/percent_rank/cume_dist WITHIN GROUP rank a value that is not in the set. Arguments must match ORDER BY columns. Inverse of percentile_cont: value→fraction vs fraction→value. rank(150) measured 66721 / 0.1334.

nodes.label: percentile_cont
nodes.rationale: Interpolates; can return a value not in the data (2.5 from 1,2,3,4). numeric/interval only. Must sort: 178.32 ms vs 57.41 ms for avg on 500k (3.1×). Percentiles do not compose — cannot average hourly p95s.

nodes.label: percentile_disc
nodes.rationale: Returns an actual value from the set. Works on any sortable type. percentile_disc(0.0) is min, percentile_disc(1.0) is max. NULLs ignored like every aggregate.

nodes.label: WITHIN GROUP ordered-set syntax
nodes.rationale: Fraction is the argument; the column lives in WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY ...), separate from the query's ORDER BY. percentile_cont(ARRAY[0.5, 0.9, 0.99]) sorts once and returns an array.

nodes.label: Planner Plan Rows estimate
nodes.rationale: EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON) Plan Rows: 125833 vs actual 125000 (0.7% high), zero row reads. Error is unbounded for correlated columns or stale stats. Label it approximate.

nodes.label: Exact count capped at a ceiling
nodes.rationale: count(*) FROM (SELECT 1 … LIMIT 1000). Pays only when matches are plentiful (1.46 vs 33.85 ms at 125000). With 120 matches: 3.01 vs 3.02 ms — no saving, the scan still looks everywhere.

nodes.label: pg_class.reltuples
nodes.rationale: Approximate whole-table row count maintained by VACUUM/ANALYZE. Order of magnitude only; stale between maintenance.

nodes.label: LIMIT pageSize + 1 has-more
nodes.rationale: 2.10 ms vs 2.11 ms for the plain page — free and exact. Slice the extra row before responding or the last page returns 21 items. Compose with keyset, not OFFSET.

nodes.label: count(*) OVER () plus page
nodes.rationale: WindowAgg must see every matching row before emitting the first, so LIMIT cannot stop early. 152.77 ms vs 48.83 ms for a separate count(*); plan showed WindowAgg actual rows=125000 feeding Limit 20.

nodes.label: Exact count(*) for pagination total
nodes.rationale: 48.83 ms against 2.11 ms for the page (~23×). Scales with matching rows while the page stays bounded by LIMIT. Count once when the filter changes, not on every page.

nodes.label: row_number
nodes.rationale: Consecutive integers; ties broken arbitrarily. Non-unique ORDER BY is non-deterministic — WHERE rn = 1 can pick a different row after a plan flip. Always add a unique tiebreaker. Ranking functions ignore the frame.

nodes.label: rank
nodes.rationale: Ties share; next value skips (1, 1, 3). max(rank) equals the row count, not the number of distinct values. Sporting convention: two golds, no silver.

nodes.label: dense_rank
nodes.rationale: Ties share; no gap (1, 1, 2). Use when you want the count of distinct levels rather than sporting position.

nodes.label: percent_rank and cume_dist
nodes.rationale: percent_rank is (rank-1)/(rows-1), 0 to 1. cume_dist is the proportion at or before this row, starts above 0, ends at 1.

nodes.label: ntile
nodes.rationale: Remainder goes to earliest buckets (7 into 3 → 3,2,2). Splits ties across boundaries with no peer notion — unsuitable for grading. Use percentile_cont thresholds instead.

nodes.label: WindowAgg Run Condition
nodes.rationale: PostgreSQL 15+ pushes WHERE rn <= N into WindowAgg so each partition stops after N rows. Applies to monotonic windows (row_number, rank, dense_rank, count). The Sort still processes all input rows.

nodes.label: DISTINCT ON top-1
nodes.rationale: Shortest PostgreSQL-only spelling of top-1 per key; one whole consistent row. Cannot do N > 1.

nodes.label: LATERAL LIMIT per group
nodes.rationale: Wins when groups are few and indexed; loses when groups approach a fraction of rows. 5000 groups / 500k rows: timeout without index, 906 ms with index vs 435 ms for row_number. Only form that takes OFFSET per group.

nodes.label: Non-covering window index backfire
nodes.rationale: Index (user_id, amount DESC) became Index Scan not Index Only Scan because id was not included — 500574 buffers vs 3783, 534 vs 435 ms. INCLUDE selected columns, or accept the sequential scan plus disk sort.

nodes.label: CYCLE clause
nodes.rationale: PG 14+. CYCLE id SET is_cycle USING path flags the row where the loop closed and stops. Only option that reports the cycle. A self-referencing FK does not prevent cycles.

nodes.label: SEARCH DEPTH/BREADTH FIRST
nodes.rationale: Creates a sortable ord column; you must still ORDER BY ord. DEPTH FIRST follows each branch to its end — what a rendered tree needs.

nodes.label: Recursive depth guard
nodes.rationale: WHERE t.d < N bounds work unconditionally. Cannot tell a legitimately deep tree from a loop. Measured: 8-row table produced 107 rows before d < 40 stopped it. UNION instead of UNION ALL dedups but fails if rows carry a depth/path column.

nodes.label: WITH RECURSIVE
nodes.rationale: Anchor UNION ALL recursive term joining the table to the CTE. Missing RECURSIVE is 42P01 (ordinary missing-table). Carry depth and path in the term. Reverse the join to climb. Index the join column or cost is depth × full scan.

nodes.label: WorkTable Scan / Recursive Union
nodes.rationale: Each round reads only the previous iteration's rows, not everything found so far. loops= on the recursive term is iteration count (depth). Aggregates are forbidden in the recursive term (42P19) because they would summarise a fragment.

nodes.label: Correlated subquery
nodes.rationale: References an outer column so it cannot be computed once — N+1 inside one statement. count() over empty is 0; sum/avg/min/max are NULL. Fine for a detail endpoint; rewrite as GROUP BY + LEFT JOIN for a list.

nodes.label: SubPlan loops= signature
nodes.rationale: SubPlan with high loops and Index Searches matching the outer row count is per-row work. Measured 5000 probes. If the planner already un-correlated it there is no SubPlan.

nodes.label: Correlated cost depends on visibility map
nodes.rationale: Best case after VACUUM: 145 vs 65 ms GROUP BY (2.2×). After touching 1 row in 500, Heap Fetches 0→133359 and 414 vs 90 ms (4.6×). GROUP BY barely moved because it reads the heap once.

nodes.label: NOT IN NULL trap
nodes.rationale: x NOT IN (a, NULL) is x <> a AND x <> NULL. The last comparison is unknown, so every row fails. Measured: 1 row became 0 after one NULL elsewhere. NOT EXISTS is null-safe.

nodes.label: EXISTS / NOT EXISTS
nodes.rationale: Positive IN / = ANY / EXISTS all plan as a semi join and agreed at 4. Target list inside EXISTS is never evaluated — SELECT 1 is convention. Prefer EXISTS for nullable columns and all negations.

nodes.label: = ANY($1::int[]) list parameter
nodes.rationale: One parameter regardless of list length; empty array matches nothing. Empty IN () is a syntax error. Stable statement text avoids re-planning per list size.

nodes.label: Scalar subquery
nodes.rationale: Must return one row and one column. Uncorrelated form is evaluated once for the statement. Zero rows is NULL, not an error. Derived tables in FROM need an alias and cannot see siblings without LATERAL.

nodes.label: 21000 more than one row from scalar subquery
nodes.rationale: Enforced at runtime, not plan time. LIMIT 1 without ORDER BY converts a loud error into a silently arbitrary answer. Prefer an aggregate or a unique-key constraint.

nodes.label: Row constructor comparison
nodes.rationale: (a, b) > (1, 5) is lexicographic: a > 1 OR (a = 1 AND b > 5), not AND of both. Correct spelling for keyset pagination. NULL in any component yields unknown.

nodes.label: PARTITION BY does not collapse rows
nodes.rationale: Same sums as GROUP BY, different row count: one row per group vs every input row with the group's value attached. Measured 3 grouped rows vs 5 windowed.

nodes.label: OVER () whole-result partition
nodes.rationale: Every row is one partition — the canonical way to attach a grand total or percentage without a self-join. Use 100.0 * not 100 * or integer division floors to zero. FILTER goes before OVER.

nodes.label: ORDER BY inside OVER running total
nodes.rationale: Implies RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. Inner ORDER BY changes values; outer ORDER BY only presentation. RANGE includes peers so equal keys share a running total.

nodes.label: Window sort dominates cost
nodes.rationale: One window over 500k: 530 ms, 8560 kB disk sort. Plain count(*) is 26.73 ms. Matching btree (PARTITION BY then ORDER BY) dropped it to 283 ms index-only scan, 575 buffers, no temp I/O.

nodes.label: Compatible windows share one sort
nodes.rationale: Same partition: one Sort, 999 ms. Different partitions: two Sorts, 1518 ms, 3.4× temp I/O. Second WindowAgg is not free even sharing a sort (~470 ms). Align PARTITION BY or split queries.

nodes.label: WindowAgg is not parallel-aware
nodes.rationale: No Gather in the plan. Extra cores do not help. Two 530 ms queries overlapped from the app beat one 1518 ms serial dual-window query.

nodes.label: Window evaluation pipeline
nodes.rationale: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → windows → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT. Filter on a window needs another query level. DISTINCT after windows means row_number prevents de-duplication.

nodes.label: 42P20 window functions not allowed in WHERE/HAVING
nodes.rationale: WHERE deciding which rows exist while the window depends on those rows would be circular. Fix: subquery or CTE, then filter. Planner flattens it and can push rn <= N as Run Condition.

nodes.label: Window over an aggregate
nodes.rationale: sum(count(*)) OVER () is legal: GROUP BY produces per-group counts, then the window sums those group rows. Standard percentage-of-total without a self-join.

nodes.label: Named WINDOW clause
nodes.rationale: Naming convenience between HAVING and ORDER BY; planner already merges identical definitions. Can extend with ORDER BY/frame if the named window has none; cannot override existing ORDER BY or change PARTITION BY.

nodes.label: Module-scope pg.Pool
nodes.rationale: Create one Pool at module scope and share it. Construction opens nothing; the first query opens the first connection.

nodes.label: Lazy pool connection
nodes.rationale: new Pool() performs no I/O. A bad host surfaces as ECONNREFUSED on the first query, so boot with SELECT 1.

nodes.label: pool.on('error') is mandatory
nodes.rationale: An idle connection killed by the server emits 'error' on the pool. Unhandled, that is an uncaught exception that kills the process.

nodes.label: application_name
nodes.rationale: Shows up in pg_stat_activity so every connection is attributable to a service.

nodes.label: One pool per process
nodes.rationale: Two pools of max 10 are 20 connections against a shared max_connections of 100. Exceptions: replica pool, dedicated LISTEN Client, short-lived script pool.

nodes.label: Pool vs Client
nodes.rationale: Use Pool almost always. pool.query borrows, runs, and returns; two calls may land on different connections.

nodes.label: Session state needs a checked-out client
nodes.rationale: Transactions, SET, cursors, advisory locks and named prepared statements cannot use pool.query because session state lives on one connection.

nodes.label: LISTEN needs a bare Client
nodes.rationale: The only common case for new pg.Client(): a long-lived listener with a bound handler. Pooling buys nothing and would hand the connection away.

nodes.label: Three connection config sources
nodes.rationale: URL, config object, or libpq env vars (PGHOST, PGPORT, PGUSER, PGPASSWORD, PGDATABASE). They do not merge as expected.

nodes.label: connectionString overwrites object fields
nodes.rationale: A URL plus database: 'postgres' still connects to the URL database, with no warning. Mix only pool-level options (max, timeouts, ssl object).

nodes.label: sslmode=require is changing
nodes.rationale: pg 8.x treats require as verify-full (stricter than libpq). pg 9.0 will adopt libpq semantics and silently stop verifying. Write sslmode=verify-full now.

nodes.label: Pool options string for server settings
nodes.rationale: options: '-c search_path=app,public -c statement_timeout=5000' applies on every new connection. A SET via pool.query lands on one arbitrary connection.

nodes.label: password as a function
nodes.rationale: Evaluated when a connection opens, not per query. Pair with idleTimeoutMillis shorter than an IAM token TTL.

nodes.label: Prefer 127.0.0.1 over localhost
nodes.rationale: localhost can resolve to ::1 first; a container published only on IPv4 refuses it. Node 24 autoSelectFamily hides this; the literal address does not depend on it.

nodes.label: $n placeholders
nodes.rationale: Positional and 1-based. A placeholder may repeat. More values than $n references are silently ignored.

nodes.label: ANY($1::int[]) for lists
nodes.rationale: One parameter regardless of list length, so statement text and the plan stay constant and you avoid the 65535-parameter ceiling.

nodes.label: Identifiers cannot be parameters
nodes.rationale: ORDER BY $1 sorts by a constant string and raises no error. Column names need an allowlist.

nodes.label: undefined becomes SQL NULL
nodes.rationale: A misspelled property inserts NULL instead of failing. Validate the object before building the values array.

nodes.label: Branch on err.code SQLSTATE
nodes.rationale: Never branch on err.message. Messages are localised and version-dependent. SQLSTATEs are a stable five-character contract.

nodes.label: err.detail leaks data
nodes.rationale: detail contains the submitted value and enables user enumeration. Log it; never serialise the raw error to a client.

nodes.label: Retry 40001 and 40P01
nodes.rationale: Serialization failure and deadlock are isolation machinery, not bugs. Retry the whole transaction with backoff and jitter.

nodes.label: FATAL errors arrive as events
nodes.rationale: When the server terminates a connection with no in-flight query, pg emits 'error' instead of rejecting a promise.

nodes.label: pg Result object
nodes.rationale: Public fields: rows, rowCount, command, fields. oid is legacy. Underscored fields are internal.

nodes.label: rowCount vs rows.length
nodes.rationale: rowCount is rows affected; rows.length is rows sent back. UPDATE without RETURNING is 1 and []. DDL rowCount is null, not 0.

nodes.label: SELECT * join column collapse
nodes.rationale: Duplicate column names collapse in the row object with no error. fields still lists all four; the last name wins. Alias or use rowMode array.

nodes.label: rowMode: 'array'
nodes.rationale: Rows as positional arrays. Preserves duplicate names and skips object allocation on large results.

nodes.label: pool.connect checkout
nodes.rationale: Takes a connection out of the pool until release(). A fourth request against max 3 queues; leaks present as latency, not exceptions.

nodes.label: client.release()
nodes.rationale: Returns the connection for reuse. Does not close it or roll anything back. Always call it in finally.

nodes.label: release(true) destroys the connection
nodes.rationale: Use after FATAL, client-side query_timeout, or unknown session state. Cheaper than poisoning later borrowers.

nodes.label: withTransaction helper
nodes.rationale: BEGIN/COMMIT on one checked-out client; wrap ROLLBACK so a dead connection does not mask the original error; release in finally.

nodes.label: DISCARD ALL before release
nodes.rationale: release() does not reset the session. SET search_path, temp tables and open transactions persist. DISCARD ALL cannot run inside a transaction.

nodes.label: Pool totalCount idleCount waitingCount
nodes.rationale: Sustained waitingCount > 0 means undersized pool, slow queries, or a leak. A leak also pins idleCount at 0 with totalCount at max.

nodes.label: Default pg type mapping
nodes.rationale: PostgreSQL sends text; pg converts by column OID. json arrives parsed, arrays as arrays, bytea as Buffer, NULL as null.

nodes.label: bigint and numeric arrive as strings
nodes.rationale: A JS number is exact only to 2^53-1. Number(9007199254740993) becomes 9007199254740992. numeric is for money where float rounding is unacceptable.

nodes.label: date and timestamp read in Node TZ
nodes.rationale: date becomes Date at local midnight (2026-08-12 → 2026-08-11T18:30Z under UTC+5:30). timestamp assumes local time. Only timestamptz is a real instant.

nodes.label: PostgresInterval object
nodes.rationale: Months and days are not fixed durations, so there is no correct millisecond conversion. Use extract(epoch FROM …) for a number.

nodes.label: Type OIDs as parser keys
nodes.rationale: fields[i].dataTypeID selects the parser. Array OIDs are distinct (1700 numeric vs 1231 numeric[]). Custom types get per-database OIDs.

nodes.label: pg.types.setTypeParser
nodes.rationale: A single process-wide registry including third-party pg users. Register once before opening a pool. Never called for NULL.

nodes.label: pg TypeOverrides
nodes.rationale: Scopes a parser change to one query or one pool. The safe form when a single report needs numbers.

nodes.label: Override date (1082) to string
nodes.rationale: A date is a calendar label. Converting it to Date at local midnight produces off-by-one days. The almost-always-right global override.

nodes.label: Do not parse numeric to Number
nodes.rationale: numeric exists because floats cannot represent decimal fractions. Keep the string or store integer minor units.

nodes.label: Named prepared statements
nodes.rationale: Adding name issues server-side PREPARE. Measured 1.6× on 2000 trivial lookups (772 ms unnamed vs 481 ms named).

nodes.label: Generic vs custom plan
nodes.rationale: Custom plans for the first five executions; from the sixth PostgreSQL may switch to a generic plan. Skewed data then gets the wrong plan. force_custom_plan restores per-value planning.

nodes.label: Prepared statements are per session
nodes.rationale: A statement prepared on pid 1932 is invisible to pid 1933. A pool of N prepares up to N times. Dynamic names leak server memory.

nodes.label: PgBouncer breaks named statements
nodes.rationale: Transaction/statement pooling routes consecutive queries to different backends → 26000 prepared statement does not exist. Use session pooling or disable names.

nodes.label: statement_timeout
nodes.rationale: Server-side cancel; SQLSTATE 57014; connection stays usable. The only timeout that actually stops the database doing work.

nodes.label: query_timeout
nodes.rationale: Client-side give-up; the server keeps executing. Users retry and the server accumulates work nobody is waiting for. Set slightly above statement_timeout.

nodes.label: idle_in_transaction_session_timeout
nodes.rationale: Kills a session that issued BEGIN then waited. Pins xmin and blocks VACUUM. Delivered as an 'error' event, not a rejected query.

nodes.label: lock_timeout
nodes.rationale: Give up rather than queue behind ACCESS EXCLUSIVE. An ALTER TABLE waiting for that lock is an outage for every query behind it.

nodes.label: connectionTimeoutMillis and idleTimeoutMillis
nodes.rationale: connectionTimeoutMillis covers socket open and waiting for a free pooled connection. idleTimeoutMillis should sit below intermediary idle TCP drops.

nodes.label: Simple vs extended query protocol
nodes.rationale: No values → simple protocol, multi-statement script, array of Results. A non-empty values array → extended protocol, exactly one statement or 42601.

nodes.label: Empty values array is not parameterized
nodes.rationale: query(sql, []) still uses the simple protocol and runs multi-statement text. Safety comes from bound values, not from the argument existing.

nodes.label: Multi-statement implicit transaction
nodes.rationale: A valid INSERT followed by a failing one left zero rows. The whole simple-query string is one implicit transaction.

nodes.label: pool.end()
nodes.rationale: Waits for in-flight queries then permanently retires the pool. A 300 ms query held end() 319 ms. A second end() throws.

nodes.label: Shutdown order: server then pool
nodes.rationale: server.close() first, then wait for in-flight requests, then pool.end(). Reversed, deploys burst 500s.

nodes.label: client.end() vs release()
nodes.rationale: end() closes a standalone Client. A pooled client from pool.connect() gets release(). Calling end() on a pooled client is a bug.

nodes.label: LISTEN / NOTIFY
nodes.rationale: PostgreSQL push to a connected client. Treat as a hint to look, never as a queue: nothing is stored.

nodes.label: LISTEN dedicated Client
nodes.rationale: LISTEN is session state. pool.query('LISTEN …') returns the connection with no handler; notifications are lost.

nodes.label: NOTIFY delivers on COMMIT
nodes.rationale: Zero delivered while the transaction is open, one after COMMIT, none after ROLLBACK. Notify inside the same transaction as the write.

nodes.label: NOTIFY dedup and 8000-byte payload
nodes.rationale: Identical channel/payload pairs in one transaction fold (3 became 1). Payload over 8000 bytes is 22023. Send an id, not the data.

nodes.label: NOTIFY plus poll queue table
nodes.rationale: The queue table is the truth; NOTIFY only removes latency. FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED makes several workers safe. Reconnect and re-LISTEN, then poll once.

nodes.label: pg-cursor streaming
nodes.rationale: Needs a checked-out client. read(n) until empty array, then close() then release(). Live set is one batch regardless of result size.

nodes.label: pool.query buffers the whole result
nodes.rationale: 300000 rows grew the heap by 101 MB, proportional to row count. The first row is unavailable until the last arrives.

nodes.label: DECLARE cursor needs a transaction
nodes.rationale: FETCH after COMMIT is 34000 cursor does not exist. WITH HOLD materialises the whole result at commit. pg-cursor uses a protocol portal bound to the connection.

nodes.label: Keyset batching instead of a cursor
nodes.rationale: Each chunk is a short pooled transaction: no long snapshot, no held client, interruptible. A cursor is right only when the export must reflect one point in time.

nodes.label: Long cursor pins xmin horizon
nodes.rationale: A twenty-minute stream is twenty minutes of no VACUUM database-wide. Hidden cost of streaming a large result.

nodes.label: postgres.js tagged templates
nodes.rationale: ${} inside the tag is a bind parameter, never SQL text. The safe path is the default path. Result is the array itself with .count.

nodes.label: pg vs postgres.js
nodes.rationale: Do not migrate an existing pg codebase for the API. Tooling expects a pg Pool. Neither driver changes schema, indexes or plans. Good default for greenfield ESM.

nodes.label: Per-row INSERT cost
nodes.rationale: 10000 autocommit inserts: 20165 ms. One transaction: 2559 ms (WAL flush once). One unnest statement: 84 ms. 240× spread.

nodes.label: INSERT … SELECT unnest
nodes.rationale: One array parameter per column; statement text is constant. Casts are required. Supports ON CONFLICT and RETURNING. Materialises everything in JS (201 MB heap at 500k rows).

nodes.label: 65535 parameter ceiling
nodes.rationale: Wire protocol encodes the count in 16 bits. 21845 rows × 3 columns succeeds; 21846 fails with 08P01 that does not mention the limit. Batch by floor(65535 / columns).

nodes.label: COPY vs unnest from Node
nodes.rationale: unnest beat pg-copy-streams by 2.7–3× at 10k/100k/500k because CSV formatting in JS dominates. COPY wins on streaming memory and unlimited size.

nodes.label: Generated TypeScript types from schema
nodes.rationale: A hand-written interface is a guess. Generate from the live schema so a dropped column is a type error. Commit the output and fail CI on git diff.

nodes.label: pool.query<User> is an assertion
nodes.rationale: pg does not validate rows against User. A dropped or renamed column still compiles. Table-level types also let SELECT projections compile as full rows.

nodes.label: Three type-generation approaches
nodes.rationale: Introspect the live database, derive from a tool schema, or infer from queries. Query inference types the actual SELECT projection and needs a DB at build time.

nodes.label: pg-copy-streams COPY FROM STDIN
nodes.rationale: Turns client.query into a writable stream. Needs a checked-out client; COPY puts the connection in a distinct protocol mode.

nodes.label: pipeline not .pipe() for COPY
nodes.rationale: pipeline propagates errors and destroys both ends. .pipe() leaves the connection stuck mid-COPY and returns a broken client to the pool.

nodes.label: COPY csv vs text format
nodes.rationale: Default is text (tab, \N for NULL). Feeding CSV to default COPY puts the whole line in the first column. In CSV an unquoted empty field is NULL; "" is empty string.

nodes.label: UNLOGGED staging table for COPY
nodes.rationale: COPY is all-or-nothing with no skip. Load all-text UNLOGGED staging, then INSERT … SELECT with validation, ON CONFLICT and rejects inspectable.

nodes.label: Creating tables from Node
nodes.rationale: pg will run CREATE TABLE. The question is when: from a replayable migration, never from a request handler and never from application startup.

nodes.label: DDL from Node three chunks
nodes.rationale: 01 issuing DDL through the driver; 02 DDL locks and blocking; 03 startup races and advisory locks.

nodes.label: IF NOT EXISTS is not a migration system
nodes.rationale: Idempotent, not concurrency-safe, not a definition check, and leaves no version record. Migrations fail loudly when a database is in an unexpected state.

nodes.label: CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS race
nodes.rationale: 228 of 500 concurrent attempts failed with 23505 on pg_type_typname_nsp_index. Catalog check and insert are not one atomic step.

nodes.label: IF NOT EXISTS is a name-only check
nodes.rationale: Does not compare columns, types, constraints or indexes. ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS with a different type is a silent no-op and a type mismatch.

nodes.label: Local PostgreSQL in Podman/Docker
nodes.rationale: Pin postgres:18-alpine on host port 55432. POSTGRES_* vars apply only on first data-directory init.

nodes.label: Connect on 127.0.0.1 never localhost
nodes.rationale: Node resolves localhost to ::1 first. A container published on IPv4 only is not listening there.

nodes.label: Wait on pg_isready not sleep
nodes.rationale: The container reports running before TCP accepts. First-time init starts the server twice. A fixed sleep is flaky or slow.

nodes.label: alpine vs debian collation
nodes.rationale: Same PostgreSQL 18.4 and en_US.utf8: musl sorts by byte value, glibc applies locale rules. ORDER BY changes if the base image does not match production.

nodes.label: Migration tools
nodes.rationale: Every tool implements a tracking table. Choose on workflow assumption, not feature list. Own-runner until CONCURRENTLY or baselining; node-pg-migrate for raw SQL; schema-derived tools only with their client.

nodes.label: The four migration models
nodes.rationale: node-pg-migrate and graphile-migrate: you write SQL. Prisma Migrate and drizzle-kit: the tool diffs a schema file. Split: do you write the schema, or does the tool derive it?

nodes.label: node-pg-migrate
nodes.rationale: v9.0.0. SQL or JS files, optional down. You own the schema; SQL is source of truth. Natural next step from a hand-written runner.

nodes.label: graphile-migrate
nodes.rationale: v1.4.1. One idempotent current.sql re-run on save, then committed as a numbered file. Fits functions/triggers/views/RLS; poor fit for incremental ALTER TABLE.

nodes.label: Prisma Migrate
nodes.rationale: v7.9.1. schema.prisma is source of truth; migrations are generated by diff. Do not use without Prisma Client.

nodes.label: drizzle-kit
nodes.rationale: v0.31.10. TypeScript schema objects; SQL generated by diff. Same derived-schema trade-off as Prisma.

nodes.label: Baselining an existing database
nodes.rationale: pg_dump --schema-only as one baseline, mark applied without running. History before the baseline is no longer replayable.

nodes.label: Migrations
