nodes.rationale: Anything else is coerced to a string. o[1] and o['1'] are the same property; two plain objects collide on [object Object]. Map is the answer for identity or non-string keys.

nodes.label: Three-tier property enumeration order
nodes.rationale: Integer-index keys first, ascending; then other strings by insertion; then symbols by insertion. An object keyed by numeric IDs reorders itself.

nodes.label: Integer-index keys
nodes.rationale: Only the canonical string form of a non-negative integer. -1, 01, 1.5 and 1e2 are ordinary strings. Zero-padded IDs sort into a different tier.

nodes.label: Enumeration method comparison
nodes.rationale: Object.keys is own enumerable strings. Reflect.ownKeys is the only one-call way to get all own keys including symbols. for...in walks the prototype chain.

nodes.label: Map for identity and ordered keys
nodes.rationale: The moment keys are not naturally strings — objects, or numbers you care about as numbers — use a Map. Map is insertion-ordered for every key type.

nodes.label: __proto__ colon form prototype setter
nodes.rationale: Only the literal colon form sets [[Prototype]]. A non-object non-null value does nothing at all. Shorthand and computed forms create ordinary properties. Duplicate colon forms are a SyntaxError.

nodes.label: JSON __proto__ is an ordinary key
nodes.rationale: JSON.parse is safe: __proto__ becomes a plain own property. Pollution happens in a later recursive merge that assigns through Object.prototype's accessor.

nodes.label: Prototype pollution
nodes.rationale: Assigning target['__proto__'] from untrusted JSON pollutes Object.prototype for every object, including ones created earlier. Defend with Object.create(null), skip dangerous keys, or defineProperty.

nodes.label: Object.create(null) dictionary
nodes.rationale: No inherited keys and no __proto__ accessor. Cost: no toString or hasOwnProperty; string conversion throws. Prefer Map unless you need a plain-object shape.

nodes.label: Object literals
nodes.rationale: Three surprises: method shorthand is not a function-valued property; { __proto__: x } is not a property; key order is not insertion order.

nodes.label: in operator
nodes.rationale: True for own or inherited properties, including Object.prototype names. Right for capability detection. Throws on primitives; does not auto-box.

nodes.label: Object.hasOwn
nodes.rationale: Modern default for data. Own-only, works on null-prototype objects, immune to shadowing, coerces primitives. ES2022 static method.

nodes.label: hasOwnProperty
nodes.rationale: Broken on Object.create(null) and on objects that shadow the method. MDN prefers Object.hasOwn. Fallback is Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call.

nodes.label: in for behaviour, hasOwn for data
nodes.rationale: Use in for feature detection where inheritance should count. Never use in for user-supplied keys.

nodes.label: undefined versus missing key
nodes.rationale: in and Object.hasOwn treat a key holding undefined as present. !== undefined, ?. and ?? cannot tell that from absence. Matters in PATCH and options objects.

nodes.label: ?? versus ||
nodes.rationale: ?? falls back only on null/undefined; || falls back on every falsy value. Mixing ?? with || or && is a SyntaxError without parentheses.

nodes.label: Array holes three states
nodes.rationale: Present, present holding undefined, and a hole. Reading the last two is undefined. map/forEach skip holes; spread/for...of visit them as undefined. Never create holes deliberately.

nodes.label: #field in obj brand check
nodes.rationale: Asks whether the object was constructed by this class. More trustworthy than instanceof. Only legal inside the declaring class body. Avoids try/catch around private access.

nodes.label: delete operator
nodes.rationale: Removes an own property only. Does not free memory, remove variables, touch the prototype chain, or change array length. true does not mean anything was deleted.

nodes.label: delete on an array leaves a hole
nodes.rationale: length is unchanged. Use splice, filter or toSpliced. V8 notes array functions are considerably slower on objects with slow elements.

nodes.label: V8 HiddenClass and dictionary mode
nodes.rationale: Frequent add/delete can generate HiddenClass overhead. Dictionary-mode properties are typically slower because inline caches do not work. No documented multiplier; one delete is not stated to demote.

nodes.label: Rest destructuring instead of delete
nodes.rationale: const { password, ...safeUser } = user builds a fresh stable-shape object. If you are calling delete in a loop, you wanted a Map.

nodes.label: Existence checks and delete
nodes.rationale: Four answers disagree on purpose along two axes: whether the prototype chain counts, and whether a property holding undefined counts as present.

nodes.label: Shallow copy
nodes.rationale: Top-level properties become independent; nested objects are shared by reference. Spread, Object.assign, slice and Array.from are all shallow.

nodes.label: Spread drops the prototype
nodes.rationale: Spreading a class instance yields fields with no methods. Map, Date, Set and RegExp keep data in internal slots, so { ...new Map(...) } is {}.

nodes.label: Copy the path you are changing
nodes.rationale: Idiomatic React/Redux updates share untouched branches. That identity sharing is what makes prev === next and memoisation work. Deep-cloning state defeats it.

nodes.label: structuredClone
nodes.rationale: Built-in deep clone via the structured clone algorithm. Rebuilds cycles to point at the clone. Preserves Map, Set, Date, RegExp and typed arrays.

nodes.label: structuredClone silent losses
nodes.rationale: Drops the prototype chain, descriptors, getters/setters, private elements and RegExp.lastIndex. A frozen object comes back writable.

nodes.label: DataCloneError
nodes.rationale: Functions and DOM nodes throw DataCloneError. Throwing at the clone is better than JSON silently dropping functions.

nodes.label: structuredClone transfer option
nodes.rationale: Moves transferable objects instead of copying them. The original ArrayBuffer is detached and byteLength becomes 0. Only use when nothing still reads the source.

nodes.label: JSON round-trip clone
nodes.rationale: JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)) is still the most-written deep clone and is lossy in seven documented ways. Acceptable only when data is already JSON-shaped with no cycles.

nodes.label: JSON.stringify seven losses
nodes.rationale: undefined/functions/symbols dropped in objects and nulled in arrays; NaN/Infinity become null; Date becomes a string; Map/Set become {}; BigInt and cycles throw; symbol keys and non-enumerable properties ignored.

nodes.label: Hand-written deep clone with WeakMap
nodes.rationale: Register the clone in a WeakMap before recursing so cycles terminate and shared identity is preserved. Handle Date, RegExp, Map and Set with their constructors. In production call structuredClone.

nodes.label: Shallow vs deep copy
nodes.rationale: Copy is not one operation. Everything convenient is shallow. structuredClone is deep and loses types. JSON is deep and loses seven things. Pick by what you can afford to lose.

nodes.label: Prototype chain
nodes.rationale: Every object has an internal [[Prototype]] link. Lookup walks until it finds a name or reaches null, then returns undefined. Nothing is copied onto instances.

nodes.label: Property shadowing
nodes.rationale: The first match wins and own properties are always first. The prototype's value is untouched and still reachable via Object.getPrototypeOf.

nodes.label: A miss traverses the entire chain
nodes.rationale: Accessing a non-existent property walks to null. A miss is the most expensive lookup, not the cheapest.

nodes.label: this is the receiver not the home
nodes.rationale: An inherited method is found on the prototype but this is the object it was called on. Finding the method and resolving each property are two separate lookups.

nodes.label: prototype vs [[Prototype]]
nodes.rationale: [[Prototype]] is an internal slot on every object. Fn.prototype is an ordinary property only functions have, the object new will install. A function's own prototype is Function.prototype.

nodes.label: What new actually does
nodes.rationale: Creates a fresh object whose [[Prototype]] is Fn.prototype, calls Fn with this bound to it, and returns it. No methods are copied; instances share one function object.

nodes.label: constructor back-reference
nodes.rationale: An own property of Fn.prototype pointing back at Fn. Replacing prototype wholesale discards it. Writable and forgeable — never use it for type checks.

nodes.label: Object.create
nodes.rationale: Sets [[Prototype]] directly with no constructor call. Descriptor defaults are all false. Object.create(null) gives no chain at all.

nodes.label: class is the same lookup machinery
nodes.rationale: Class methods go on Ctor.prototype. class adds private fields, extends wiring, strict bodies, non-enumerable methods and a constructor that throws without new.

nodes.label: A write creates an own property
nodes.rationale: Reads walk the chain; writes do not. Assignment shadows a prototype data property. The prototype and other inheritors are untouched.

nodes.label: Shared mutable prototype state
nodes.rationale: Fn.prototype.items = [] is one array shared by every instance. push is a read then a mutation, so no shadowing own property is created. Create per-instance fields instead.

nodes.label: Inherited setters intercept writes
nodes.rationale: If the chain has a setter for that key, the setter runs and no own property is created. A read-only inherited property throws TypeError in strict mode instead of shadowing.

nodes.label: Object.setPrototypeOf deoptimization
nodes.rationale: Engines optimise the chain at creation time. Changing it causes recompile for de-optimization. Set the chain at creation with { __proto__: proto } or Object.create.

nodes.label: Keep the prototype chain short
nodes.rationale: A miss visits every level. Two or three levels is normal; ten is a smell. Extending built-in prototypes lengthens the chain for every object of that type.

nodes.label: The prototype chain topic
nodes.rationale: An object is own properties plus a link. This topic makes class stop being magic and comes before topic 06 deliberately.

nodes.label: What class desugars to
nodes.rationale: The wiring is identical: methods go on Ctor.prototype. class is sugar for prototype wiring and a genuine language feature for everything else.

nodes.label: Five non-sugar class features
nodes.rationale: Always-strict body; TypeError without new; non-enumerable methods; TDZ and block scope; private elements with no desugaring.

nodes.label: Instance field versus prototype method
nodes.rationale: A field is an own enumerable property per instance. A method is one shared non-enumerable function on Ctor.prototype. items = [] must be a field.

nodes.label: Arrow-function class field
nodes.rationale: Own property per instance whose this is lexical. Survives being detached as a callback. Cost: one function per instance and it cannot be super-called.

nodes.label: Derived class field initialisation order
nodes.rationale: Base fields run at the start of the constructor. Derived fields run immediately before super() returns, so an overridden method called from the parent constructor sees them still undefined.

nodes.label: class
nodes.rationale: class is half syntactic sugar over prototypes; the false half is the part worth knowing.

nodes.label: Five class features that are not sugar
nodes.rationale: Always strict; TypeError without new; methods non-enumerable; block-scoped TDZ; private elements have no desugaring.

nodes.label: Where class members live
nodes.rationale: Instance field = own per instance; method() = Ctor.prototype; static = class object; #field = private slot, not inherited.

nodes.label: static members
nodes.rationale: static puts a member on the class object itself, not on instances or the prototype. instance.staticThing is undefined because the instance chain never passes through Ctor.

nodes.label: this in a static method
nodes.rationale: this is the class it was called on. new this(...) in a factory returns the subclass because extends links class objects.

nodes.label: Polymorphic static factory
nodes.rationale: Use new this(...) not new Model(...) so User.create() builds a User. Statics inherit through the class-object chain.

nodes.label: Static initialization blocks
nodes.rationale: Run statements (loops, try/catch) and access private scope during class evaluation. Evaluated at the class statement, not first construction.

nodes.label: Class getters and setters
nodes.rationale: Accessors go on the prototype like methods. Pair a #private field with a public get/set. static get/set put the accessor on the class object.

nodes.label: Accessor infinite-recursion trap
nodes.rationale: get name() { return this.name; } calls itself until RangeError. Backing store must be a different name (#name).

nodes.label: Static fields evaluated at class evaluation
nodes.rationale: MDN: evaluated during class evaluation with this set to the class. A throwing block prevents the class existing; expensive work is paid at module load.

nodes.label: Private elements
nodes.rationale: The one class feature with no desugaring. # prefix; privacy enforced by JavaScript itself, in the grammar.

nodes.label: Private access SyntaxError outside class
nodes.rationale: obj.#field outside the declaring class is a parse-time SyntaxError, so the file never runs. Not equivalent to _underscore.

nodes.label: Private access TypeError on wrong object
nodes.rationale: Inside the class, access on a non-instance throws TypeError: Cannot read private member #x from an object whose class did not declare it.

nodes.label: #x in obj brand check
nodes.rationale: Asks whether the object has that private element without throwing. Stronger than instanceof because privates cannot be forged or added later.

nodes.label: Private elements are not inherited
nodes.rationale: Not part of the prototypical inheritance model. A subclass cannot read the parent's #field. JS has no protected. Same name in parent and child are independent slots.

nodes.label: Private identifier unique namespace
nodes.rationale: All private identifiers in a class must be unique; namespace shared between static and instance. Only get/set pairs may repeat. #constructor is reserved.

nodes.label: Private elements are encapsulation not security
nodes.rationale: A debugger shows them. Guarantee is that other code cannot accidentally depend on internals — a maintenance property, not secrecy.

nodes.label: Private elements are not serialisable
nodes.rationale: JSON.stringify cannot see them; structuredClone does not duplicate them. A class with private state needs its own toJSON and clone.

nodes.label: this inside methods
nodes.rationale: A method is not attached to its object. this is decided by how it is called — the binding is created by the dot.

nodes.label: this is decided by the call site
nodes.rationale: MDN: if the call is obj.f(), this refers to obj. Same function object, different this depending on the receiver. Nothing travels when extracted.

nodes.label: Method borrowing
nodes.rationale: Assigning bird.sayHi = car.sayHi and calling it gives this === bird. A feature of the same rule that makes extracting a method dangerous.

nodes.label: Sloppy-mode this substitution
nodes.rationale: In non-strict mode undefined/null this is replaced with globalThis. Writes silently create globals. Strict (modules, classes) throws TypeError instead.

nodes.label: Four ways a method loses this
nodes.rationale: Assign to a variable; pass as a callback; destructure it out; re-attach to a different object. Callbacks are the most common form.

nodes.label: thisArg on iteration methods
nodes.rationale: forEach, map, filter, some, every, find, findIndex, flatMap take optional thisArg. reduce, reduceRight and sort do not. Arrows sidestep it.

nodes.label: this in a class field initialiser
nodes.rationale: Already bound — to the instance for an instance field, to the class for a static one. Why an arrow field captures the instance permanently.

nodes.label: bind in the constructor
nodes.rationale: Creates a new function with this fixed and stores it as an own property that shadows the prototype method. Binding is permanent.

nodes.label: Arrow class field
nodes.rationale: Field initialiser runs with this bound to the instance; the arrow captures it lexically. Own property per instance; not overridable; no super.

nodes.label: Wrap at the call site
nodes.rationale: () => this.m() leaves the method a plain prototype method, costs nothing, stays overridable. Best default except removable listeners.

nodes.label: call / apply / thisArg for one call
nodes.rationale: Sets this for one call, not permanently. Not a fix for the detached-method problem if you are already at the call site.

nodes.label: bind only works once
nodes.rationale: A bound function's this is permanent. Re-binding does nothing; call/apply cannot override it.

nodes.label: removeEventListener identity trap
nodes.rationale: Removal matches by function identity. An inline arrow is a new function each time, so removeEventListener silently does nothing.

nodes.label: Per-instance cost of bound or arrow methods
nodes.rationale: bind-in-constructor and arrow fields create one function object per instance and take the method off the prototype, blocking override and super.

nodes.label: Object.keys / values / entries / fromEntries
nodes.rationale: Three methods share one definition: own enumerable string-keyed properties. fromEntries performs the reverse of entries.

nodes.label: Own enumerable string-keyed
nodes.rationale: MDN's phrase for entries/keys/values. Skips inherited, non-enumerable, and symbol keys. Same set JSON.stringify serialises.

nodes.label: Object.keys
nodes.rationale: Returns own enumerable string keys. Default over for...in because it does not walk the prototype chain.

nodes.label: Object.entries
nodes.rationale: Array of [key, value] pairs for own enumerable string-keyed properties. Keys come back as strings.

nodes.label: for...in vs Object.keys
nodes.rationale: for...in enumerates the prototype chain as well. That single difference is why Object.keys should be the default.

nodes.label: Integer-index enumeration order
nodes.rationale: Integer-index keys come out ascending regardless of insertion. {100,2,7} yields 2, 7, 100. Objects keyed by numeric ID are not ordered collections.

nodes.label: Object.keys throws on null and undefined
nodes.rationale: Non-objects are coerced except null and undefined, which throw TypeError. Guard with ?? {}.

nodes.label: Reflect.ownKeys
nodes.rationale: Returns every own property including symbols and non-enumerables. getOwnPropertyNames adds non-enumerable strings only.

nodes.label: Object.fromEntries
nodes.rationale: Transforms any iterable of key-value pairs into a plain object. Reverse of Object.entries. Does not use this; always a plain object.

nodes.label: entries → map/filter → fromEntries
nodes.rationale: Objects have no map or filter. Convert to pairs, use array methods, convert back. A pick built this way is safer than delete.

nodes.label: Map ↔ Object conversion
nodes.rationale: Object.fromEntries(map) and new Map(Object.entries(obj)). The bridge into real insertion order and non-string keys.

nodes.label: URLSearchParams to object is lossy
nodes.rationale: Repeated keys cannot live on an object. tag=a&tag=b becomes {tag:'b'}. Use getAll or keep URLSearchParams.

nodes.label: entries/fromEntries round-trip losses
nodes.rationale: Drops symbols, non-enumerables, inherited, prototype, accessors (getters invoked), descriptors, and numeric key order. Shallow.

nodes.label: Phase 5 — The built-in library
nodes.rationale: 26 topics grouped by object. Master-first: 01, 02, 04, 05, 06, 07, 09, 10 complete. Documentation-validated; no new sandboxes.

nodes.label: Array creation and shape
nodes.rationale: new Array(n) creates holes so .map() does nothing. length is writable and is one more than the highest index.

nodes.label: Never create holes
nodes.rationale: If you never create holes the hole-behaviour table stops mattering. Use splice to remove, Array.from({length:n}, fn) to allocate, Array.of when arity is dynamic.

nodes.label: Array constructor arity trap
nodes.rationale: new Array(3) is length 3 with holes; new Array(1,2) is [1,2]. One numeric argument is a length. Hazard when argument count is dynamic.

nodes.label: Array.of
nodes.rationale: Always treats arguments as elements. Array.of(3) is [3]. Exists because Array() changes meaning by argument count.

nodes.label: Array.from
nodes.rationale: Creates a shallow-copied Array from an iterable or array-like. Only built-in that accepts both protocols. Spread requires Symbol.iterator.

nodes.label: Array.from mapFn
nodes.rationale: Maps during construction: no intermediate array. Callback gets (element, index) only — no third array argument because the array is still being built.

nodes.label: {length: n} range idiom
nodes.rationale: Array.from({length:n}, (_,i)=>...) never creates a sparse array. new Array(n).map skips holes. Standard way to build a range.

nodes.label: Array length is writable
nodes.rationale: Writable nonnegative integer < 2^32. Shrinking truncates; growing appends holes. arr.length=0 empties in place. Invalid lengths throw RangeError.

nodes.label: Three states of an array index
nodes.rationale: Present with a value; present holding undefined; a hole (property absent). Reading gives undefined for the last two; only in/hasOwn distinguish them.

nodes.label: Four ways to create holes
nodes.rationale: new Array(n); elision [1,,3]; arr.length = larger; delete arr[i] (length unchanged). All avoidable.

nodes.label: Methods that skip holes
nodes.rationale: Skip: forEach, map, filter, some, every, reduce, reduceRight. Treat as undefined: for...of, spread, Array.from, find, findIndex, includes, join, sort, fill, entries.

nodes.label: includes vs indexOf on holes
nodes.rationale: includes treats holes as undefined (true); indexOf skips holes (-1). Sharpest form of the hole-behaviour split.

nodes.label: length is not a count of elements
nodes.rationale: length is one more than the highest index. a[99]='x' makes length 100 with one value. Object.keys(a).length is the real count.

nodes.label: Adding and removing array elements
nodes.rationale: Adders return a length; removers return an element. The front is fundamentally more expensive. splice with missing deleteCount throws away the tail.

nodes.label: Array.prototype.push
nodes.rationale: Adds at the back; returns the new length, not the array. Cannot be chained.

nodes.label: Array.prototype.pop
nodes.rationale: Removes the last element; returns it, or undefined if empty. Constant work.

nodes.label: Array.prototype.shift
nodes.rationale: Removes the first element and shifts all remaining values left by 1. Work proportional to length.

nodes.label: Array.prototype.unshift
nodes.rationale: Inserts at the front by re-indexing everything. Returns the new length.

nodes.label: O(n²) queue via shift in a loop
nodes.rationale: n shifts each re-index the remaining array. Fix: index cursor, or reverse once and pop. Specified algorithm, not a measured multiplier.

nodes.label: push(...huge) argument limit
nodes.rationale: Spread turns every element into an argument and can throw RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded. Loop with push, or concat.

nodes.label: Non-mutating add/remove equivalents
nodes.rationale: push → [...arr,x]; unshift → [x,...arr]; pop → slice(0,-1); shift → slice(1). Default unless the array is local. Identity change is what React detects.

nodes.label: Array.prototype.splice
nodes.rationale: Removes, inserts, and replaces in place. Returns the removed elements as an array, not the modified array.

nodes.label: Omitted splice deleteCount deletes to the end
nodes.rationale: splice(2) truncates from index 2. splice(2,0) inserts without removing. Most damaging splice mistake.

nodes.label: splice vs delete on arrays
nodes.rationale: delete leaves a hole and length unchanged. splice removes the element, closes the gap, decrements length.

nodes.label: Never splice inside a forward loop
nodes.rationale: Removing at i shifts later elements down, so i++ skips the next. Iterate backwards, or filter (the default).

nodes.label: Array.prototype.toSpliced
nodes.rationale: Non-mutating counterpart: same arguments, returns the new array. Produces a dense array; splice preserves sparseness.

nodes.label: indexOf + splice(-1) trap
nodes.rationale: indexOf miss is -1; splice(-1,1) removes the last element. Guard with i !== -1, or use filter.

nodes.label: Array iteration methods
nodes.rationale: Eight methods; pick by what you want back. They differ in return value, early stop, and whether they visit holes.

nodes.label: Array.prototype.forEach
nodes.rationale: Always returns undefined and is not chainable. No way to stop other than throwing. Wrong tool if you need break/await.

nodes.label: Array.prototype.map
nodes.rationale: New array, same length, callback return values. Misused as a loop it allocates an array of undefined.

nodes.label: Array.prototype.filter
nodes.rationale: New array of matches; visits every element. filter(...)[0] is a common misuse of find.

nodes.label: Array.prototype.find
nodes.rationale: First matching element or undefined; stops at the match. findLast searches from the end.

nodes.label: Array.prototype.findIndex
nodes.rationale: Index of first match, or -1. if (i) is inverted: 0 is falsy and -1 is truthy. Always compare !== -1.

nodes.label: Array.prototype.some
nodes.rationale: true if any element matches; stops on first true. Empty array → false.

nodes.label: Array.prototype.every
nodes.rationale: true if all match; stops on first false. Empty array returns true (vacuous). Gates need length > 0 &&.

nodes.label: every is vacuously true on []
nodes.rationale: MDN: for-all over the empty set. cart.every(inStock) passes for an empty cart.

nodes.label: for...of for control flow
nodes.rationale: break, continue, return, and await work in for...of and none of them work in forEach. Use the loop when the body is control flow.

nodes.label: Iteration callback (element, index, array)
nodes.rationale: Every iteration method passes three arguments. Passing a named function whose later params mean something misfires.

nodes.label: map(parseInt) radix bug
nodes.rationale: ["1","2","3"].map(parseInt) is [1, NaN, NaN] because index arrives as parseInt radix.

nodes.label: find visits holes; forEach skips them
nodes.rationale: MDN: find is invoked for every index, treating holes as undefined. forEach skips empty slots. Same sparse array: 7 visits vs 3.

nodes.label: Mutating an array while iterating
nodes.rationale: Range is fixed before the first callback. Appended elements are not visited; removals cause skips. Build a new array.

nodes.label: async forEach discards promises
nodes.rationale: forEach expects a synchronous function and does not wait for promises. MDN example prints 0 instead of 14. filter(async) filters nothing because every promise is truthy.

nodes.label: for...of await vs Promise.all(map)
nodes.rationale: for...of + await is sequential. Promise.all over map is concurrent. Pick by independence and load.

nodes.label: Array.prototype.reduce
nodes.rationale: Collapses an array into one value. MDN has a section on when not to use it. Mechanism is small; judgement is the hard part.

nodes.label: reduce callback and initial value
nodes.rationale: callback(accumulator, currentValue, currentIndex, array). Second parameter of reduce is initialValue, so there is no thisArg.

nodes.label: reduce without initialValue
nodes.rationale: First element becomes the accumulator; iteration starts at index 1; empty array throws TypeError; single element returns it with no callback call.

nodes.label: Always pass a reduce initial value
nodes.rationale: An empty array is the first render, a filtered-to-nothing list, an API with no rows. Initial value also declares the accumulator type.

nodes.label: reduce skips holes not undefined
nodes.rationale: [1,2,,4] sums to 7; [1,2,undefined,4] is NaN. Clearest demonstration that a hole is not undefined.

nodes.label: Missing return in reduce callback
nodes.rationale: Most common reduce bug. Next accumulator is undefined; failure appears on the second iteration.

nodes.label: reduceRight
nodes.rationale: Same method from the end. Matters only when the operation is not associative (compose, string building).

nodes.label: reduce is a for...of loop
nodes.rationale: MDN equivalence: any reduce you cannot immediately rewrite as that loop should have been the loop.

nodes.label: Spreading the reduce accumulator is O(N²)
nodes.rationale: MDN anti-pattern: {...allNames, [name]: n} copies the whole object every iteration. Mutate the private accumulator or use for...of.

nodes.label: Better-named methods than reduce
nodes.rationale: flat, Object.groupBy/Map.groupBy, flatMap, Array.from(new Set), find/some, filter. Grouping is the most common legitimate-looking misuse.

nodes.label: Object.groupBy / Map.groupBy
nodes.rationale: Prefer Map.groupBy — any key type and insertion order. Replaces the hand-written grouping reduce.

nodes.label: pipe and asyncPipe via reduce
nodes.rationale: Fold over functions, not data. asyncPipe sequences promises with acc.then(fn). Genuine reduce: scalar fold or fold over functions.

nodes.label: 07.2 · The fixes, and which to choose
08.1 · What they include and what they skip
Four sort rules
nodes.rationale: Always pass a numeric comparator; copy before sorting shared arrays; keep the comparator total and consistent; undefined and holes always go last.

nodes.label: Default sort is UTF-16 string order
nodes.rationale: Elements are converted to strings then compared as UTF-16 code units, so [1, 30, 4, 21, 100000] becomes [1, 100000, 21, 30, 4].

nodes.label: sort compareFn contract
nodes.rationale: Negative means a before b, positive after, zero or NaN equal. Only the sign matters, which is why a - b works.

nodes.label: Well-formed comparator requirements
nodes.rationale: Pure, stable, reflexive, anti-symmetric, transitive. Violations do not throw; they yield implementation-defined order.

nodes.label: Fisher–Yates shuffle
nodes.rationale: sort(() => Math.random() - 0.5) breaks every consistency requirement and is a biased, engine-dependent shuffle.

nodes.label: String.prototype.localeCompare
nodes.rationale: Default UTF-16 order puts Z before a and mis-sorts accents. localeCompare returns a signed number that plugs into compareFn.

nodes.label: Intl.Collator
nodes.rationale: Build one Collator and reuse compare; creating one per comparison is wasteful on large lists.

nodes.label: Multi-key || comparator chain
nodes.rationale: A tie returns 0, which is falsy, so evaluation falls through. Negate one term for a descending key.

nodes.label: Decorate–sort–undecorate
nodes.rationale: An expensive key computed inside compareFn runs O(n log n) times and a variable key violates stability. Map to {item, key}, sort, map back.

nodes.label: sort mutates and returns the same array
nodes.rationale: const sorted = arr.sort() is the same reference, so change detection sees no new identity and shared callers are reordered.

nodes.label: Array.prototype.toSorted
nodes.rationale: ES2023 non-mutating counterpart: returns a shallow-copied sorted array. [...arr].sort() is the portable form.

nodes.label: ES2019 sort stability
nodes.rationale: Equal elements keep original relative order since ES2019. Earlier engines varied by array length, which is why old code carries index tiebreaks.

nodes.label: Two-pass multi-column sort
nodes.rationale: Sort secondary first then primary; stability preserves the secondary inside each primary group. Use the || chain for a one-shot sort.

nodes.label: undefined and holes sort last
nodes.rationale: Comparator is never called for them. Missing properties on objects still reach it. Map to a sentinel to put missing values first.

nodes.label: ES2023 non-mutating array family
nodes.rationale: toSorted, toReversed, toSpliced and with leave the original alone and produce dense arrays.

nodes.label: Array.prototype.reverse
nodes.rationale: Like sort, reverse mutates in place and returns the same reference.

nodes.label: Strings are immutable
nodes.rationale: Every string method returns a new string, so no defensive copy is needed.

nodes.label: String.prototype.substring
nodes.rationale: Treats negatives as 0 and swaps start > end, hiding bugs behind a plausible substring.

nodes.label: Use slice, not substring
nodes.rationale: slice matches Array.prototype.slice, supports negative indices, and returns empty when start > end so mistakes surface.

nodes.label: String.prototype.at
nodes.rationale: Accepts negative indices; bracket notation does not. Out of range returns undefined, unlike charAt which returns empty string.

nodes.label: String.prototype.split
nodes.rationale: No separator returns [whole string]. limit truncates and discards the remainder. Capture groups in a regex separator are included.

nodes.label: empty string split is [""]
nodes.rationale: "".split(",") is [""] not [], so field counts are 1 for empty CSV input.

nodes.label: split("") splits UTF-16 code units
nodes.rationale: Emoji and other non-BMP characters become surrogate halves. [...str] and Array.from yield code points.

nodes.label: Intl.Segmenter
nodes.rationale: Code points are not graphemes; skin-tone and family emoji are several code points that display as one character.

nodes.label: Array.prototype.join
nodes.rationale: null and undefined become empty strings, so missing values silently become empty CSV fields.

nodes.label: String trim family
nodes.rationale: Removes Unicode whitespace, takes no argument, and belongs at the input boundary. Use Start/End names, not Left/Right.

nodes.label: String.prototype.padStart
nodes.rationale: First argument is target total length. Already-long strings are unchanged; multi-character pads are repeated then cut.

nodes.label: String.prototype.repeat
nodes.rationale: Negative count throws RangeError. Replaces the old new Array(n+1).join(str) idiom.

nodes.label: String.prototype.replace
nodes.rationale: A string pattern replaces only the first occurrence — the most common string bug.

nodes.label: String.prototype.replaceAll
nodes.rationale: Throws TypeError if a regex lacks the g flag. Equivalent to replace with a global regex; the difference exists only for string patterns.

nodes.label: Never build a regex from user input
nodes.rationale: A string in replaceAll matches literally. new RegExp(userInput) treats metacharacters as syntax and is a backtracking DoS vector.

nodes.label: Replacement $ patterns
nodes.rationale: $&, $1 and $<name> are interpreted in a replacement string. Use the function form when the replacement is data-derived.

nodes.label: Locale-dependent case mapping
nodes.rationale: Turkish i uppercases to dotted İ. Prefer localeCompare with sensitivity accent over lowercasing both sides.

nodes.label: JSON.stringify is silently lossy
nodes.rationale: It sees the same own enumerable string-keyed set as Object.keys. Prototype, symbols and non-enumerables are gone.

nodes.label: undefined omitted in objects, nulled in arrays
nodes.rationale: undefined, functions and symbols vanish from objects and become null in arrays — same values, opposite treatment.

nodes.label: Date.toJSON ISO string
nodes.rationale: The most common JSON bug: a parsed clone holds a string, so .getTime() throws far from the serialisation.

nodes.label: Map and Set stringify as {}
nodes.rationale: Contents live in internal slots, not own enumerable properties.

nodes.label: stringify throws on BigInt and cycles
nodes.rationale: BigInt refusal forces an explicit serialisation. A cycle is a hard limit; structuredClone clones but does not produce a string.

nodes.label: toJSON hook
nodes.rationale: The return value is serialised instead of the object. Lives with the type, unlike a per-call-site replacer.

nodes.label: JSON.stringify replacer
nodes.rationale: Function form returning undefined omits a key at every level. Array form is a deny-by-default allowlist. Symbol keys stay ignored.

nodes.label: stringify is not deep equality
nodes.rationale: Key order follows enumeration, so same content in different insertion order produces different strings.

nodes.label: JSON.parse SyntaxError
nodes.rationale: Trailing commas, single quotes and empty bodies throw. JSON is stricter than object-literal syntax.

nodes.label: Reviver must return value
nodes.rationale: Returning undefined deletes the property. Doing so for the root deletes the entire result.

nodes.label: Reviver is innermost-first
nodes.rationale: Depth-first: children are transformed before parents. Root is called last with key "".

nodes.label: Reviving Date from JSON
nodes.rationale: Match ISO strings or key.endsWith("At"). A loose pattern turns version strings into dates.

nodes.label: reviver context.source
nodes.rationale: value is already a double past MAX_SAFE_INTEGER. context.source is the original text, only for primitives.

nodes.label: JSON.parse is not prototype pollution
nodes.rationale: "__proto__" is an ordinary own property in JSON. Pollution happens later if a merge assigns through that key.

nodes.label: Use Map when keys are data
nodes.rationale: Keys from user input, non-strings, open-ended sets, frequent add/remove, insertion order or size want Map. Fixed typed keys and JSON edges want objects.

nodes.label: The six Map vs object differences
Object accidental inherited keys
nodes.rationale: A Map has no default keys. An object dictionary keyed by user input inherits toString and friends.

nodes.label: Map keys can be any value
nodes.rationale: Object keys stringify, so 1 collides with "1" and any two objects become [object Object]. Map compares object keys by identity.

nodes.label: Map insertion order vs object order
nodes.rationale: Integer-like object keys enumerate ascending first. A Map keyed by numeric IDs keeps insertion order.

nodes.label: Map is directly iterable
nodes.rationale: for...of over a Map yields [k, v] pairs. Objects need Object.entries and are not iterable.

nodes.label: Map add/remove performance
nodes.rationale: If you are calling delete in a loop, you wanted a Map. No multiplier is claimed.

nodes.label: SameValueZero key equality
nodes.rationale: NaN equals NaN and 0 equals -0. Same algorithm as Set and Array.prototype.includes.

nodes.label: Map does not serialise
nodes.rationale: Biggest reason objects survive at network and storage edges. JSON.stringify([...map]) keeps key types; fromEntries stringifies them.

nodes.label: Map has no structural typing
nodes.rationale: A Map of string keys cannot catch config.get("retires") the way config.retires would.

nodes.label: Map.groupBy vs Object.groupBy
nodes.rationale: Grouping keys are data. Map.groupBy keeps any key type and insertion order; Object.groupBy stringifies and re-sorts numeric keys.

nodes.label: WeakMap
nodes.rationale: Holds keys weakly so entries die with the key object. A plain Map in that role is a memory leak. Not iterable, no size.

nodes.label: Array vs object destructuring
nodes.rationale: Arrays match by position, objects by name. Object rename syntax is key-left, binding-right — opposite an object literal.

nodes.label: Destructuring defaults apply to undefined only
nodes.rationale: JSON payloads use null for missing values because stringify drops undefined, so every default is routinely bypassed. Follow with ??.

nodes.label: Nested destructuring
nodes.rationale: Intermediate names are paths, not bindings. A missing level applies the inner pattern to undefined and throws.

nodes.label: Object rest omit-a-key
nodes.rationale: const { password, ...safeUser } = user builds a new object without mutating. Shallow; own enumerable only.

nodes.label: Destructuring swap idiom
nodes.rationale: The right-hand array is fully evaluated before assignment, so no temporary is needed.

nodes.label: Parentheses for object assignment
nodes.rationale: A statement starting with { is a block. ({ a, b } = obj) forces expression position. Array patterns have no such problem.

nodes.label: Destructuring null or undefined throws
nodes.rationale: Throws even with empty patterns. Guard with ?? {} or a parameter default of = {}.

nodes.label: Options object as named arguments
nodes.rationale: Order-independent, self-documenting, and addable without touching callers. Worth the allocation past two or three parameters.

nodes.label: Destructured parameter = {}
nodes.rationale: function f({ a }) {} throws on f() because the parameter is undefined. Any optional destructured parameter needs = {}.

nodes.label: Promise.all array destructuring
nodes.rationale: Positional binding is right when order is the call order. Reordering silently reassigns same-typed results.

nodes.label: Destructuring detaches this
nodes.rationale: const { start } = timer is assignment, same as const f = obj.f. APIs meant to be destructured return closures.

nodes.label: Destructuring and fn.length
nodes.rationale: A destructured parameter counts as one. A default stops the count, so adding = {} drops arity from 1 to 0.

nodes.label: for...in
nodes.rationale: Iterates enumerable string keys including inherited ones. An Object.hasOwn guard is the signal to switch to Object.keys.

nodes.label: for...of
nodes.rationale: Iterates values via Symbol.iterator. Strings yield code points. Works on Map and Set directly.

nodes.label: Array.prototype.forEach
nodes.rationale: Index is a number. Skips holes. Cannot break. Does not await.

nodes.label: Never for...in on an array
nodes.rationale: Indices arrive as strings, non-index properties are included, and property enumeration skips holes that for...of visits.

nodes.label: Plain objects are not iterable
nodes.rationale: A record is not a sequence. Object.entries states whether you want keys, values or pairs.

nodes.label: Control flow and choosing a loop
Loop capability table
nodes.rationale: Need break, continue, enclosing return or await? forEach and array methods are out. Produce a value with map/filter/find.

nodes.label: return inside forEach
nodes.rationale: Returns from the callback like continue, not from the enclosing function. findUser always returns null.

nodes.label: for...of await vs Promise.all map
nodes.rationale: forEach(async) discards promises. Sequential for...of bounds load; Promise.all starts every request at once.

nodes.label: Labelled break
nodes.rationale: outer: for (...) { break outer } exits both loops. No labelled escape from forEach.

nodes.label: Iterating while modifying
nodes.rationale: forEach fixes its range up front. for...of re-reads length, so push inside the same array is an infinite loop.

nodes.label: Array and call spread
nodes.rationale: Requires Symbol.iterator. [...obj] throws on a plain object. [...new Set(items)] is the idiomatic dedupe.

nodes.label: Object spread
nodes.rationale: Copies own enumerable properties. {...map} is {}. Spreading false or undefined is a silent no-op that enables ...(cond && { k }).

nodes.label: Spread is a shallow copy
nodes.rationale: Multidimensional arrays are not safe to copy with spread. structuredClone is for a genuinely independent graph.

nodes.label: Spread versus rest
nodes.rationale: Same dots, opposite direction. Rest collects and must be last; spread expands in a call or literal.

nodes.label: Spread replacing apply
nodes.rationale: Composes with fixed arguments and works with new, which apply cannot. apply remains only for setting this.

nodes.label: Spread argument-count RangeError
nodes.rationale: Math.max(...hugeArray) and arr.push(...huge) pass each element as an argument. Use reduce, a loop, or concat.

nodes.label: Later spreads win
nodes.rationale: Object spread is a replace, not a deep merge. A spread after an explicit key overrides it.

nodes.label: Immutable updates with spread
nodes.rationale: Copy only changed levels and share untouched branches so prev.items === next.items remains a valid change check.

nodes.label: Array.from vs spread
nodes.rationale: Array.from accepts array-likes without an iterator, maps while converting, and builds n slots.

nodes.label: Spread inside a growing loop is quadratic
nodes.rationale: out = [...out, x] copies the whole accumulation each iteration. Use map or push.

nodes.label: Phase 7 — Asynchronous JavaScript
nodes.rationale: Syllabus centre of gravity: eleven Master topics; if only one phase is finished to Master depth, finish this one.

nodes.label: Single-threaded JavaScript
nodes.rationale: True of your code, false of the platform. Network, timers, disk, crypto and rendering run elsewhere.

nodes.label: Run-to-completion
nodes.rationale: A function cannot be preempted. Buys no locks; costs a frozen UI for any long synchronous job.

nodes.label: Concurrency vs parallelism
nodes.rationale: Concurrency is several operations in progress; parallelism is simultaneous execution. Promise.all is concurrency; workers are parallelism.

nodes.label: await does not block the thread
nodes.rationale: await suspends the async function, not the thread. It cannot slice a long synchronous computation.

nodes.label: Worker as separate agent
nodes.rationale: Own thread, heap and event loop. Communication is structured-cloned message passing; isolation preserves run-to-completion.

nodes.label: Never-blocking exceptions
nodes.rationale: Atomics.wait over SharedArrayBuffer can halt an agent (dedicated/shared workers only). Sync APIs — readFileSync, execSync, alert, localStorage — stop the world.

nodes.label: Event loop
nodes.rationale: An agent has a heap of objects, a LIFO stack of execution contexts, and a FIFO queue of jobs. The loop pulls one job, runs until the stack is empty, then pulls the next.

nodes.label: Heap
nodes.rationale: Large unstructured memory region populated as objects are created. No order.

nodes.label: Call stack
nodes.rationale: LIFO execution contexts. Finite; V8 does not implement proper tail calls. An async continuation starts a fresh stack.

nodes.label: Job queue
nodes.rationale: FIFO jobs from platform completions and from .then, queueMicrotask and await. Enables async while remaining single-threaded.

nodes.label: A job is complete when the stack is empty
nodes.rationale: MDN definition of run-to-completion. Nothing else — timer, event, rendering — runs until the call stack fully unwinds.

nodes.label: setTimeout delay is a minimum
nodes.rationale: The callback also waits for the current job, every job queued ahead, and the entire microtask queue. A floor, not a schedule.

nodes.label: No tail-call optimisation in V8
nodes.rationale: The spec defines proper tail calls; V8 does not implement them. Deep recursion overflows regardless of how it is written.

nodes.label: Node vs browser event loops
nodes.rationale: libuv phases plus process.nextTick versus the HTML loop with rendering. Only 'microtasks before tasks' is asserted for both.

nodes.label: Microtask
nodes.rationale: Created by .then/.catch/.finally, await continuations, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver. Entire queue drains after the current task.

nodes.label: Task (macrotask)
nodes.rationale: One job per event-loop turn. Created by setTimeout, setInterval, event dispatch, the initial script. A task yields; a microtask does not.

nodes.label: Microtask drain until empty
nodes.rationale: A task runs one job. A microtask drain runs every microtask, including ones queued during the drain.

nodes.label: Microtask starvation
nodes.rationale: A self-re-arming microtask chain never returns to the task queue — no timers, events or rendering. Worse than while(true) because it looks async.

nodes.label: await is microtask scheduling
nodes.rationale: Code before the first await is synchronous. await on a non-promise still yields a microtask, never a task, so an await loop still starves rendering.

nodes.label: Rendering between tasks
nodes.rationale: The browser schedules a rendering opportunity between tasks, after the microtask queue is empty. Yield a task to paint.

nodes.label: requestAnimationFrame
nodes.rationale: Neither a task nor a microtask — a separate callback list in the rendering step, just before layout and paint.

nodes.label: process.nextTick
nodes.rationale: Node-only queue drained before the promise microtask queue. setImmediate is a check-phase task.

nodes.label: queueMicrotask
nodes.rationale: Runs after the current execution context exits but before event handlers and timeouts. Prefer over Promise.resolve().then: no allocation, exceptions surface as uncaught errors.

nodes.label: Releasing Zalgo (sometimes-async)
nodes.rationale: A function should be always-async or never-async. Cache-hit sync vs miss async fires events before listeners attach. Defer the fast path with queueMicrotask.

nodes.label: length === 1 microtask batching
nodes.rationale: First call schedules the flush; later calls in the same turn join the array. Runs after all sync code and before paint — the mechanism behind framework batching.

nodes.label: Callback
nodes.rationale: A function passed as an argument and invoked by the outer function. You write it; the caller decides when, how often, and with what arguments.

nodes.label: Synchronous vs asynchronous callbacks
nodes.rationale: Syntax is identical. map/forEach/sort are sync; setTimeout/then are not. Only the callee's documentation answers timing.

nodes.label: Error-first callback convention
nodes.rationale: An async callback cannot throw — the stack is gone — so the error travels as data in position zero. On success the first argument is null, not omitted.

nodes.label: Missing return after if (err)
nodes.rationale: Unlike catch, an if does not end the block. Fall-through starts the success path with undefined and points the stack trace at the wrong function.

nodes.label: Inversion of control (callbacks)
nodes.rationale: The rest of your program is a function in a third party's hands. Failures — too early, too late, never, twice, wrong args, swallowed — are all silent.

nodes.label: once() wrapper
nodes.rationale: A called flag that ignores a second invocation. Exactly what a promise provides structurally — it settles once.

nodes.label: MDN promise guarantees
nodes.rationale: Never invoked before the current event-loop run ends; invoked even if attached after settling; multiple then handlers in insertion order. Promises fixed the contract, not the indentation.

nodes.label: Callback hell / pyramid of doom
nodes.rationale: Forced because a callback API returns nothing to sequence on. Real cost is per-level if (err) return, not indentation.

nodes.label: Named functions do not fix callback hell
nodes.rationale: Flattens indentation, hides sequence, loses closures, keeps per-level error branches, and leaves every trust problem in place.

nodes.label: Promise for one result, callback for many
nodes.rationale: Use a promise for one result later; a callback for a function to run or many results over time. Promises are one-shot.

nodes.label: Promise
nodes.rationale: An object representing eventual completion or failure. You attach callbacks to a returned object instead of passing them into a function.

nodes.label: Promise three states
nodes.rationale: pending, fulfilled, rejected. Settled means fulfilled or rejected. Transition happens at most once and is irreversible.

nodes.label: Resolved vs fulfilled
nodes.rationale: Resolved is the decision, not the outcome — settled or locked onto another promise. resolve(inner) can leave the outer pending. The executor parameter is named resolve, not fulfill.

nodes.label: Thenable
nodes.rationale: Any object with a callable then. Promise.resolve and await assimilate thenables. A data field named then is accidentally adopted.

nodes.label: Promise state is not readable
nodes.rationale: No promise.state or promise.value. A synchronous isSettled() would reintroduce Zalgo. The only read is attaching a handler.

nodes.label: then always runs asynchronously
nodes.rationale: Even on an already-settled promise the handler is a microtask. The returned promise is always pending when returned.

nodes.label: Identity and thrower default handlers
nodes.rationale: Missing onFulfilled is (x) => x; missing onRejected is (x) => { throw x; }. Error propagation is the default thrower firing per link.

nodes.label: catch is then(undefined, onRejected)
nodes.rationale: No separate error channel. A rejection is the second argument's turn. catch internally calls then.

nodes.label: catch restores the chain
nodes.rationale: A catch that returns normally fulfils, so later then handlers run. Re-throw to keep failing. A log-only catch swallows the error as undefined.

nodes.label: finally transparency
nodes.rationale: onFinally receives no argument; a return is ignored and the original outcome passes through. A throw or rejected return replaces the outcome, destroying the original error.

nodes.label: Promise adoption
nodes.rationale: Return a value and it is wrapped; return a promise or thenable and it is adopted, never nested. Lets a handler switch between sync and async without callers changing.

nodes.label: Forgotten return / floating promise
nodes.rationale: A handler that returns nothing fulfils immediately with undefined. The inner promise floats: sequencing breaks and its rejection becomes unhandled.

nodes.label: then returns a new promise
nodes.rationale: Each link represents the previous step and the handler. Combined with adoption, that is why a chain is flat where a callback pyramid was not.

nodes.label: A promise chain is sequential
nodes.rationale: Each link waits for the previous to settle. Chaining independent fetches is an accidental waterfall; Promise.all is the composition tool.

nodes.label: reduce sequential composition
nodes.rationale: [f1,f2,f3].reduce((p, f) => p.then(f), Promise.resolve()). Seed is an already-fulfilled promise; pass functions by reference.

nodes.label: Chain error propagation modeled after try
nodes.rationale: Promises catch all errors, even thrown exceptions and programming errors. A TypeError in a handler lands in the same catch as a network failure.

nodes.label: then(f, g) is not then(f).catch(g)
nodes.rationale: Two-argument then handles only upstream rejections. A throw inside f rejects the next promise. Trailing catch handles both.

nodes.label: Nesting to scope a catch
nodes.rationale: A nested catch only swallows failures in its scope. Flat mid-chain catch would swallow critical errors too. Nesting is a scoping tool, not a style.

nodes.label: finally is a link, not a clause
nodes.rationale: It runs when the promise it attaches to settles, not at the end of the chain. Transparency means it does not mark a rejection handled.

nodes.label: Promise executor runs synchronously
nodes.rationale: new Promise(fn) calls fn immediately on the current stack. Wrapping slow work in a promise does not make it non-blocking.

nodes.label: Every chain link costs a microtask
nodes.rationale: A three-link chain over an already-resolved promise takes three ticks. A long chain of sync handlers freezes the frame the way a loop does.

nodes.label: async function always returns a promise
nodes.rationale: No path out is not a promise. return wraps or adopts; throw becomes a rejection.

nodes.label: async function never throws synchronously
nodes.rationale: try { asyncFn() } without await catches nothing. Synchronous argument checks must live in a non-async wrapper.

nodes.label: return p vs Promise.resolve(p) identity
nodes.rationale: Promise.resolve(p) returns the same native promise; an async function must create its own. Breaks caches keyed by promise reference.

nodes.label: async/await desugars to a promise chain
nodes.rationale: await 1 becomes Promise.resolve(1).then(() => undefined). Non-promises are wrapped; code after await is a continuation.

nodes.label: async/await like generators plus promises
nodes.rationale: The function suspends and resumes; the awaited promise decides when. Gain is real try/catch, ordinary loops, and locals instead of threaded handler arguments.

nodes.label: Async body is synchronous until the first await
nodes.rationale: An async function is not asynchronous until it reaches an await. Top-level code, up to and including the first await, runs synchronously on the caller's stack.

nodes.label: await evaluates its expression immediately
nodes.rationale: The expression runs now; only the waiting is deferred. That is why starting work before awaiting it turns a waterfall into parallel work.

nodes.label: await suspends and returns control to the caller
nodes.rationale: After the expression is evaluated, the rest of the body is registered as a continuation and control exits the function.

nodes.label: await always costs at least one tick
nodes.rationale: Even when the promise is already fulfilled, execution still pauses until the next tick. There is no fast path.

nodes.label: await continuation is a microtask
nodes.rationale: An await loop never yields to rendering, because rendering happens between tasks.

nodes.label: await converts non-promises via Promise.resolve
nodes.rationale: The value comes back unchanged, so await is safe on a value that may or may not be a promise — but it is converted, not skipped, which is why the tick is spent either way.

nodes.label: Thenables are assimilated by await
nodes.rationale: await cares about the shape, not the class. An object with an unrelated then field gets assimilated rather than returned.

nodes.label: Top-level await
nodes.rationale: A module that awaits at the top level delays evaluation of every module that imports it. Not available in CommonJS because require is synchronous.

nodes.label: await-split pieces share one scope
nodes.rationale: user is an ordinary const visible to every later line, where a chain would have to thread it through handler arguments.

nodes.label: Three-pass ordering method
nodes.rationale: Walk the synchronous path, drain the microtask queue, then run one task. The interview question is always an ordering question.

nodes.label: Each await re-queues at the back of the microtask queue
nodes.rationale: A function with two awaits does not resume all at once — it rejoins the back of the queue at each one, which is why interleaving with other microtasks is possible.

nodes.label: await suspends the function, not the thread
nodes.rationale: await cannot rescue a synchronous hot loop. Once the continuation resumes, it runs to completion like any other job.

nodes.label: Two async functions interleave
nodes.rationale: Both run synchronously to their first await, then resume in queue order. Concurrency without parallelism: one thread, two suspended functions taking turns.

nodes.label: await in a for loop is sequential
nodes.rationale: Each iteration suspends until its request settles. The loop is the correct shape when each step depends on the previous one, and the wrong shape when the steps are independent.

nodes.label: await inside forEach does nothing
nodes.rationale: forEach discards the callback's return value, so the promises are never awaited and their rejections float free.

nodes.label: async/await is syntax over chaining with shared scope
nodes.rationale: Syntax over the machinery of chaining, with one thing genuinely added: the pieces share a scope.

nodes.label: An async function never throws synchronously
nodes.rationale: A throw becomes a rejection, so a bare try/catch around the call catches nothing.

nodes.label: Waterfalls are a choice, not a consequence
nodes.rationale: await evaluates its expression immediately and defers only the code that depends on it.

nodes.label: Engine versus host
nodes.rationale: V8/SpiderMonkey/JSC execute the language; window, document and process come from the host, not from JavaScript.

nodes.label: Phase 2 — Operators, expressions and control flow
Phase 7 — Asynchronous JavaScript
nodes.rationale: If you only ever finish one phase to Master depth, finish that one — it is what every interview probes and what every production incident traces back to.

nodes.label: Phase 8 — Modules, errors, memory and the toolchain
Phase 11 — Network, storage and data transfer
fetch does not reject on 404 or 500
Phase 13 — Complexity and JavaScript's real costs
Phase 14 — Core data structures in JavaScript
Phase 16 — Dynamic programming and the harder set
Phase 17 — Machine coding: implement it yourself
nodes.rationale: The brief's custom functions requirement: writing map, bind, debounce, Promise.all and an LRU from an empty file.

nodes.label: Phase 18 — Building the store front end
nodes.rationale: Framework-free on purpose. When React's version breaks at 2 a.m., you know what it was doing.

nodes.label: URL as the single source of truth
Search box three bugs
nodes.rationale: Debounce the input, abort the in-flight request, and discard out-of-order responses.

nodes.label: Cart as a state machine
nodes.rationale: Immutable updates, derived totals; the total is computed rather than stored.

nodes.label: Idempotency from the client
nodes.rationale: Disabling the button is not a fix for a double-submitted checkout.

nodes.label: Node.js 24 Active LTS
nodes.rationale: Build on Node 24 LTS in production; Node 26 to learn what's next. Maintained through 30 Apr 2028.

nodes.label: v27 one major per year, every release LTS
nodes.rationale: The odd/even unstable vs stable rule ends with v27. October 2026 is when the v27 alpha opens, not when v27 ships.

nodes.label: Do not skip Phase 0
nodes.rationale: Every Node is weird complaint traces back to skipping the runtime model.

nodes.label: Do not start Express before Phase 5
nodes.rationale: Express is a thin layer over node:http. Learning it first means learning the abstraction without the thing it abstracts.

nodes.label: Node.js is a runtime, not a language
nodes.rationale: A program that runs JavaScript outside the browser and gives it access to your computer. Same language. Different powers.

nodes.label: V8
nodes.rationale: V8 is the brain: parses, compiles and garbage-collects JavaScript and only does one thing at a time.

nodes.label: libuv
nodes.rationale: libuv is the hands: the event loop and the ability to wait for files and sockets without freezing.

nodes.label: The event loop is the program
nodes.rationale: Your file is the setup for the program. The process does not exit when the file ends; the loop keeps running as long as work is pending.

nodes.label: process.versions
nodes.rationale: Proof that Node is a bundle of C libraries — V8, libuv, OpenSSL — not one thing.

nodes.label: One thread, and never let it wait
nodes.rationale: Cheap concurrency for I/O-heavy work, paid for with a hard rule: never make that one thread do anything slow.

nodes.label: One callback at a time, no locks
nodes.rationale: Two functions can never execute simultaneously. The guarantee stops at every await.

nodes.label: Read-modify-write race across await
nodes.rationale: The function yields at await; a second request can run the same code and both write back a value computed from the same stale read.

nodes.label: Network I/O uses no extra threads
nodes.rationale: Sockets are handled by epoll/kqueue/IOCP. The libuv pool is for filesystem, dns.lookup, parts of crypto, and zlib.

nodes.label: Sequential await waterfall
nodes.rationale: Three 300ms queries sequential ~902ms, Promise.all ~301ms. Sequential await in a loop is the single most common performance bug in Node code.

nodes.label: One slow function slows every request
nodes.rationale: The users who suffer are not the ones who called the slow endpoint. They are everyone else.

nodes.label: monitorEventLoopDelay
nodes.rationale: Values are in nanoseconds. Healthy web process: mean delay under a few milliseconds, p99 under ~50ms.

nodes.label: Sync suffix in a request path is a bug
nodes.rationale: Sync is fine at startup — reading a config file before the server listens blocks nothing.

nodes.label: Four fixes for a blocked loop
nodes.rationale: Use the async version; chunk and yield with setImmediate; move to worker_threads; queue it and return 202.

nodes.label: Wrapping blocking code in async does not unblock it
nodes.rationale: async only changes how the function returns a value. Unless you await something that genuinely yields, the code still runs to completion on the main thread.

nodes.label: Four spare threads to block on your behalf
nodes.rationale: Portable filesystem calls block, so libuv hands the call to a worker thread and posts the result back. Network I/O uses no threads.

nodes.label: UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE
nodes.rationale: Default 4, max 1024. Created lazily on first use; size is fixed from then on. Set it in the environment before the process starts.

nodes.label: dns.lookup uses the thread pool
nodes.rationale: Every outbound fetch, http.request and database connection resolves through dns.lookup by default, so a burst of HTTP can make unrelated fs reads slow.

nodes.label: dns.resolve does not use the thread pool
nodes.rationale: resolve4 talks to a DNS server directly and ignores /etc/hosts. The usual fix for pool pressure is a DNS cache in front of lookup, not swapping to resolve.

nodes.label: Thread pool versus worker_threads
nodes.rationale: The pool is internal and runs C/C++ only. worker_threads each run their own V8 isolate and JavaScript.

nodes.label: Same language, different host
nodes.rationale: The browser supplies the DOM and a strict sandbox; Node supplies filesystem, sockets, processes and no sandbox at all.

nodes.label: CORS is a browser policy
nodes.rationale: Node has no origin and no cookies to protect, so it never enforces CORS. A successful Node request proves nothing about whether the browser will be allowed to read it.

nodes.label: fetch relative URL throws in Node
setTimeout returns a Timeout object in Node
process.env values are always strings
nodes.rationale: DEBUG=false is the truthy string 'false'. Convert at the edge, once, and validate at startup.

nodes.label: process.exit versus process.exitCode
nodes.rationale: process.exit is immediate and abandons pending work. Set exitCode and let the event loop drain.

nodes.label: SIGTERM graceful shutdown
nodes.rationale: SIGTERM is what Docker and Kubernetes send before they kill you. Without a handler, in-flight requests are dropped on every deploy.

nodes.label: __dirname versus process.cwd
nodes.rationale: Relative paths resolve against the current working directory, not the file that contains them. Use __dirname or import.meta.dirname for files that ship with the code.

nodes.label: Run the Active LTS in production
nodes.rationale: The rule is whatever is Active LTS, not whatever is newest. Feature set is frozen and it receives backported fixes for 30 months from release.

nodes.label: Odd/even LTS rule ends at v27
Pin the version in the repo
nodes.rationale: .nvmrc, engines, a pinned Dockerfile tag, and CI reading the same file. Anything relying on a person remembering will drift.

nodes.label: Node flags must come before the script name
nodes.rationale: A misplaced flag is silently ignored rather than rejected. Confirm with process.execArgv.

nodes.label: --env-file
nodes.rationale: A variable already in the environment wins. No variable expansion. A missing file is a hard error unless --env-file-if-exists is used.

nodes.label: NODE_OPTIONS
nodes.rationale: Flags that decide what to run (--eval, --print, --test, --env-file) are rejected so an inherited variable cannot hijack every Node process.

nodes.label: Build on Node for production fullstack work
nodes.rationale: Not because it is the fastest, but because compatibility gaps are the expensive kind of problem and most apps are bound by the database anyway.

nodes.label: Deno permission model
nodes.rationale: No file, network or env access unless granted. Deno 2 added npm, package.json and node_modules while keeping the sandbox.

nodes.label: Bun on JavaScriptCore
nodes.rationale: Startup difference is real and matters for serverless and CLI. Throughput usually does not, because the bottleneck is almost never the runtime.

nodes.label: Bun as a development tool on a Node deploy
Deoptimization
nodes.rationale: A function that keeps flipping between optimised and interpreter — a deopt loop — can be slower than one that was never optimised.

nodes.label: Hidden classes
nodes.rationale: Give objects all their properties at construction and do not delete properties from hot objects. Do not restructure for shape stability until a profiler points here.

nodes.label: V8 micro-optimisation is last
nodes.rationale: For a typical Node web service the ranking is database, network, blocking the loop, serialisation, algorithms, then V8.

nodes.label: --max-old-space-size
nodes.rationale: Raise it when you have proven a legitimately large working set — not to postpone a memory leak.

nodes.label: Phase 0 gate
nodes.rationale: Explain why a 3-second for loop stalls every incoming request but a 3-second database query does not, and name three ways to fix the first one.

nodes.label: Named versus default exports
nodes.rationale: The default export is just a named export whose name happens to be default. Prefer named exports so grep and refactors work.

nodes.label: ESM import extension is required
nodes.rationale: ESM does not guess .js or /index.js. That is what makes resolution fast and cacheable.

nodes.label: Imports are hoisted and run first
ESM live read-only bindings
nodes.rationale: An import is a view onto the exporting module's variable, not a copy. CommonJS destructure copies the number once and never sees the update.

nodes.label: ESM top-level await
nodes.rationale: Every importer waits for it, transitively, and the module cannot be require()d from CommonJS (ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE).

nodes.label: Dynamic import()
nodes.rationale: Returns a promise for the module namespace. The module is still evaluated once no matter how many times you import it.

nodes.label: CommonJS
nodes.rationale: Node's original module system: synchronous, dynamic, and cached by resolved path. Not deprecated; most of npm is still published this way.

nodes.label: CommonJS module wrapper
nodes.rationale: Node wraps every CJS file in a function(exports, require, module, __filename, __dirname). Those five names are parameters, not globals, which is why they do not exist in ESM.

nodes.label: module.exports vs exports
nodes.rationale: exports starts as a second name for the same object as module.exports. Only module.exports is what require returns.

nodes.label: Never assign to bare exports
nodes.rationale: exports = {…} rebinds the local parameter and exports {}. Use module.exports everywhere.

nodes.label: require.cache
nodes.rationale: A module body runs once per resolved path per process. Later requires return the same object. Core modules are not in require.cache.

nodes.label: CommonJS module singleton
nodes.rationale: Module-scope state is process-wide. That is how you get one connection pool, and how one test leaks state into the next.

nodes.label: require is synchronous
nodes.rationale: require reads and compiles on the main thread, blocking the event loop. Fine at startup; a latency spike inside a request handler. Also why CJS cannot load ESM with top-level await.

nodes.label: CommonJS has no live bindings
nodes.rationale: require returns an object; destructuring copies values at that moment. Export a function or getter, or read through the module object.

nodes.label: node: prefix
nodes.rationale: Marks a specifier as a built-in. Node returns it immediately — no node_modules walk, no filesystem probing.

nodes.label: Prefix-only built-ins
nodes.rationale: On Node 24 four built-ins exist only as node:sea, node:sqlite, node:test, node:test/reporters. Bare names fall through to npm packages.

nodes.label: Core modules resolve before node_modules
nodes.rationale: A package named path or fs cannot hijack require('path') or require('fs'). Core wins already in both CJS and ESM.

nodes.label: module.builtinModules
nodes.rationale: Array of every built-in name. Node 24 has 72 built-ins; four names start with node:.

nodes.label: Prefixed imports as bundler signal
nodes.rationale: Bundlers and edge runtimes use the prefix to tell a Node built-in from a package, producing better errors when node:fs does not exist.

nodes.label: CJS ↔ ESM interop
nodes.rationale: Both directions work on Node 24. require(esm) shed its experimental label in v24.15.0. One hard boundary remains: top-level await.

nodes.label: cjs-module-lexer named exports
nodes.rationale: Node statically analyses CJS source to synthesise named exports. Computed keys, loops, and conditionals are invisible. Default-import and destructure.

nodes.label: require() of an ES module
nodes.rationale: Returns the module namespace object, not the default export. A default is at .default. Unflagged in v23.0.0 / v22.12.0 / v20.19.0.

nodes.label: __esModule marker
nodes.rationale: Node sets __esModule: true on the namespace from require(esm) so interop code can distinguish it from a plain CJS export object.

nodes.label: ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE
nodes.rationale: require cannot load an ESM graph that contains top-level await anywhere in the subtree. Use await import() or --experimental-print-required-tla.

nodes.label: createRequire
nodes.rationale: Build a working require inside ESM via createRequire(import.meta.url). Escape hatch that reintroduces synchronous loading.

nodes.label: JSON import attribute
nodes.rationale: import data from './x.json' with { type: 'json' }. Mandatory security requirement; the old assert spelling is gone.

nodes.label: Dual package hazard
nodes.rationale: Separate CJS and ESM builds can both load in one process. Module-scope state then exists twice.

nodes.label: Module resolution
nodes.rationale: How a string in an import becomes a file on disk. Node decides from specifier shape before anything else.

nodes.label: Three kinds of specifier
nodes.rationale: Built-in (node:fs/fs), relative/absolute path, or bare package name. Only bare specifiers search node_modules.

nodes.label: node_modules walk
nodes.rationale: For a bare specifier Node looks in node_modules in the importing file's directory, then parents to the filesystem root. First match wins.

nodes.label: Hoisting makes undeclared dependencies work
nodes.rationale: npm flattens the tree so a transitive lodash sits in root node_modules. It breaks the day that dependency drops it.

nodes.label: CJS vs ESM resolution
nodes.rationale: CommonJS probes .js/.json/.node and directory index.js. ESM resolves the exact URL and fails with ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND or ERR_UNSUPPORTED_DIR_IMPORT.

nodes.label: Nearest package.json type field
nodes.rationale: Resolution finds the file; the nearest package.json decides how to parse it. .mjs is always ESM, .cjs always CommonJS.

nodes.label: MODULE_TYPELESS_PACKAGE_JSON
nodes.rationale: Since v22.7.0 / v20.19.0 a typeless .js that fails as CommonJS is reparsed as ESM, with a warning about the cost.

nodes.label: require.resolve
nodes.rationale: Runs the resolution algorithm and returns the filename without loading the module.

nodes.label: Circular dependencies
nodes.rationale: A requires B, B requires A. Neither module system hangs. Neither outcome is one you want to design around.

nodes.label: CommonJS partial exports object
nodes.rationale: When B requires A while A is still executing, the cache holds whatever A has assigned so far. Behaviour depends on statement order.

nodes.label: ESM cycle temporal dead zone
nodes.rationale: ESM links bindings before evaluating. Reading a const export during the cycle throws ReferenceError. A crash at startup beats a silent undefined.

nodes.label: Function declarations survive cycles
nodes.rationale: Function declarations are hoisted at link time. A cycle can sit for years and break the day someone converts a function to a const arrow.

nodes.label: Extract the shared piece
nodes.rationale: Two modules that each need the other are usually one concept that got split. Extract, invert the dependency, or only then defer with await import().

nodes.label: package.json essentials
nodes.rationale: The file that decides how code is parsed, what ships, and what runs. Six fields carry almost all of it.

nodes.label: package.json type field
nodes.rationale: Decides how every .js file in the package is parsed. Set it explicitly; module for new work.

nodes.label: main vs exports
nodes.rationale: main is the old single entry point. exports takes precedence wherever both exist.

nodes.label: files allowlist
nodes.rationale: Without it npm publishes everything except a small default-ignored set. README, LICENSE and package.json always ship; node_modules never does.

nodes.label: engines as a floor
nodes.rationale: A declaration, not enforcement, unless engine-strict=true. State a floor, not a ceiling.

nodes.label: Avoid postinstall scripts
nodes.rationale: pre/post hooks run implicitly. postinstall executes on every npm install of your package — a supply-chain concern.

nodes.label: dependencies vs devDependencies vs peerDependencies
nodes.rationale: Runtime vs build/test vs host-supplied. Production installs with --omit=dev skip devDependencies.

nodes.label: node --run
nodes.rationale: Runs package.json scripts without the npm process. No pre/post scripts, no .npmrc resolution.

nodes.label: exports map
nodes.rationale: Defines the package public surface and makes everything else unreachable. Turns an open directory into a declared interface.

nodes.label: Subpath exports
nodes.rationale: Left side is the public name, right side is the file. Once exports exists the only valid specifiers are listed keys, including the real path.

nodes.label: ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED
nodes.rationale: Thrown for any path not listed. Adding an exports map is a major version if consumers were deep-importing.

nodes.label: Conditional exports
nodes.rationale: Node picks the first matching condition in written order. types must be first; default must be last.

nodes.label: Dual package hazard
nodes.rationale: Shipping both CJS and ESM builds means an app can load both. Caches, registries and instanceof disagree. Ship ESM only or keep state out of module scope.

nodes.label: Subpath imports (#internal)
nodes.rationale: Private aliases inside the package. Keys must start with #. Node resolves them natively with no build step, and they accept conditions.

nodes.label: Semantic versioning
nodes.rationale: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH records the maintainer's intent, not a guarantee. A patch that fixes a bug your code depended on is still a break for you.

nodes.label: Caret vs tilde ranges
nodes.rationale: ^1.2.3 allows <2.0.0; ~1.2.3 allows <1.3.0. For 0.x, ^ tightens to patch-level because the minor slot carries breaking changes.

nodes.label: package-lock.json
nodes.rationale: Records exact version, resolved URL and integrity hash for every package. package.json ranges do not describe what you are running.

nodes.label: Lockfile integrity hash
nodes.rationale: Makes the install verifiable, not just reproducible. A tampered tarball fails even if the version number matches.

nodes.label: npm ci
nodes.rationale: Installs the lockfile exactly, never writes it, deletes node_modules first, and fails if package.json and the lockfile disagree. Use in CI, Docker, production.

nodes.label: Commit the lockfile
