nodes.rationale: 256 kB against a plain view's 0 bytes. Needs its own indexes. Not automatically faster if the view already pushes down.

nodes.label: REFRESH CONCURRENTLY unique index
nodes.rationale: CONCURRENTLY diffs old against new and needs a key. Without a unique index it raises 55000. 1.6× slower than plain REFRESH.

nodes.label: Plain REFRESH AccessExclusiveLock
nodes.rationale: Readers waited 32 ms of a 142 ms plain REFRESH. CONCURRENTLY waited 2 ms. No incremental refresh exists.

nodes.label: Matview staleness is yours to manage
nodes.rationale: Nothing refreshes it. Prefer a scheduled refresh. A trigger-driven full recompute inside a write is almost always wrong.

nodes.label: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW WITH NO DATA
nodes.rationale: Querying before populate raises 55000. Check pg_class.relispopulated in a health check.

nodes.label: LANGUAGE sql inlining vs plpgsql black box
nodes.rationale: sql inlines and sees real statistics (60 rows). plpgsql is a Function Scan with a fixed 1000-row guess that wrecks joins.

nodes.label: Function volatility IMMUTABLE STABLE VOLATILE
nodes.rationale: VOLATILE is the default and blocks inlining even for LANGUAGE sql. Lying about IMMUTABLE gives wrong answers, not errors. Index expressions need IMMUTABLE (42P17).

nodes.label: Trigger functions must be plpgsql
nodes.rationale: NEW, OLD, RETURN NEW/NULL, TG_OP/TG_NAME/TG_LEVEL are the vocabulary. The honest list for plpgsql is trigger bodies plus rare data-heavy loops.

nodes.label: RAISE EXCEPTION USING ERRCODE
nodes.rationale: Without an explicit SQLSTATE everything is P0001. Use 23xxx integrity codes so the app maps them like constraint violations.

nodes.label: pg_notify from a trigger
nodes.rationale: AFTER trigger so the announced row exists. PERFORM rather than SELECT. Row-level 500 inserts → 500 notifications; statement-level → 1.

nodes.label: NOTIFY identifier vs pg_notify string
nodes.rationale: NOTIFY folds unquoted names; pg_notify uses the string exactly and can compute a channel. Prefer pg_notify from application or trigger code.

nodes.label: 8 GB notification queue
nodes.rationale: A stuck listener is database-wide: the queue cannot truncate past it and NOTIFY errors for everyone. Monitor pg_notification_queue_usage().

nodes.label: LISTEN/NOTIFY is at-most-once
nodes.rationale: A notification sent while nobody is listening is discarded. Fine as a hint; unacceptable for exactly-once. Combine with an outbox.

nodes.label: RANGE LIST HASH partitioning
nodes.rationale: RANGE for time series, LIST for tenant/region/status, HASH to spread writes. Parent holds no rows.

nodes.label: Partition pruning
nodes.rationale: With the key in WHERE: 15.6 ms one partition. Without: 32.9 ms Parallel Append of all five — about 2× not 5×. An index would have done more.

nodes.label: DETACH and DROP partition for retention
nodes.rationale: DETACH 5 ms, DROP 103353 rows in 10 ms. The real payoff is cheap bulk deletion, not query speed.

nodes.label: DEFAULT partition safety net
nodes.rationale: No matching range without DEFAULT raises 23514. Attaching a new range that overlaps the default scans it under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE.

nodes.label: Partition key must be in every unique constraint
nodes.rationale: PRIMARY KEY (id) is rejected. No global index across partitions. A partition-key UPDATE is DELETE + INSERT and cannot be HOT.

nodes.label: Procedure can COMMIT mid-body
nodes.rationale: The same COMMIT inside a FUNCTION raises 2D000. A function runs inside the caller's transaction and may not end it.

nodes.label: CALL vs SELECT for procedures
nodes.rationale: SELECT a procedure raises 42809. Procedures return no rows and cannot appear in a query.

nodes.label: Procedure transaction control only when outermost
nodes.rationale: CALL inside an explicit BEGIN raises 2D000. Inside an application withTransaction wrapper a procedure behaves like a function.

nodes.label: Foreign data wrappers — postgres_fdw and dblink
postgres_fdw foreign table
nodes.rationale: Looks like a table and is a query against another server. User mapping holds a password in the catalog.

nodes.label: FDW Remote SQL pushdown
nodes.rationale: Full pushdown 2.9 ms vs 41.9 ms with a VOLATILE predicate (14×). EXPLAIN VERBOSE Remote SQL is the only tool that matters.

nodes.label: FDW has no two-phase commit
nodes.rationale: Local commit can succeed while the remote fails. Treat FDW as a read tool, not a write path.

nodes.label: dblink autonomous query
nodes.rationale: No foreign tables, no pushdown. Still useful for a query on another database that is not part of your transaction.

nodes.label: IMPORT FOREIGN SCHEMA
nodes.rationale: Snapshot of remote definitions. Does not track later schema changes; re-import after remote migrations.

nodes.label: pgvector is not in the stock image
nodes.rationale: Absent from postgres:18-alpine, not merely uninstalled. Needs pgvector/pgvector:pg18 or a provider that ships it.

nodes.label: vector distance operators
nodes.rationale: <-> L2, <=> cosine, <#> negative inner product. All are distances so ORDER BY ASC is nearest-first. Dimension mismatches raise 22000.

nodes.label: HNSW approximate index
nodes.rationale: 50000 384-dim vectors: exact 88 ms → HNSW 2.1 ms (42×). Build 22.9 s, index 98 MB vs 78 MB table. Results are approximate.

nodes.label: ef_search recall knob
nodes.rationale: On well-separated clusters recall was 10/10 at every setting; raising ef_search only added latency 1.2→4.5 ms. Measure recall on your vectors.

nodes.label: HNSW 2000-dimension cap
nodes.rationale: vector column holds up to 16000 dimensions; HNSW indexes cap at 2000 (54000 at 2001). halfvec indexes up to 4000.

nodes.label: Dual write bug
nodes.rationale: No transaction spans database and queue. Measured: order committed, enqueue failed, jobs = 0. Reversing order just moves the failure.

nodes.label: Outbox table in the same transaction
nodes.rationale: Business row and event row commit or neither does. Partial index on published_at IS NULL keeps the relay query small.

nodes.label: SKIP LOCKED relay claim
nodes.rationale: Three workers, 20 rows: 20 unique claims, 94 ms. Without SKIP LOCKED: 189 ms serialised behind one row.

nodes.label: Outbox is at-least-once
nodes.rationale: Relay can publish then crash before setting published_at. Exactly-once effect needs an idempotent consumer.

nodes.label: Idempotent consumer ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
nodes.rationale: Unique idempotency key; rowCount 0 means already handled. Naive job sent 2 emails, idempotent sent 1.

nodes.label: AFTER row audit trigger
nodes.rationale: Attached to the table so migrations, psql and other services cannot bypass it. to_jsonb(OLD/NEW) survives schema changes. Cost ~1.24×.

nodes.label: WHEN OLD IS DISTINCT FROM NEW
nodes.rationale: <> is NULL when either side is NULL so NULL→value would not audit. WHEN is cheaper (0.86×) because the body never runs.

nodes.label: SET LOCAL app.user_id
nodes.rationale: current_setting(..., true) returns NULL if unset (avoids 42704). Plain SET behind a pooler lands on another backend.

nodes.label: Phase 12 gate columns vs jsonb and FTS
tsvector tsquery and @@
nodes.rationale: Documents become tsvector; queries become tsquery; @@ matches them. Most apps never need a separate search server.

nodes.label: The app role should not own the schema
Two connection strings owner vs app
nodes.rationale: Migrations connect as owner; the service must not be able to read MIGRATION_DATABASE_URL. Two variables in one .env is the pattern without the protection.

nodes.label: DDL is an ownership right
nodes.rationale: No GRANT DROP or GRANT ALTER. App role with DML still gets 42501 on DROP TABLE. Does not protect rows; TRUNCATE is grantable and should be withheld.

nodes.label: GRANT USAGE not CREATE on schema
nodes.rationale: CREATE is grantable; objects the app creates are then owned by the app and the boundary erodes.

nodes.label: ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE owner
nodes.rationale: Stops a manual grant on every new table. A hand-created table with a different owner never receives those defaults.

nodes.label: First matching pg_hba rule wins
nodes.rationale: No fall-through. If that method fails the connection fails. Reversing reject and scram inverted the outcome.

nodes.label: pg_hba_file_rules parsed view
nodes.rationale: Resolves includes and numbers rules. error column names a bad line. Reload keeps old rules; restart with a syntax error takes the server down.

nodes.label: pg_hba auth methods
nodes.rationale: scram-sha-256 is the correct password method. trust authenticates any password. md5 rule can use a SCRAM-stored password; a scram rule cannot use an md5-stored one.

nodes.label: Non-existent role same as wrong password
nodes.rationale: Prevents role enumeration. Check pg_roles yourself; the error will never say the role is misspelled.

nodes.label: Six libpq sslmodes
nodes.rationale: prefer is the default and silently falls back to plaintext. allow tries plaintext first. require encrypts but verifies nothing.

nodes.label: verify-full hostname check
nodes.rationale: verify-ca accepted CN=devbible-pg-hba while connecting to 127.0.0.1; verify-full rejected it. Production should use verify-full.

nodes.label: hostssl hostnossl enforce TLS on the server
nodes.rationale: Client sslmode is the client's choice. hostnossl reject plus hostssl scram is the only version of require-TLS that survives a misconfigured service.

nodes.label: pg rejectUnauthorized false is require
nodes.rationale: ssl: true is not verify-full. Pass the CA explicitly with rejectUnauthorized: true. Check pg_stat_ssl per connection.

nodes.label: Logical vs physical replication
nodes.rationale: Physical copies WAL bytes of the whole cluster, same major, read-only. Logical copies decoded row changes, per table, writable, cross-major.

nodes.label: PUBLICATION and SUBSCRIPTION
nodes.rationale: wal_level = logical requires a restart. Snapshot then stream in commit order. Schema must already exist on the subscriber.

nodes.label: What logical replication does not copy
nodes.rationale: DDL/schema, sequence data, large objects; only tables. TRUNCATE is replicated but fails if FKs point outside the subscription.

nodes.label: Replica identity
nodes.rationale: Without a PK or marked unique index, INSERTs replicate and the first UPDATE/DELETE fails. REPLICA IDENTITY FULL breaks for types like point/box.

nodes.label: Abandoned replication slot fills publisher disk
nodes.rationale: A slot whose subscriber is gone retains WAL forever. Alert on pg_replication_slots; set max_slot_wal_keep_size to sacrifice the subscriber.

nodes.label: Logical replication is not for HA
nodes.rationale: Schema, sequences and replica identity are all manual. Every one of those is a step that will not have been done at 4am failover.

nodes.label: Minor vs major upgrade
nodes.rationale: 18.3→18.4 is binaries plus restart. 17→18 changes on-disk format. Minor upgrades carry security fixes and should be applied promptly.

nodes.label: pg_upgrade catalog migration
nodes.rationale: --check works with the old server running. Install new extension .so files but do not CREATE EXTENSION on the new cluster.

nodes.label: pg_upgrade --link and --swap destroy rollback
nodes.rationale: --link makes the old cluster unusable once the new one starts. --swap destructively modifies the old cluster once transfer begins. Verified backup is a precondition.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL 18 transfers most optimizer statistics
nodes.rationale: Pre-18 transferred none. CREATE STATISTICS objects still do not transfer. Keep vacuumdb --analyze-in-stages in the runbook.

nodes.label: Logical-replication upgrade cutover
nodes.rationale: Near-zero downtime across majors. Advance sequences as an explicit cutover step or the first insert raises 23505.

nodes.label: An untested backup is a belief
nodes.rationale: Having backups, being able to restore, and being able to restore in time under pressure are three different claims. Only rehearsal establishes the third.

nodes.label: Measured RTO from a drill
nodes.rationale: Logical restore measured at 4× dump time. -j 4 bought nothing when one table held 97% of the data. If RTO exceeds the business assumption, that is the finding.

nodes.label: Most likely disaster is a bad write
nodes.rationale: Replicas faithfully replicate a bad DELETE. Only PITR with a long enough retention window helps. Retention is chosen against how long a bug might go unnoticed.

nodes.label: Disaster runbook outside the system
nodes.rationale: Exact commands, who decides, credentials, verification queries, endpoint change, measured timings. Someone who did not write it must be able to follow it.

nodes.label: Phase 13 complete 18 of 18
nodes.rationale: Topics 07–18 validated against official docs under the no-new-sandboxes rule. No page carries a console block that was not produced by a real run.

nodes.label: Least privilege model
nodes.rationale: A role is an identity, a privilege is a verb on one object, ownership outranks both, and effective privileges are the union over every inherited role.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL role
nodes.rationale: There is no user type. LOGIN is an attribute. CREATE USER is CREATE ROLE … LOGIN. A group is a role nobody logs in as.

nodes.label: pg_authid cluster-wide roles
nodes.rationale: Roles live in pg_authid and are shared by every database. A pg_dump contains grants but not roles unless pg_dumpall --roles-only ran first.

nodes.label: INHERIT and SET ROLE
nodes.rationale: INHERIT (default) activates group privileges automatically. NOINHERIT or WITH INHERIT FALSE leaves membership available until SET ROLE. SET ROLE is not SET SESSION AUTHORIZATION and leaks on a pooled connection until RESET ROLE or DISCARD ALL.

nodes.label: VALID UNTIL and CONNECTION LIMIT
nodes.rationale: Role attributes, not grants. CONNECTION LIMIT 1 yields 53300. Expired VALID UNTIL reports 28P01, identical to a wrong password, and only affects password auth.

nodes.label: SCRAM-SHA-256 verifier
nodes.rationale: Since PostgreSQL 14 the default store is a verifier in pg_authid.rolpassword, not the password. The exposure is CREATE ROLE … PASSWORD plaintext in logs and pg_stat_activity; \password computes the verifier client-side.

nodes.label: REASSIGN OWNED then DROP OWNED
nodes.rationale: DROP ROLE fails with 2BP01 while the role owns objects or holds grants. REASSIGN then DROP OWNED, in that order, in every database; reverse order drops the objects. DROP ROLE is cluster-wide.

nodes.label: Separate owner and app roles
nodes.rationale: Separate roles cost a bootstrap step and a second connection string for migrations. A leaked app credential is then bounded by a readable grant list instead of superuser.

nodes.label: Schema USAGE before table verbs
nodes.rationale: GRANT SELECT on a table is unreachable until USAGE on the schema passes. The error noun is the diagnosis: permission denied for schema vs for table.

nodes.label: TRUNCATE is not DELETE
nodes.rationale: DELETE is MVCC row removal; TRUNCATE takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE and discards the file. Withholding TRUNCATE from the app role turns an injected TRUNCATE into 42501.

nodes.label: MAINTAIN privilege
nodes.rationale: PostgreSQL 17+ delegates VACUUM, ANALYZE, REINDEX, CLUSTER and REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW without ownership. VACUUM without MAINTAIN returns OK and only warns, so nightly jobs can succeed while vacuuming nothing.

nodes.label: Identity vs serial sequence grant
nodes.rationale: An identity sequence is owned by the column so INSERT needs no USAGE on the sequence. A serial DEFAULT nextval() is an ordinary sequence call and needs GRANT USAGE ON SEQUENCE.

nodes.label: Column grants are additive
nodes.rationale: A column grant adds access; table-wide SELECT from any inherited role makes the column list irrelevant. SELECT * and predicates on ungranted columns fail; count(*) needs no column privilege.

nodes.label: UPDATE needs SELECT to read
nodes.rationale: UPDATE covers writing only. WHERE, RETURNING and SET x = x + 1 read columns and need SELECT. A write-only role cannot run a qualified update.

nodes.label: Ownership outranks privileges
nodes.rationale: REVOKE from the owner succeeds and is not a boundary: ownership carries the right to GRANT it back. There is no GRANT DROP; DDL is an ownership right.

nodes.label: EXECUTE to PUBLIC on new functions
nodes.rationale: proacl NULL means the built-in default, not no access. Combined with SECURITY DEFINER this is the classic privilege-escalation shape. There is no DENY; revoke from PUBLIC and re-grant.

nodes.label: View as a column boundary
nodes.rationale: Column grants only widen. A view exposes named columns and cannot be widened by an unrelated group membership.

nodes.label: GRANT ON ALL TABLES is a snapshot
nodes.rationale: It expands to the tables that exist at execution and stores one ACL each. A table created afterwards is 42501. You also need ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES for future objects.

nodes.label: ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES
nodes.rationale: Stores a rule applied when new objects are created; not retroactive. Keyed on the creating role (defaclrole). Omit FOR ROLE and a DBA records a rule for postgres, not the migration role.

nodes.label: relacl privilege string
nodes.rationale: grantee=privileges/grantor. rwadDxtm map to SELECT UPDATE INSERT DELETE TRUNCATE REFERENCES TRIGGER MAINTAIN. relacl NULL is the built-in default, not locked down. Empty grantee is PUBLIC.

nodes.label: public schema CREATE removed in PG15
nodes.rationale: PUBLIC now has USAGE only on public. Apps that created tables in public as a non-owner fail after upgrade with 42501. pg_database_owner resolves to whoever owns the current database.

nodes.label: has_*_privilege boot assertion
nodes.rationale: These functions resolve group membership and inheritance, which reading relacl does not. Assert the app can SELECT and cannot TRUNCATE, CREATE or be superuser, at boot.

nodes.label: Pool object connectionString leak
nodes.rationale: pool.options.password is undefined but connectionString still holds the credential. JSON.stringify and util.inspect reproduce it. pg error objects carry no password.

nodes.label: pg_stat_activity.query text
nodes.rationale: Any superuser or pg_read_all_stats member can read the running statement, including the last statement of an idle session. Bound parameters appear as $1 in the view.

nodes.label: log_statement logs bound parameters
nodes.rationale: Parameters stay out of statement text and pg_stat_activity but log_statement=all adds DETAIL: Parameters. log_parameter_max_length defaults to -1 (unlimited).

nodes.label: ALTER ROLE PASSWORD plaintext in the log
nodes.rationale: The database stores a SCRAM verifier while the logger writes the plaintext statement. Use \password or SET LOCAL log_statement=none around the change.

nodes.label: URL password encoding
nodes.rationale: / and # in a password throw ERR_INVALID_URL with *****REDACTED*****. @ : and space parse. encodeURIComponent or pass discrete host/user/password fields.

nodes.label: Safe connection identity readout
nodes.rationale: Log current_user, current_database(), inet_server_addr() and is_superuser instead of the connection string. is_superuser=on is an alert.

nodes.label: application_name
nodes.rationale: Empty by default. Set it on the pool so pg_stat_activity, pg_stat_statements and the server log attribute work to a service.

nodes.label: Short-lived credentials
nodes.rationale: A leak with a deadline beats storage choice. pg accepts a password function invoked per new connection for IAM tokens. VALID UNTIL revokes without a deploy.

nodes.label: Logical backup
nodes.rationale: SQL that recreates one database from a consistent snapshot. Portable and selective, and about four times slower to restore than to take.

nodes.label: Dump formats and what is in them
Custom dump format -Fc
nodes.rationale: Default choice: compressed, indexed, selective and parallel restore, one file. Same size as gzipped plain text; unlike -Fp the format cannot be changed after the dump.

nodes.label: pg_restore table of contents
nodes.rationale: pg_restore -l lists restorable items. TABLE vs TABLE DATA enables schema-only or data-only. SEQUENCE SET captures identity positions; skip them and the first insert duplicates keys.

nodes.label: Roles are not in pg_dump
nodes.rationale: The GRANT is dumped; CREATE ROLE is not. A complete logical backup is pg_dumpall --roles-only plus pg_dump. Also absent: tablespaces, other databases, postgresql.conf, pg_hba.conf, replication slots.

nodes.label: pg_dump version compatibility
nodes.rationale: pg_dump may be newer than the server, never older. Restoring into an older major is unsupported. Downgrading is a logical-replication job.

nodes.label: Restore costs far more than dump
nodes.rationale: Measured 2.55 s dump vs 10.29 s restore. Restore inserts rows, rebuilds every index, revalidates constraints and writes WAL.

nodes.label: pg_restore -j parallelises across items
nodes.rationale: One dominant table cannot be split. -j 4 was 10.06 s vs 10.29 s serial. Parallel dump requires -Fd; -Fc -j is a hard error.

nodes.label: pg_restore continues after errors
nodes.rationale: relation already exists is reported and the run keeps going. Use --exit-on-error in automation, --clean --if-exists to replace, or restore into a new database and rename.

nodes.label: Selective restore leaves indexes behind
nodes.rationale: pg_restore -t restores the table item, not separate index and constraint items. The table accepts duplicates with no error.

nodes.label: pg_dump REPEATABLE READ snapshot
nodes.rationale: 1000 rows inserted during the dump appeared in the source and zero in the restore. Parallel workers share the leader snapshot via pg_export_snapshot. The long transaction holds the xmin horizon.

nodes.label: pg_dump ACCESS SHARE lock
nodes.rationale: Reads and writes proceed; ALTER/DROP/TRUNCATE/VACUUM FULL wait. A waiting ALTER then blocks everything queued behind it. Do not run migrations and dumps in the same window.

nodes.label: Process-per-connection
nodes.rationale: postgres forks a backend per connection with its own caches, prepared statements and snapshot. Isolation is the gain; memory and fork cost are why max_connections=500 is almost never the answer.

nodes.label: max_connections
nodes.rationale: Default 100, postmaster context, restart-only. Sizes shared memory whether slots are used. superuser_reserved_connections=3 is the last-resort admin reserve. Failure is FATAL: sorry, too many clients already.

nodes.label: replicas × pool max
nodes.rationale: pg.Pool max is per process. Ten replicas × 10 is the whole default max_connections before workers and admin sessions. A rolling deploy doubles it.

nodes.label: pg.Pool vs PgBouncer
nodes.rationale: pg.Pool bounds one Node process. PgBouncer bounds total backends across every client. They are complementary, not alternatives.

nodes.label: Transaction pooling
nodes.rationale: Server connection returns when the transaction finishes. Measured: 40 sequential clients used 1 backend; 40 concurrent used exactly default_pool_size=5. Session mode pins a backend for the client lifetime and saves nothing behind pg.Pool.

nodes.label: Session features broken in transaction mode
nodes.rationale: SET/RESET, LISTEN/NOTIFY, WITH HOLD cursors, SQL PREPARE, temp tables, LOAD and session advisory locks never work. Failures are intermittent because they appear only when the next transaction lands on a different backend.

nodes.label: SET LOCAL on a pooled connection
nodes.rationale: Plain SET persists across a pooled handoff; SET LOCAL does not. A leaked tenant id is a cross-tenant exposure. Use pg_advisory_xact_lock, not session advisory locks.

nodes.label: Protocol-level prepared statements
nodes.rationale: Since PgBouncer 1.21.0, named extended-protocol statements work in transaction mode when max_prepared_statements is non-zero (default 200). SQL-level PREPARE is still unsupported.

nodes.label: server_reset_query unused in transaction mode
nodes.rationale: DISCARD ALL runs in session mode on client disconnect. In transaction pooling it is not used; there is no automatic cleanup between transactions.

nodes.label: query_wait_timeout
nodes.rationale: Default 120 s. With pool size 5, two extra clients holding BEGIN waited 120204 ms then 08P01. Upstream timeouts fire first, so the symptom is the service hanging.

nodes.label: Idle-in-transaction pool exhaustion
nodes.rationale: In transaction pooling the backend is held for the whole transaction. Five open transactions filled a pool of 5. Set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout and statement_timeout; both default to 0 (disabled).

nodes.label: A smaller pool is usually faster
nodes.rationale: Past cores × 2, extra backends add contention not throughput. Size default_pool_size small and query_wait_timeout short, or neither. Large max_client_conn, small default_pool_size.

nodes.label: max_client_conn vs default_pool_size
nodes.rationale: max_client_conn (default 100) bounds cheap connections to PgBouncer. default_pool_size (default 20) bounds expensive backends per user/database pair.

nodes.label: The Node side, observing, and alternatives
connectionTimeoutMillis
nodes.rationale: Unset by default, so pool.connect() waits forever on a saturated pool. Set it shorter than the upstream HTTP timeout.

nodes.label: client.release() in finally
nodes.rationale: A client never released on the error path is the most common way to produce pool exhaustion.

nodes.label: SHOW POOLS
nodes.rationale: cl_waiting and maxwait are the leading indicator of the 120-second failure. Pair with pg_stat_activity state = idle in transaction for the cause.

nodes.label: Read-your-writes
nodes.rationale: A client must see its own committed writes. Async replicas replay after the primary commits, so a post-save read can return the old value with no error. Load-dependent and invisible in development.

nodes.label: Physical streaming replica
nodes.rationale: A byte-identical whole-cluster copy permanently in recovery. Writes return 25006. It replays VACUUM and DDL. pg_is_in_recovery() is true on a standby.

nodes.label: Four WAL LSN stages
nodes.rationale: sent_lsn, write_lsn, flush_lsn, replay_lsn on pg_stat_replication. The flush-to-replay gap is durability without visibility. Lag columns revert to NULL when caught up and idle.

nodes.label: replay_lag
nodes.rationale: On an async standby, approximates the delay before recent transactions became visible. now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() grows without bound on an idle primary; compare receive vs replay LSN for health.

nodes.label: synchronous_commit
nodes.rationale: Per-transaction. on is not synchronous replication unless synchronous_standby_names is set. Only remote_apply waits for replay. A slow synchronous standby stalls commits on the primary.

nodes.label: remote_apply
nodes.rationale: COMMIT returns once WAL is replayed and visible on the synchronous standby. Apply per transaction with SET LOCAL; a global setting couples write availability to replica health.

nodes.label: Recovery conflict 40001
nodes.rationale: Replay of primary VACUUM would remove row versions a standby query still needs. Default max_standby_streaming_delay is 30 s then canceling statement due to conflict with recovery. SQLSTATE 40001 is retryable. Some conflicts terminate the session.

nodes.label: hot_standby_feedback
nodes.rationale: Default off. The standby reports its oldest snapshot so primary VACUUM defers cleanup. Cost is table bloat on the primary — the same xmin-horizon problem as a long transaction. vacuum_defer_cleanup_age was removed in PG16.

nodes.label: Read routing hierarchy
nodes.rationale: Same-request and post-write reads, and any read that feeds a write decision, stay on the primary. Lists, search, feeds and analytics may go to a replica.

nodes.label: Sticky-to-primary and LSN wait
nodes.rationale: Sticky window longer than typical replay_lag is simple. Capturing pg_current_wal_lsn() and requiring pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() >= that LSN is exact. Not reading from replicas is often correct.

nodes.label: pg_stat_activity
nodes.rationale: One row per server process. Filter backend_type = client backend and state <> idle, order by xact_start. xact_age vs query_age distinguishes a slow statement from idle in transaction. Remembers nothing.

nodes.label: idle in transaction
nodes.rationale: BEGIN then the application went away. Holds locks, pins the vacuum horizon, and occupies a pooled backend. query shows the last statement, the clue to the missing COMMIT or release().

nodes.label: Wait events
nodes.rationale: Lock means find the blocker. Client/ClientRead means the application is slow, not the database. IO is disk-bound.

nodes.label: pg_blocking_pids
nodes.rationale: Returns pids holding locks the waiter needs. Fix the root of the chain, not the queue. pg_locks is the detail when lock mode and object matter.

nodes.label: pg_cancel_backend vs pg_terminate_backend
nodes.rationale: Cancel stops the running query and keeps the session; it does nothing to idle in transaction. Terminate closes the session and rolls back. Prefer cancel first; set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout so humans are the fallback.

nodes.label: total_exec_time beats mean time
nodes.rationale: A 4 ms lookup run 500000 times costs far more than an 8 s nightly report. Slow-query logging never shows the cheap-but-constant query.

nodes.label: shared_preload_libraries restart
nodes.rationale: The module needs a restart, then CREATE EXTENSION per database. Both halves are required. Enable it before the incident where you first wish you had it.

nodes.label: Query normalisation
nodes.rationale: Literals become $n so one shape aggregates. String concatenation fills pg_stat_statements.max (default 5000) and evicts useful rows. queryid is not stable across major versions.

nodes.label: Cumulative counters need a delta
nodes.rationale: A single snapshot is since last reset, possibly months. Monitoring products sample and report rates. pg_stat_statements_reset() is unrecoverable.

nodes.label: stddev_exec_time
nodes.rationale: Large relative to mean on a high-call statement signals parameter-dependent plans, lock waits or data skew. An average hides it.

nodes.label: pg_read_all_stats
nodes.rationale: Non-superusers see only their own query text. Granting this role to monitoring is the read-only observability privilege. The same membership can read every session's SQL via pg_stat_activity.

nodes.label: Monitoring views
nodes.rationale: Three questions, three views: live activity, aggregate cost, and quiet deterioration. Using the wrong view spends an outage reading averages.

nodes.label: Three questions three views
nodes.rationale: Now = pg_stat_activity/pg_locks; aggregate cost = pg_stat_statements; quietly worse = pg_stat_user_tables/pg_stat_database.

nodes.label: Oldest transaction age as leading indicator
nodes.rationale: Bloat, lock waits, pool exhaustion and replication conflicts all trace back to a transaction open too long. Monitor this after disk space.

nodes.label: Table health
nodes.rationale: Views that tell you something is wrong before anyone notices: dead tuples, unused indexes, whether autovacuum is keeping up.

nodes.label: pg_stat_user_tables
nodes.rationale: One row per table: seq_scan, idx_scan, n_live_tup, n_dead_tup, last_autovacuum, write mix. Cheap, approximate, for trends and triage.

nodes.label: High seq_scan is a hint not a verdict
nodes.rationale: Sequential scans are often optimal for small tables or queries that touch most rows. Treat them as EXPLAIN candidates; adding an index can make a query slower.

nodes.label: Dead tuples vs autovacuum pace
nodes.rationale: Rising n_dead_tup with recent last_autovacuum means not keeping pace (tune per-table scale_factor). Old or NULL last_autovacuum means blocked by a long-open transaction.

nodes.label: Unused indexes via idx_scan = 0
nodes.rationale: Exclude unique/PK. Check stats_reset, replica stats, and idx_scan lag before DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY.

nodes.label: VACUUM silent skip without MAINTAIN
nodes.rationale: Missing MAINTAIN privilege: VACUUM warns, skips the table, and exits successfully. Nightly jobs that lost their grant never fail.

nodes.label: Statistics counters are estimates
nodes.rationale: n_live_tup and n_dead_tup are approximate; stats report after statements complete. Exact counters would need sync on every row operation.

nodes.label: Database health and alerting
nodes.rationale: Database-level statistics plus the 3am alert list: disk, connections, oldest xact, idle-in-transaction, lag, dead tuples, deadlocks, temp_bytes.

nodes.label: pg_stat_database
nodes.rationale: One row per database: cache hit, temp spills, deadlocks, rollback ratio, stats_reset. Read stats_reset first.

nodes.label: Cache hit ratio understates OS cache
nodes.rationale: blks_read counts shared-buffer misses, many served from the OS page cache. A sharp drop matters; 97% is not a RAM purchase.

nodes.label: temp_bytes spill signal
nodes.rationale: Sorts or hashes exceeded work_mem. Gather this trend before raising work_mem.

nodes.label: Defensible production alert set
nodes.rationale: Alert on few things: connections >80% of max, oldest xact >5 min, idle-in-transaction, lag, dead tuples >20%, deadlock rate, rising temp_bytes, disk >80%.

nodes.label: Disk space and WAL fill
nodes.rationale: PostgreSQL handles a full disk badly. A stuck replication slot accumulating WAL can fill one surprisingly fast.

nodes.label: Database statistics are approximate by design
nodes.rationale: Cumulative, approximate, reported after statements complete, reset with stats_reset. For trends and triage, not accounting.

nodes.label: Key configuration
nodes.rationale: Reason about what a managed provider already set. Four facts: work_mem per operation, effective_cache_size allocates nothing, random_page_cost=4 models spinning disk, context tells restart vs reload.

nodes.label: The memory settings
nodes.rationale: Four settings account for most tuning; only one allocates the memory people think it does. Phase 0 shared_buffers benchmark was confounded and is not reused.

nodes.label: shared_buffers
nodes.rationale: Allocated once at startup (postmaster, restart). Default 128 MB. Dedicated server guidance ~25% of RAM because OS page cache is the second tier.

nodes.label: work_mem per sort or hash operation
nodes.rationale: Worst case ≈ work_mem × operations × concurrent queries. Raising globally is the classic OOM path. SET LOCAL or ALTER ROLE, never plain SET on a pool.

nodes.label: effective_cache_size allocates nothing
nodes.rationale: Planner hint for shared buffers plus OS page cache. Higher makes index scans look cheaper. Default 4 GB on a large server biases sequential scans.

nodes.label: maintenance_work_mem
nodes.rationale: One maintenance op per session — safer to raise than work_mem. Autovacuum multiplies it by worker count; decouple with autovacuum_work_mem.

nodes.label: autovacuum_work_mem
nodes.rationale: Caps background vacuum so N workers cannot each claim the large maintenance_work_mem used for interactive index builds.

nodes.label: hash_mem_multiplier
nodes.rationale: Default 2.0: hash nodes may use work_mem × multiplier. Hashes degrade worse on spill than sorts.

nodes.label: max_connections forces work_mem down
nodes.rationale: Each backend can allocate work_mem several times. Higher max_connections lowers the safe work_mem. Strongest argument for a pooler.

nodes.label: Planner costs, WAL, and changing a setting
nodes.rationale: Settings that decide whether the planner picks an index are one-line, no-restart changes. pg_settings.context values sandbox-measured on PG 18.4.

nodes.label: random_page_cost = 4 models spinning disk
nodes.rationale: On SSD/NVMe use 1.1. Leaving 4.0 over-costs index scans so the planner ignores indexes. Highest-value one-line change; test with EXPLAIN first.

nodes.label: default_statistics_target
nodes.rationale: Default 100. Raise per-column (SET STATISTICS 250–500) for skewed data rather than globally. Correlated columns want CREATE STATISTICS.

nodes.label: jit default on
nodes.rationale: Helps long analytics; can add overhead to short queries mis-costed above the JIT threshold. Test SET jit = off after upgrades.

nodes.label: max_wal_size checkpoint loop
nodes.rationale: 1 GB default on write-heavy systems forces frequent checkpoints and full-page write bursts. Raise to several GB; cost is longer crash recovery.

nodes.label: fsync = off risks corruption
nodes.rationale: Never off on real data. synchronous_commit = off is the safe durability trade: can lose recent commits, no corruption.

nodes.label: synchronous_commit
nodes.rationale: Safe way to trade durability for speed. With empty synchronous_standby_names, remote_apply/remote_write/local behave like on.

nodes.label: lock_timeout
nodes.rationale: Default 0 (wait forever). Essential for safe DDL. User context; set per role so migrations are not killed by web limits.

nodes.label: statement_timeout
nodes.rationale: Bounds a single statement. Default 0. Set per role, not globally. Not a substitute for lock_timeout.

nodes.label: idle_in_transaction_session_timeout
nodes.rationale: Kills transactions left open. Default 0. Worst blockers of vacuum and DDL hold locks while doing nothing.

nodes.label: Changing a setting
nodes.rationale: A reload that silently does nothing wastes an afternoon. Check context and pending_restart first.

nodes.label: pg_settings.context
nodes.rationale: postmaster=restart (shared_buffers, max_connections); sighup=reload (ssl, random_page_cost); user/superuser=SET. pending_restart shows staged changes. Measured PG 18.4.

nodes.label: ALTER SYSTEM vs postgresql.conf
nodes.rationale: Writes postgresql.auto.conf, read after postgresql.conf and overrides it. RESET undoes. Reload is refused on syntax error; restart with a bad file fails to start.

nodes.label: Setting precedence order
nodes.rationale: postgresql.conf → auto.conf → ALTER DATABASE → ALTER ROLE → SET → SET LOCAL. Narrowest scope wins.

nodes.label: Tuning start order for PERN
nodes.rationale: 1 random_page_cost 1.1, 2 effective_cache_size ~75% RAM, 3 timeouts per role, 4 work_mem with spill evidence, 5 max_wal_size, 6 shared_buffers last (restart).

nodes.label: Logging slow queries
nodes.rationale: PostgreSQL logs almost nothing useful by default, and the one setting people turn on leaks secrets.

nodes.label: Monitoring three-legged stool
nodes.rationale: pg_stat_activity (now), pg_stat_statements (aggregate), the log (which execution was slow). Production wants all three.

nodes.label: What to log and what it costs
nodes.rationale: Defaults disable duration, statement, lock-wait and temp-file logging. Each is a one-line reload.

nodes.label: log_min_duration_statement
nodes.rationale: Default -1 disabled. 1000 ms is a web starting point. Sample the merely-slow band with log_min_duration_sample + log_statement_sample_rate.

nodes.label: log_line_prefix
nodes.rationale: Default is only timestamp and PID. Add %u@%d %a %e. %a only works if services set application_name.

nodes.label: log_lock_waits
nodes.rationale: Default off. Logs waits longer than deadlock_timeout. Best diagnostic for a freeze that then recovered — invisible to pg_stat_activity afterwards.

nodes.label: log_temp_files
nodes.rationale: Default -1. Set 0 to log every spill past work_mem, naming the statement behind rising temp_bytes.

nodes.label: log_statement
nodes.rationale: all fills disks and logs bound parameters. ddl is the safe continuous production value.

nodes.label: jsonlog destination
nodes.rationale: Structured JSON per line. Prefer over regex on log_line_prefix when shipping logs.

nodes.label: logging_collector
nodes.rationale: Captures stderr into rotating files. Requires a restart. In containers, stderr to the container log is often preferred.

nodes.label: Parameters do not protect the log
nodes.rationale: Measured: pg_stat_activity shows $1, but log_statement=all writes DETAIL Parameters. log_parameter_max_length defaults to -1 (full). Treat logs as credential-bearing.

nodes.label: ALTER ROLE PASSWORD logs plaintext
nodes.rationale: SCRAM stores a verifier; the statement still contains the literal. log_statement=ddl captures it. Use psql \password to send only the verifier.

nodes.label: auto_explain
nodes.rationale: Logs the plan at the moment a query was slow. Load via shared_preload_libraries (restart), session_preload_libraries, or LOAD.

nodes.label: auto_explain.log_analyze instruments every statement
nodes.rationale: Docs warn of extremely negative impact: per-node timing applies to all statements, not only logged ones. Mitigate with log_timing=off or sample_rate; enable only while investigating.

nodes.label: log_parameter_max_length_on_error defaults to 0
nodes.rationale: Failed statements do not log parameters by default. Why many developers never see parameter logging and conclude it never happens.

nodes.label: Zero-downtime schema changes
nodes.rationale: The migration that takes the site down is fast; it spends its time waiting. Deployment view; statement timings live in Phase 3.

nodes.label: Waiting ACCESS EXCLUSIVE blocks the queue
nodes.rationale: New queries do not jump the queue. A DDL blocked by one slow reader makes the table unavailable before it has run. lock_timeout is not optional.

nodes.label: Schema change and code deploy are never simultaneous
nodes.rationale: During a rolling deploy old and new code share one schema. Never remove in the same step that adds a replacement.

nodes.label: The lock queue
nodes.rationale: A 5 ms ALTER can cause a 30-second outage because ACCESS EXCLUSIVE queues and later ACCESS SHARE cannot jump it.

nodes.label: ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock queue
nodes.rationale: Default ALTER TABLE lock conflicts with every mode including SELECT's ACCESS SHARE. Blast radius is the longest transaction on the table, not DDL duration.

nodes.label: lock_timeout plus retry on 55P03
nodes.rationale: SET LOCAL lock_timeout, retry lock_not_available with backoff. statement_timeout does not reliably bound lock wait. Cancel the blocker, not the migration.

nodes.label: ADD COLUMN constant default is catalog-only
nodes.rationale: Since PG 11 a non-volatile default is stored in metadata. Volatile defaults, identity, stored generated, and constrained domains still rewrite.

nodes.label: VALIDATE CONSTRAINT uses SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE
nodes.rationale: Does not block reads or writes. ADD FOREIGN KEY is SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE and still blocks writes on both tables.

nodes.label: Transactional DDL holds locks until commit
nodes.rationale: One transaction wrapping five ALTERs holds the first ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for all five. Split scans/rewrites. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run in a transaction.

nodes.label: Expand and contract
nodes.rationale: Expand additively, migrate data and dual-write, contract later. Every deploy compatible with schema before and after; every migration compatible with code before and after.

nodes.label: NOT VALID then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT
nodes.rationale: Skips the lengthy scan; new rows are enforced immediately. Do not leave convalidated=false indefinitely.

nodes.label: SET NOT NULL via validated CHECK
nodes.rationale: CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID → VALIDATE → SET NOT NULL. Since PG 12 the validated check lets SET NOT NULL skip its ACCESS EXCLUSIVE scan.

nodes.label: Batched backfill with SKIP LOCKED
nodes.rationale: LIMIT + ORDER BY + FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, commit per batch, pause so autovacuum keeps up. One huge UPDATE bloats and loses work on failure.

nodes.label: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY
nodes.rationale: No write-blocking lock. Cannot run in a transaction. Scans twice and waits for existing transactions. Slower than a regular build.

nodes.label: Invalid indexes after CONCURRENTLY failure
nodes.rationale: indisvalid=false: ignored for queries, still maintained on every write. Drop and retry or REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY. Check post-migration.

nodes.label: Never rename a column in one step
nodes.rationale: No instant when old and new code agree on the name. Add, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, drop later. Same for int→bigint.

nodes.label: Zero-downtime migration checklist
nodes.rationale: lock_timeout, no ACCESS EXCLUSIVE scans, NOT VALID constraints, CONCURRENTLY indexes, batched backfills, both-code compatibility, rollback without restore.

nodes.label: Managed PostgreSQL
nodes.rationale: Which of the previous twelve topics are still your job. Provider facts checked 2026-08-13 and move fast.

nodes.label: Managed hosting removes sysadmin not application work
nodes.rationale: Backups, replicas, failover, patching become theirs. Missing indexes, long transactions, connection exhaustion and locking migrations remain yours — and cause most incidents.

nodes.label: Managed role is not SUPERUSER
nodes.rationale: RDS gives rds_superuser, not PostgreSQL superuser. No postgresql.conf, pg_hba, often no ALTER SYSTEM, no arbitrary extensions, no server-side COPY from a path.

nodes.label: Parameter groups replace config files
nodes.rationale: Default RDS parameter group cannot be edited. Custom group + attach; static vs dynamic is the same restart/reload distinction as pg_settings.context.

nodes.label: Extension allowlist
nodes.rationale: CREATE EXTENSION only for vetted extensions. pg_stat_statements is usually already in shared_preload_libraries. Check niche extensions before designing around them.

nodes.label: Provider backups do not make restore yours
nodes.rationale: Provider guarantees a backup exists, not a practised restore, adequate retention, or coverage of a correct-but-wrong-rows migration. Keep pg_dump.

nodes.label: Illusion of delegation
nodes.rationale: Automated backups, failover and instance tuning do not imply durability, availability or performance are handled. Most managed incidents are application-side.

nodes.label: Direct vs pooled endpoints
nodes.rationale: Wrong endpoint fails only under load. Serverless uses pooled; migrations, LISTEN/NOTIFY and admin use direct.

nodes.label: Neon pooled endpoint via PgBouncer
nodes.rationale: Hostname token -pooler. transaction pool_mode, up to 10k clients. Protocol-level prepared statements supported (PgBouncer 1.21+).

nodes.label: Supabase Supavisor ports
nodes.rationale: 5432 direct/session, 6543 transaction. Transaction mode does not support prepared statements. Direct is IPv6 by default.

nodes.label: Serverless connection pattern
nodes.rationale: Always pooled endpoint; module-scope pool; max 1–2 per instance; connectionTimeoutMillis set. Optional HTTP driver for one-shot queries.

nodes.label: sslmode=verify-full on managed TLS
nodes.rationale: Traffic crosses a network you do not control. require encrypts but verifies nothing. Pass the provider CA; never rejectUnauthorized: false.

nodes.label: Migrations must use the direct endpoint
nodes.rationale: Need session semantics, advisory locks, and CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY. Transaction-mode poolers produce intermittent failures.

nodes.label: Row-level security
nodes.rationale: Authorization that cannot be forgotten. Know tier generally; Master on Supabase where it is the entire authorization model.

nodes.label: RLS default-deny empty table
nodes.rationale: ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY with no policy: queries succeed and return zero rows. Not an error.

nodes.label: USING versus WITH CHECK
nodes.rationale: USING filters existing rows; WITH CHECK validates the row after a write. UPDATE needs both or a user can reassign owner_id. USING alone is copied into WITH CHECK.

nodes.label: Permissive OR restrictive AND
nodes.rationale: PERMISSIVE grants (OR); RESTRICTIVE constrains (AND) and grants nothing alone. Tenant isolation is the canonical restrictive policy.

nodes.label: Table owners bypass RLS by default
nodes.rationale: Superusers, BYPASSRLS, and table owners skip policies. Connecting as schema owner makes RLS a no-op and tests pass while proving nothing.

nodes.label: FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY
nodes.rationale: Makes the owner subject to policies. Real fix is connecting as a non-owner. Verify relrowsecurity and relforcerowsecurity.

nodes.label: SET LOCAL for RLS identity
nodes.rationale: Plain SET persists on a pooled backend into the next tenant's request — measured ex54. This is a cross-tenant leak, not a style issue.

nodes.label: set_config is_local for parameterized identity
nodes.rationale: SET LOCAL name = $1 is 42601. set_config(name, value, true) accepts parameters. current_setting(name, true) returns NULL if unset.

nodes.label: Index policy predicate columns
nodes.rationale: A policy is a silent predicate on every query. Tenant tables want (tenant_id, …) leading indexes. Confirm with EXPLAIN.

nodes.label: current_setting is STABLE
nodes.rationale: May be evaluated once per statement. Helper functions must be STABLE, not IMMUTABLE (wrong cache) or VOLATILE (per-row).

nodes.label: RLS leakproofness limit
nodes.rationale: Strong on rows returned, weaker on inference. Non-leakproof user predicates may not be pushed below the barrier. SECURITY DEFINER is the common practical hole.

nodes.label: Test RLS as the application role
nodes.rationale: Owner-run tests always pass. Assert negatives: other tenant 0 rows, cross-tenant INSERT/UPDATE rejected, missing context empty or error.

nodes.label: BYPASSRLS job role
nodes.rationale: Exactly one unfiltered role, named for that purpose; the application must not use it. Implicit owner bypass hides unrestricted access.

nodes.label: Filter in the app and enable RLS underneath
nodes.rationale: App WHERE is clearer and faster; RLS converts a forgotten tenant_id into an empty result and covers psql. On Supabase, RLS is the whole mechanism.

nodes.label: Base backups and WAL archiving
nodes.rationale: Managed providers do this; you still decide RPO/RTO. Logical restore measured 4× dump because indexes rebuild.

nodes.label: Logical vs physical backups
nodes.rationale: Logical: portable, per-table, no PITR, slow restore. Physical: whole cluster, same major/arch, PITR, fast restore. Production wants both.

nodes.label: Point-in-time recovery
nodes.rationale: Restore base backup, replay archived WAL to any later second. Base need not be a consistent snapshot; log replay repairs it like crash recovery.

nodes.label: archive_command
nodes.rationale: Must return non-zero on failure or WAL is deleted locally and never stored. test ! -f refuses overwrite. archive_mode=on requires a restart.

nodes.label: archive_timeout
nodes.rationale: Default 0. Quiet databases may not fill a WAL segment for hours, so last hours are unarchived. Forces a switch and bounds RPO.

nodes.label: pg_basebackup -X stream
nodes.rationale: Streams WAL generated during the backup so it is restorable standalone. PG 18 incremental backups recombine with pg_combinebackup.

nodes.label: pg_stat_archiver failed_count
nodes.rationale: Growing failed_count is an emergency: recovery window stops advancing and unreycled WAL fills pg_wal until the disk is full.

nodes.label: Physical backup and PITR
nodes.rationale: Base backup plus every WAL record since equals the ability to land on any second. The base backup need not be filesystem-consistent because log replay repairs it, the same mechanism as crash recovery. A managed provider runs this, but RPO and RTO remain product decisions.

nodes.label: Failing archive_command is an outage
nodes.rationale: WAL that cannot be archived is retained until the disk fills. Alert on pg_stat_archiver.failed_count.

nodes.label: Point-in-time recovery
nodes.rationale: Stop the server, move the old data directory aside, restore the base backup, set restore_command and a recovery_target_*, touch recovery.signal, then start. The target must be after the end of the base backup.

nodes.label: recovery_target_action pause default
nodes.rationale: Default pause stops recovery so you can connect and confirm the landing point before promoting. Immediate promote forecloses a retry. Combined with timelines, a wrong attempt can be repeated.

nodes.label: recovery.signal versus standby.signal
nodes.rationale: recovery.signal performs recovery then becomes a normal read-write server. standby.signal keeps the server in continuous recovery as a replica.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL timelines
nodes.rationale: When recovery completes, PostgreSQL starts a new timeline so post-recovery WAL does not overwrite original history. recovery_target_timeline (default latest) selects which branch to follow. A wrong PITR is not fatal.

nodes.label: Recovery point objective
nodes.rationale: How much data may we lose. Set by archive frequency, archive_timeout, and replication mode. Continuous archiving: last archived WAL segment (seconds to minutes). Nightly pg_dump: up to 24 hours.

nodes.label: Recovery time objective
nodes.rationale: How long may we be down. Set by backup size, restore speed, and whether anyone has practised. A restore never timed is a hope, not a plan.

nodes.label: Oldest recoverable point is backup end
nodes.rationale: The recovery target must be after the end of the base backup. You cannot recover into a backup that was still in progress. Base backup frequency sets the recovery floor.

nodes.label: Managed provider restore duties
nodes.rationale: Choose retention against how long a corrupting bug might go unnoticed. Keep logical dumps for per-table recovery. Snapshot restore usually yields a new endpoint. The provider guarantees the backup exists, not that you can use it.

nodes.label: PITR trades procedure for precision
nodes.rationale: A logical restore is one command; PITR is a stopped server, restored directory, configured target, signal file, and verification. All value is contingent on rehearsal.

nodes.label: Phase 2 — Data types and the relational model
nodes.rationale: Target PostgreSQL 18.4, Node 24, pg. Seventeen topics from integer widths through modelling money.

nodes.label: Phase 2 gate — bigint text timestamptz numeric
nodes.rationale: Move on when you default to bigint + text + timestamptz + numeric for money, and you never write = NULL.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL integer types
nodes.rationale: smallint 2 bytes ±32767, integer 4 bytes ±2.1e9, bigint 8 bytes ±9.22e18. No unsigned variant; use CHECK (n >= 0). Overflow raises 22003 rather than wrapping.

nodes.label: bigint for surrogate primary keys
nodes.rationale: Measured 17 MB vs 21 MB and same PK index on 500k two-column rows. Exhausting an int sequence is 2200H and a full ACCESS EXCLUSIVE rewrite. Foreign keys must match referenced width or a cast kills the index.

nodes.label: GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY
nodes.rationale: Standard SQL preferred over serial/bigserial, which expand to column plus sequence plus default. ALWAYS prevents explicit inserts from desynchronising the sequence.

nodes.label: pg returns bigint as a string
nodes.rationale: int8 exceeds Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER. Measured 9007199254740993 arrived as a string. Compare as strings or BigInt. setTypeParser(20, parseInt) is a global decision.

nodes.label: numeric vs float
nodes.rationale: numeric is exact software decimal; double precision and real are approximate IEEE floats. 1000 additions of 0.01 gave 9.999999999999831 in float8 and 10.00 in numeric. numeric(p,s) overflow is 22003; extra scale rounds silently.

nodes.label: Money never in float
nodes.rationale: 0.01 has no exact binary form. An unbalanced ledger costs more than any query. Default numeric(12,2); move to integer cents only when a measurement says you must.

nodes.label: Integer cents in bigint
nodes.rationale: Exact and as fast as float: 27.7 ms vs 76.8 ms for 300k-row sum, 8 bytes vs 10. Units become implicit; a missed conversion is a 100× error.

nodes.label: pg returns numeric as a string
nodes.rationale: Converting to a JavaScript number would throw away exactness. Prefer SQL arithmetic or a decimal library. Never setTypeParser(1700, parseFloat).

nodes.label: numeric rounds half away from zero
nodes.rationale: 2.5::numeric(2,0) is 3. Float-to-int uses half-to-even (2.5 → 2). numeric NaN compares equal to itself so it can be sorted and indexed.

nodes.label: text vs varchar vs char
nodes.rationale: Same implementation for text and varchar. Measured identical 13 MB and ~26 ms on 300k rows. char(50) pads: 51 bytes vs 4 for the same three characters, 24 MB vs 13 MB.

nodes.label: Use text by default
nodes.rationale: varchar(n) bakes a guessed number into physical structure. Widening is 2.4 ms metadata; narrowing rewrites under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE (305 ms / 200k rows). Prefer text plus CHECK (length(col) <= n).

nodes.label: varchar cast truncates silently
nodes.rationale: INSERT into varchar(50) raises 22001. Explicit ::varchar(50) truncates with no warning. A CHECK cannot be cast away.

nodes.label: char(n) padding semantics
nodes.rationale: Comparison ignores trailing spaces; concatenation after implicit text cast does not. Acceptable only for genuinely fixed-width codes.

nodes.label: timestamptz vs timestamp
nodes.rationale: Both 8 bytes; neither stores a zone. timestamptz is a UTC instant converted on input/output. timestamp keeps the digits and means a different instant to every reader.

nodes.label: AT TIME ZONE bidirectional conversion
nodes.rationale: timestamptz AT TIME ZONE zone yields timestamp (clock reading there). timestamp AT TIME ZONE zone yields timestamptz (interpret those digits as that zone). Direction depends on input type.

nodes.label: now() versus clock_timestamp()
nodes.rationale: now()/CURRENT_TIMESTAMP is frozen at transaction start. clock_timestamp() is wall clock and changes every call. Use now() for created_at so one transaction shares a timestamp.

nodes.label: DST: 1 day versus 24 hours
nodes.rationale: Same wall-clock time tomorrow and 24 hours from now differ across a DST boundary in a local zone. On UTC-normalised timestamptz they agree.

nodes.label: date to JavaScript Date midnight trap
nodes.rationale: pg turns date into a Date at local midnight. In Asia/Calcutta that is 18:30 UTC the previous day, so toISOString prints the day before. Fix with to_char or setTypeParser(1082).

nodes.label: Session TimeZone setting
nodes.rationale: Display and interpretation, not storage. Affects timestamptz printing, bare timestamp literals, current_date, date_trunc, and ::date. Precedence: SET, PGTZ/options, postgresql.conf, OS at initdb. Pin server and database to UTC.

nodes.label: GROUP BY day depends on session zone
nodes.rationale: Events at 21:00Z and 23:30Z on 15 June bucket to 15 June in UTC and 16 June in Asia/Kolkata. Always name the zone: date_trunc('day', at AT TIME ZONE ...).

nodes.label: IANA time zone names
nodes.rationale: Abbreviations like IST are ambiguous. Fixed offsets miss DST. Store users' zones as IANA names so history and legislation are applied correctly.

nodes.label: Pin the pg pool to UTC
nodes.rationale: options: '-c timezone=UTC'. Plain SET leaks across pooled release(). SET LOCAL TIME ZONE $1 fails 42601; use set_config(name, value, true) or put AT TIME ZONE in the query.

nodes.label: NULL three-valued logic
nodes.rationale: NULL is absence. NULL = NULL is unknown. WHERE keeps only true, so col = NULL matches nothing. Use IS NULL or IS NOT DISTINCT FROM.

nodes.label: NOT IN with NULL returns nothing
nodes.rationale: 2 NOT IN (1, NULL) is NULL because it expands to true AND (2 <> NULL). Prefer NOT EXISTS, which handles NULL and usually plans as an anti-join.

nodes.label: UNIQUE allows many NULLs
nodes.rationale: NULLs are not equal, so they do not conflict. Measured three NULLs accepted. UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT (PostgreSQL 15+) allows at most one.

nodes.label: Aggregates ignore NULL
nodes.rationale: count(*) counts rows; count(col) counts non-nulls. sum() over no rows or all NULLs is NULL, not 0 — wrap with coalesce. NULLs sort last ASC and first DESC.

nodes.label: Empty string is not NULL
nodes.rationale: Oracle conflates them; PostgreSQL does not. || with a NULL operand yields NULL; concat() and concat_ws() skip NULLs. undefined parameters become NULL in pg.

nodes.label: uuid v4 versus uuid v7
nodes.rationale: 200k inserts: bigint 947 ms / 4408 kB index; v4 1727 ms / 8552 kB; v7 1356 ms / 6184 kB. Random keys scatter B-tree writes. uuidv7 first 48 bits are a millisecond timestamp.

nodes.label: B-tree locality for sequential keys
nodes.rationale: Sequential keys append to the rightmost leaf, stay in cache, and fill completely. Random keys split pages half-empty and make the working set the entire index.

nodes.label: uuidv7() built-in
nodes.rationale: PostgreSQL 18 built-in, no extension. uuid_extract_timestamp recovers creation time — a free created_at and a leak of when the row was created. Use v4 for public ids when timing is sensitive.

nodes.label: Never store a UUID as text
nodes.rationale: 16 bytes as uuid, 40 as text, plus string comparison and no format validation. Common middle path: bigint PK for joins, uuid unique column for public ids.

nodes.label: jsonb vs json
nodes.rationale: json stores exact text. jsonb parses to binary: keys sorted, last duplicate wins, whitespace dropped. json has no equality operator (42883). jsonb was larger on a small object (112 vs 56 bytes).

nodes.label: GIN index on jsonb
nodes.rationale: 200k rows: jsonb ->> 33.6 ms vs json 98.7 ms unindexed; @> with GIN 9.4 ms. json cannot be GIN-indexed (42704). ->> equality does not use default GIN; use @> or a B-tree expression index.

nodes.label: Promote queried jsonb keys to columns
nodes.rationale: A jsonb key has no CHECK, FK, statistics, or cheap B-tree. Use jsonb for schemaless payloads; promote keys you filter or join. A generated column is the migration-free middle step. Pass objects to pg; JSON.stringify double-encodes.

nodes.label: boolean type
nodes.rationale: 1 byte. true/t/yes/y/on/1 and false/f/no/n/off/0; else 22P02. Three-valued unless NOT NULL. Count trues with count(*) FILTER (WHERE b); sum(b::int) is NULL-poisoned.

nodes.label: date arithmetic
nodes.rationale: 4 bytes, no time or zone. date - date is an integer day count. date + integer is a date. date + interval is a timestamp. Month arithmetic clamps: 31 Jan + 1 month = 28 Feb, and is not associative.

nodes.label: interval comparison versus addition
nodes.rationale: 16 bytes: months, days, microseconds. interval '1 month' = interval '30 days' is true for comparison, but addition uses the calendar. Compare timestamps (created_at < now() - interval '1 month'), not intervals. age() is a human calendar breakdown; subtraction is an exact duration.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL arrays
nodes.rationale: Any type can be an array. 1-based; out-of-range subscript is NULL, not an error. Prefer cardinality() (0 for empty) over array_length() (NULL for empty). pg maps JS arrays natively.

nodes.label: GIN @> not ANY for array membership
nodes.rationale: 200k rows: @> 73.2 ms seq scan → 4.8 ms with GIN. 't42' = ANY(tags) is not GIN-indexable (41.8 ms parallel seq scan). Write tags @> ARRAY['t42']. Scalar id = ANY($1) is a different, indexable IN-list idiom.

nodes.label: Array versus child table
nodes.rationale: No FK from array elements (42804). No per-element constraints or extra columns. Any element change rewrites the whole MVCC row. Arrays for values that travel with the row; child tables for entities.

nodes.label: enum vs CHECK vs lookup table
nodes.rationale: Invalid value SQLSTATEs: enum 22P02, CHECK 23514, FK 23503. Enum 4-byte OID, ~18% smaller (7080 vs 8656 kB / 200k). All three arrive in Node as strings.

nodes.label: Enum cannot drop values
nodes.rationale: 0A000 dropping an enum value is not implemented. ALTER TYPE ADD VALUE then using it in the same transaction is 55P04, breaking atomic migrations. Enums sort by declaration order.

nodes.label: Default to a lookup table
nodes.rationale: Adding a value is an INSERT (3.4 ms), not DDL, and can carry label, colour, sort_order, is_terminal. CHECK re-validates every row (62.9 ms / 200k) unless NOT VALID then VALIDATE.

nodes.label: Cast the literal, never the column
nodes.rationale: acct = '12345' index-only 0.199 ms vs acct::bigint = 12345 seq scan 47.9 ms (241×). created::date = current_date 65.4 ms vs a range on the bare column 1.2 ms. The index stores the column, not the cast.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL 42883 type mismatch
nodes.rationale: No text = integer operator. Treat 42883 as a type-mismatch bug, not an inconvenience to cast away. pg sends untyped text so a JS number against a text column still uses the index; hand-written :: on the column is the danger.

nodes.label: Implicit, assignment, and explicit casts
nodes.rationale: Implicit only where lossless (int + numeric). Assignment on store. Explicit ::, CAST, and type-named functions are equivalent. '42.7'::int is 22P02; 42.7::int rounds to 43. Invalid dates are 22008.

nodes.label: bytea
nodes.rationale: Binary round-trips to a Node Buffer. Measured 102400 bytes in and out, identical. Hex text form is 2×; pg uses the binary protocol so Buffers are unaffected. Use octet_length().

nodes.label: TOAST for bytea
nodes.rationale: Above ~2 KB, attstorage x compresses and moves the value to a side table. Measured pg_column_size 1185 for a compressible 100 KB buffer. Queries that omit the column never read the blob.

nodes.label: Object storage instead of large bytea
nodes.rationale: Backups, WAL, and replicas grow with blobs; values materialise whole in memory; no range requests or signed URLs. Keep metadata and sha256 in PostgreSQL, bytes in object storage, reconcile deletes with a queue. Prefer bytea over large objects (not deleted with the row).

nodes.label: inet versus cidr
nodes.rationale: inet holds a host optionally with a mask (10 bytes vs 16 as text). cidr is a network only and rejects host bits (22P02 for 192.168.1.10/24). << containment is GiST-indexable. inet normalises IPv6 so equivalent forms compare equal.

nodes.label: Built-in geometric types
nodes.rationale: point, box, polygon, circle and friends with <->, @>, &&, GiST-indexable. Cartesian only — distances on lat/long degrees are not metres. Use PostGIS geography for Earth. point arrives in Node as {x, y}.

nodes.label: citext
nodes.rationale: Case-insensitive text via CREATE EXTENSION citext. UNIQUE rejects case variants with 23505. A forgotten lower() on a text column silently misses rows. Folds case, not Unicode composition.

nodes.label: Domain type
nodes.rationale: Base type plus reusable CHECK, e.g. CREATE DOMAIN email AS citext. Violations 23514 name the domain constraint. Inherits base behaviour. Cannot hold FKs or deferred constraints. Adding a CHECK validates every table using it.

nodes.label: Composite type
nodes.rationale: A row shape used as a column. No per-field constraints, FKs, or cheap indexes. ADD ATTRIBUTE rewrites every using table. pg returns the raw literal ("1 High St",London,"E1 6AN"). Appropriate as a function return type; every table has an implicit composite.

nodes.label: Avoid composites for storage
nodes.rationale: Use prefixed columns with real constraints, a child table for one-to-many, or jsonb if the shape is unknown. Unpack with (addr).city or to_jsonb(addr).

nodes.label: Range types
nodes.rationale: First-class values with @>, &&, <<, -|-. Half-open [) by default; discrete types canonicalise [1,10] to [1,11). range(x,x) is empty. pg returns the text form '[1,10)'.

nodes.label: Exclusion constraint
nodes.rationale: EXCLUDE USING gist (room WITH =, during WITH &&) means no two rows share a room and overlapping times. Violations 23P01. Enforced by an index, so concurrent read-then-write cannot both succeed. Needs btree_gist for the scalar equality.

nodes.label: Multirange
nodes.rationale: A plain range must be contiguous; [1,5)+[10,15) is 22000. PostgreSQL 14+ multiranges hold disjoint ranges as one value, for availability windows with gaps.

nodes.label: Amount plus currency
nodes.rationale: An amount alone is not money. Store numeric(14,2) plus char(3) currency. A composite FK (invoice_id, currency) referencing invoices (id, currency) makes mismatched lines impossible. Always declare scale; unconstrained numeric allows 16383 fractional digits.

nodes.label: Do not use the money type
nodes.rationale: Locale-dependent via lc_monetary; dump/restore can break across locales; no currency identity. The documentation's own best-practice note prefers numeric.

nodes.label: ISO 4217 minor units
nodes.rationale: Not every currency has two decimals: JPY has none, some have three. Hard-coded ÷100 is wrong by 10 or 100. Store minor_units per currency. Unit prices need more scale than totals.

nodes.label: Round once at the charging boundary
nodes.rationale: Rounding at each step discards fractions that compound. Carry full precision through; store both inputs and the rounded charge so a historical invoice can be reproduced and explained. Implement jurisdiction-specific rules explicitly.

nodes.label: Largest-remainder allocation
nodes.rationale: 100/3 → 33.33×3 = 99.99. No rounding rule fixes indivisibility. Floor each share in minor units, then give leftover units to the largest remainders (33.34, 33.33, 33.33). Assert parts sum to the whole.

nodes.label: Store the FX rate with the transaction
nodes.rationale: Without fx_rate and fx_rate_at, next year's report reconverts at today's rate. Never convert for comparison on the fly. Rates need numeric(18,8) against amounts numeric(14,2).

nodes.label: Append-only ledger
nodes.rationale: Do not store a mutable balance. Immutable signed entries; derive the balance with SUM. When reads get slow, add a materialised snapshot plus entries since. A wrong UPDATE permanently corrupts a mutable balance and loses history.

nodes.label: Never parseFloat numeric
nodes.rationale: pg returns numeric as a string on purpose. parseFloat or overriding the type parser reintroduces IEEE-754 imprecision. Compute in SQL or a decimal library. Mixing SQL and JS-float totals is how two parts of one system disagree.

nodes.label: Modelling money
nodes.rationale: An amount is not a number and arithmetic on it is not ordinary arithmetic. The bugs are the ones that make accounts fail to balance.

nodes.label: Five money modelling rules
nodes.rationale: numeric plus currency; round once; allocate remainders; store the FX rate used; keep it a string in JavaScript. Never double precision (1000×0.01 = 9.999999999999831) or the locale-dependent money type.

nodes.label: numeric rounds 2.5 away from zero
nodes.rationale: numeric 2.5 → 3 (away from zero); double precision 2.5 → 2 (to even). A second independent reason money is never float.

nodes.label: Phase 3 DDL tables constraints schema design
nodes.rationale: Design a 1-N and N-N schema with identity PKs, FKs, and CHECKs without an ORM. Target PostgreSQL 18.4, Node 24, pg.

nodes.label: CREATE TABLE
nodes.rationale: Writes the contract every client must obey. Type changes on a large table rewrite it under a lock that blocks everything.

nodes.label: text plus CHECK not varchar or enum
nodes.rationale: text and varchar(n) have identical performance; narrowing varchar rewrites (433 ms / 200k). Enums cannot drop or reorder values.

nodes.label: timestamptz not timestamp
nodes.rationale: timestamp stores no zone so the same value means different instants. timestamptz stores an instant. Converting later rewrites the table.

nodes.label: char(n) blank-pads
nodes.rationale: char(3) holding 'US' compares and returns as 'US '. Use only for genuinely fixed-width codes; prefer text.

nodes.label: now() is transaction start time
nodes.rationale: Two inserts 150ms apart in one transaction share created_at. Use clock_timestamp() for per-row wall-clock time. now() cannot be a generated column (42P17).

nodes.label: Schema-qualify DDL in migrations
nodes.rationale: Unqualified CREATE TABLE follows search_path ("$user", public). A role with its own schema silently creates tables elsewhere.

nodes.label: Liberal constraints conservative types
nodes.rationale: Constraints can be relaxed with ALTER and NOT VALID. Type changes that alter on-disk representation rewrite under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE.

nodes.label: GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY
nodes.rationale: SQL-standard key. Refuses a manual id with 428C9 so the sequence cannot drift. Catalog property is_identity, not column_default.

nodes.label: serial
nodes.rationale: Not a type: integer plus owned sequence plus default. Accepts manual ids without advancing the sequence, later 23505.

nodes.label: bigint primary key
nodes.rationale: int stops at 2147483647 and sequences advance on attempts. int→bigint is a full rewrite under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE (431 ms / 200k).

nodes.label: pg returns bigint as a string
nodes.rationale: 64-bit exceeds JavaScript safe integer range. user.id + 1 yields '11'. Treat ids as opaque strings; do not install a global int8 parser.

nodes.label: Natural key
nodes.rationale: Right for immutable reference data (ISO 4217). Needing ON UPDATE CASCADE is the signal the key is mutable and wrong.

nodes.label: Surrogate key
nodes.rationale: Settles identity, not uniqueness. A users table with id and no UNIQUE(email) accumulates duplicate accounts.

nodes.label: UUIDv7
nodes.rationale: Time-ordered UUID restores insert locality. Random v4 scatters btree inserts. 16 bytes vs 8. Adding uuid DEFAULT gen_random_uuid() rewrites (902 ms / 200k).

nodes.label: Composite primary key
nodes.rationale: Natural fit for a join table. The pair is the uniqueness rule. Index serves the leading column only.

nodes.label: Foreign key
nodes.rationale: The database refuses a row that points at nothing. Application check-then-insert cannot close the concurrency window.

nodes.label: ON DELETE actions
nodes.rationale: NO ACTION 23503, RESTRICT 23001, CASCADE deletes children, SET NULL, SET DEFAULT. Map both error codes to HTTP 409.

nodes.label: NO ACTION vs RESTRICT
nodes.rationale: Difference appears only when deferred. NO ACTION can check at COMMIT; RESTRICT always fires immediately.

nodes.label: Index every FK referencing column
nodes.rationale: PostgreSQL indexes the referenced side only. Unindexed child FK: parent delete 33.6 ms vs 8.7 ms indexed at 300k children.

nodes.label: Application cannot enforce referential integrity
nodes.rationale: Between findParent and insertChild another transaction can delete the parent. Only the database evaluates the constraint as part of the write.

nodes.label: CHECK constraint
nodes.rationale: Rejects only when the expression is false. SQLSTATE 23514. Pair with NOT NULL or write CHECK (col IS NULL OR …).

nodes.label: CHECK passes on NULL
nodes.rationale: NULL >= 18 is unknown, not false. Measured: CHECK (age >= 18) accepted a NULL age.

nodes.label: Explicit NULL bypasses DEFAULT
nodes.rationale: DEFAULT applies only when the column is omitted or given DEFAULT. ORMs that send null for unset fields override every default.

nodes.label: NOT NULL
nodes.rationale: Column property, not DEFERRABLE. Default to NOT NULL. WHERE status != 'archived' silently excludes NULL rows.

nodes.label: Constraint SQLSTATE to HTTP map
nodes.rationale: 23502 not-null 422; 23503 FK 409; 23505 unique 409; 23514 check 422; 23001 restrict 409. Match err.constraint for field-level messages.

nodes.label: Application validation vs constraints
nodes.rationale: Application validation is UX and can collect all errors. Constraints are correctness. 20 concurrent check-then-insert workers produced 20 duplicates and zero errors.

nodes.label: ALTER TABLE
nodes.rationale: Every ALTER takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE. Catalog-only is milliseconds; a rewrite is linear in row count. Both block every reader and writer.

nodes.label: Table rewrite via relfilenode
nodes.rationale: Rewrite when on-disk representation changes: int→bigint, narrowing varchar, volatile default, SET LOGGED/UNLOGGED. Widening varchar and varchar→text do not.

nodes.label: Volatile default rewrites ADD COLUMN
nodes.rationale: Constant default is catalog-only since PG11 (4 ms). gen_random_uuid() rewrites 902 ms. now() is statement-stable and did not rewrite.

nodes.label: SET LOCAL lock_timeout
nodes.rationale: A 3 ms ALTER can outage a table: ACCESS EXCLUSIVE queues behind a long read and everything after queues behind it. 55P03 and retry is the good outcome.

nodes.label: Add backfill swap type change
nodes.rationale: Add new column, backfill in batches, keep current with a trigger, swap in a short lock_timeout transaction. Interruptible unlike one ALTER TYPE.

nodes.label: ADD CONSTRAINT NOT VALID
nodes.rationale: Skips the validation scan (3 ms). VALIDATE CONSTRAINT later takes SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE so reads and writes continue.

nodes.label: Batch ALTER subcommands
nodes.rationale: One statement is one lock acquisition and at most one rewrite pass covering all sub-commands.

nodes.label: One-to-many
nodes.rationale: FK on the many side. NOT NULL makes it mandatory. Index the referencing column. Choose ON DELETE CASCADE or RESTRICT.

nodes.label: One-to-one
nodes.rationale: Make the FK the primary key. Without uniqueness it is one-to-many wearing a 1-1 name (second profile → 23505).

nodes.label: Many-to-many join table
nodes.rationale: PRIMARY KEY (a_id, b_id) is the uniqueness rule. A surrogate id permits the duplicate you meant to forbid. Name it from the domain once it carries attributes.

nodes.label: Join table trailing-column index
nodes.rationale: PK (post_id, tag_id) serves WHERE post_id. WHERE tag_id is a Seq Scan on 20k rows until a second index exists.

nodes.label: Self-referencing tree
nodes.rationale: parent_id nullable marks a root. ON DELETE CASCADE deletes whole subtrees. Arbitrary depth needs a recursive CTE.

nodes.label: Transactional DDL
nodes.rationale: CREATE ALTER DROP roll back like any statement. Most engines commit DDL implicitly. A created table vanished after a later 42P07 in the same transaction.

nodes.label: Atomic migrations
nodes.rationale: Nothing applied and nothing recorded stay consistent. Makes forward-only migrations practical. Still holds ACCESS EXCLUSIVE until commit.

nodes.label: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY
nodes.rationale: 25001 cannot run inside a transaction. VACUUM and CREATE/DROP DATABASE also cannot. A failed CONCURRENTLY build leaves an INVALID index.

nodes.label: INVALID concurrent index
nodes.rationale: Ignored by the planner and still maintained on every write. Find with pg_index WHERE NOT indisvalid, then drop and rebuild.

nodes.label: UNIQUE accepts unlimited NULLs
nodes.rationale: Two NULLs are not equal under three-valued logic. Measured: three NULLs inserted into a unique column.

nodes.label: NULLS NOT DISTINCT
nodes.rationale: PostgreSQL 15+. Treats NULLs as equal so only one is allowed (23505). Works on constraint and index forms.

nodes.label: UNIQUE constraint vs unique index
nodes.rationale: Same btree. FK can only target a constraint. Only an index can be partial, on an expression, or built CONCURRENTLY.

nodes.label: Partial unique index
nodes.rationale: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX … WHERE deleted_at IS NULL allows re-registration after soft delete. Constraints cannot be partial.

nodes.label: Case-insensitive unique email
nodes.rationale: Index on lower(email) requires WHERE lower(email)=lower($1). Non-deterministic ICU collation makes plain equality case-insensitive but disables LIKE.

nodes.label: Adding NOT NULL safely
nodes.rationale: The obvious SET NOT NULL holds ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for a full scan. Do the long part under a weaker lock.

nodes.label: Constant default ADD COLUMN since PG11
