nodes.rationale: bool NOT NULL DEFAULT false is 4 ms catalog-only. Volatile gen_random_uuid() still rewrites 902 ms and needs the old three-step dance.

nodes.label: NOT VALID then VALIDATE for NOT NULL
nodes.rationale: ADD CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID 3 ms; VALIDATE 25 ms under SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE. Direct SET NOT NULL 36 ms ACCESS EXCLUSIVE throughout. From PG12 SET NOT NULL can use the validated CHECK as proof.

nodes.label: Batched backfill
nodes.rationale: One UPDATE over millions of rows holds row locks, huge WAL, and VACUUM's cleanup horizon. Batches of a few thousand commit and stay interruptible.

nodes.label: Schema as namespace
nodes.rationale: A namespace inside a database. Also used for extensions, staging areas, and GRANT USAGE access-control boundaries.

nodes.label: search_path
nodes.rationale: Default "$user", public. The same SELECT FROM items returned different rows under tenant_a vs tenant_b. Most dangerous session setting in a pooled app.

nodes.label: Shared tables with tenant_id
nodes.rationale: Cheapest layout; one missing WHERE leaks. Pair with row-level security so the guarantee travels with the row.

nodes.label: Schema per tenant
nodes.rationale: Wrong search_path shows an empty table, not another tenant. Stops scaling around the low thousands (1000×50 = 50000 tables).

nodes.label: Database per tenant
nodes.rationale: Strongest isolation. A connection pool per tenant; cross-tenant queries impossible.

nodes.label: Row-level security tenant isolation
nodes.rationale: USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::bigint). A rule the application can forget is not a rule.

nodes.label: SET LOCAL search_path
nodes.rationale: SET search_path persists on a pooled connection. SET LOCAL reverts on commit. Schema name cannot be $1; validate against pg_namespace then escapeIdentifier.

nodes.label: Unquoted identifiers fold to lower case
nodes.rationale: CREATE TABLE "UserAccounts" then SELECT FROM UserAccounts → 42P01 relation useraccounts does not exist. Quoted names must be quoted forever.

nodes.label: snake_case convention
nodes.rationale: What unquoted identifiers become anyway. Plural tables, singular columns, <table>_<cols>_key/fkey/check/idx matching PostgreSQL generated names.

nodes.label: Constraint names are an API
nodes.rationale: err.constraint turns 23505 + users_email_key into a field-level 409. Auto-generated names change on column rename; name them explicitly.

nodes.label: 63-byte identifier limit
nodes.rationale: Truncated silently with a NOTICE. Two long index names that differ after byte 63 collide and the second CREATE INDEX fails as a duplicate.

nodes.label: user is reserved
nodes.rationale: SELECT * FROM user returns current_user, not a table. Plural users dodges this and most reserved-word collisions.

nodes.label: First normal form
nodes.rationale: One value per column. Comma-separated product_names cannot be joined, indexed, or counted without parsing strings.

nodes.label: Second normal form
nodes.rationale: No partial dependency on part of a composite key. product_name depends only on product_id, not (order_id, product_id).

nodes.label: Third normal form
nodes.rationale: No dependency between non-key columns. customer_city belongs on customers, not orders, or a move leaves contradictory cities.

nodes.label: Depend on the key the whole key and nothing but the key
nodes.rationale: Plain-language test that replaces formal 1NF/2NF/3NF. Duplication permits contradiction two concurrent writers cannot prevent.

nodes.label: Historical price snapshot
nodes.rationale: unit_cents on the order line is a different fact from products.price_cents. Not denormalization; joining would rewrite past invoices.

nodes.label: Denormalize against a measurement
nodes.rationale: A slow read is fixable later; inconsistent data is often unfixable. Prefer generated columns and materialized views the database maintains.

nodes.label: DROP RESTRICT default
nodes.rationale: 2BP01 dependent_objects_still_exist. The error NOTICE list is the cheapest inventory of dependents.

nodes.label: DROP CASCADE
nodes.rationale: Drops views, constraints, triggers that cannot exist without the object. Child table survives; only its FK is dropped, then orphans accumulate.

nodes.label: DROP CASCADE vs ON DELETE CASCADE
nodes.rationale: Same word, different mechanism. DROP CASCADE acts on schema dependencies; ON DELETE CASCADE acts on row references.

nodes.label: Rename before drop
nodes.rationale: Two deploys: stop referencing, rename to _deprecated_DATE (42703 for stragglers), drop later. Dropping makes data unreachable immediately.

nodes.label: Sequence
nodes.rationale: Separate object whose state is deliberately outside the transaction. Every surprising sequence behaviour follows from that.

nodes.label: Sequence gaps
nodes.rationale: Four attempts produced ids 1 and 4. Required for concurrency: transactional nextval would serialise all inserts. CACHE and crash recovery also leave holes.

nodes.label: Gapless counter row
nodes.rationale: Invoice numbers cannot use a sequence. UPDATE counters SET n = n + 1 RETURNING n serialises every insert on that counter. Gapless and concurrent are mutually exclusive.

nodes.label: ALTER SEQUENCE OWNED BY
nodes.rationale: Lifecycle only: owned sequences drop with the table (serial/identity). Hand-created sequences survive DROP TABLE. Does not restrict nextval.

nodes.label: RETURNING id over currval
nodes.rationale: currval is session state (55000 if unused). lastval() silently changes if a trigger consumes another sequence. RETURNING is unambiguous and one round trip.

nodes.label: Generated column
nodes.rationale: Computed from other columns of the same row. Writing it raises 428C9 so it cannot drift. Prefer over a trigger when the value is a pure same-row function.

nodes.label: STORED generated columns only
nodes.rationale: PostgreSQL 18 has no VIRTUAL. Use a view or expression index for computed-on-read. ADD COLUMN with a generated expression rewrites the table.

nodes.label: Generated expression must be IMMUTABLE
nodes.rationale: now(), random(), nextval(), other tables, STABLE functions → 42P17. Falsely marking IMMUTABLE silently corrupts stored values.

nodes.label: UNLOGGED table
nodes.rationale: ~1.5× faster inserts (150→98 ms / 100k). Truncated on crash recovery, never replicated, empty after failover. SET LOGGED/UNLOGGED rewrites (230 ms / 200k).

nodes.label: TEMPORARY table
nodes.rationale: Private to one session (pg_temp_N). Shadows same-named permanent tables via search_path. Lives in temp_buffers (default 8 MB).

nodes.label: ON COMMIT DROP
nodes.rationale: Pooled connections reuse sessions. A leftover temp table leaks into the next request. Hold one checked-out client; prefer a CTE if the data is one-statement only.

nodes.label: COMMENT ON
nodes.rationale: Catalog documentation via obj_description/col_description. information_schema does not expose comments. \d hides them; \d+ shows them. NULL deletes.

nodes.label: Comments in migrations
nodes.rationale: Hand-typed comments vanish on rebuild. pg_dump includes them. Lost when an object is dropped and recreated; not inherited by partitions.

nodes.label: Deferrable constraint
nodes.rationale: Checked at COMMIT. Applies to UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, EXCLUDE, FK. Not NULL and CHECK in practice cannot be deferred. Cannot serve as ON CONFLICT arbiter.

nodes.label: Circular foreign keys
nodes.rationale: DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED lets both inserts succeed; immediate fails 23503. Often a modelling smell versus a nullable FK plus is_primary.

nodes.label: DEFERRABLE INITIALLY IMMEDIATE
nodes.rationale: Fail fast by default; SET CONSTRAINTS … DEFERRED opts in. Preferred declaration so nothing pays until a transaction asks.

nodes.label: Deferred unique column swap
nodes.rationale: Swapping unique positions collides mid-statement (23505). Needs a deferrable constraint, not a bare unique index.

nodes.label: Table inheritance
nodes.rationale: Predates declarative partitioning. Parent PK is not inherited: two child rows with id 1 accepted. Use essentially never for new work.

nodes.label: Primary keys are not inherited
nodes.rationale: NOT NULL and CHECK inherit. PK, UNIQUE, and FK do not. A FK pointing at the parent misses child rows. SELECT on parent sees children.

nodes.label: Declarative partitioning
nodes.rationale: Enforces the key across partitions (duplicate 23505). No matching partition → 23514. Worth it for detach-drop or partition-key pruning; not below tens of millions of rows.

nodes.label: Unique constraint must include partition key
nodes.rationale: Global uniqueness on id alone is not enforceable without checking every partition. Generate ids centrally and accept uniqueness on trust, or add the partition key.

nodes.label: ONLY excludes children
nodes.rationale: DELETE FROM parent includes children unless ONLY. pg_inherits also backs partitioning; check relkind = 'p' for a partitioned parent.

nodes.label: Choosing a tenancy model
nodes.rationale: Decision page, not mechanism. Migrations and cross-tenant reporting pull opposite isolation. Shared schema is the usual SaaS default.

nodes.label: Shared schema default
nodes.rationale: Scales to millions of tenants, migrations run once, reporting is one query. Isolation is configuration (RLS, non-owner role, SET LOCAL) not structure.

nodes.label: tenant_id leads every index
nodes.rationale: Every query is tenant-scoped, including the RLS predicate. An index on (created_at) cannot serve the filter on every query.

nodes.label: Uniqueness is per tenant
nodes.rationale: UNIQUE (tenant_id, slug). A global unique slug is unintended cross-tenant coupling. tenant_id is NOT NULL with an FK.

nodes.label: RESTRICTIVE RLS plus FORCE
nodes.rationale: RESTRICTIVE applies regardless of permissive policies. FORCE stops the table owner bypassing RLS — the role a careless app connects as.

nodes.label: set_config LOCAL app.tenant_id
nodes.rationale: Plain SET persisted across pooled handoff (ex54). SET LOCAL x = $1 is 42601; use set_config(name, value, true) inside a transaction.

nodes.label: Schema-per-tenant
nodes.rationale: Right when isolation is contractual or regulatory, schemas genuinely differ, or per-tenant restore is routine. Cost: migrations run N times, cross-tenant queries become UNION over N, catalog grows, search_path is safety-critical.

nodes.label: Database-per-tenant
nodes.rationale: Rare: a small number of large tenants needing strict isolation, per-tenant restore and resource limits. Connection pooling multiplies per database; onboarding is provisioning.

nodes.label: Shared schema with RLS
nodes.rationale: Default: cheapest operations, weakest structural isolation, most isolation bought back with RESTRICTIVE RLS plus FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY. Only reversible starting point.

nodes.label: Tenancy decision order
nodes.rationale: Contract or regulation first; then tenant count (thousands force shared); then cross-tenant query frequency; then genuine schema variation. Do not choose for hypothetical isolation.

nodes.label: Shared-to-separated migration asymmetry
nodes.rationale: Shared to separated is filter-and-copy. Separated to shared remaps colliding identity values everywhere they are referenced.

nodes.label: SET LOCAL mandatory for tenant context
nodes.rationale: Plain SET persists on a pooled connection into the next request. With RLS keyed on app.tenant_id this is a concurrency-only leak. Use set_config(..., true).

nodes.label: tenant_id leads every index
nodes.rationale: Every query is tenant-scoped in application code and via the RLS predicate, so an index that does not lead with tenant_id cannot serve the filter on every query.

nodes.label: Tenant onboarding
nodes.rationale: Shared schema is an INSERT; schema-per-tenant is CREATE SCHEMA plus migrations; database-per-tenant is provisioning. Must be idempotent and transactional.

nodes.label: Deleting a tenant completely
nodes.rationale: Separated models DROP SCHEMA CASCADE or DROP DATABASE. Shared schema DELETEs every table in FK order, ideally ON DELETE CASCADE plus information_schema-generated lists. Backups still hold data for the retention window.

nodes.label: Noisy neighbours
nodes.rationale: PostgreSQL offers no intra-database isolation. Mitigate with per-role statement_timeout and work_mem, separate pools per tier, app rate limits, a reporting replica, or move a large tenant out.

nodes.label: Hybrid tenancy
nodes.rationale: Long tail on shared schema, dedicated databases for the largest or contractually separated few. Arriving from shared is the reversible direction.

nodes.label: BYPASSRLS analytics role
nodes.rationale: Global billing and admin queries must bypass RLS via a dedicated named role, not the table owner, so unrestricted access is explicit.

nodes.label: application_name includes the tenant
nodes.rationale: pg_stat_statements normalises tenant id into a parameter and aggregates across tenants. application_name gives pg_stat_activity and the slow-query log per-tenant attribution.

nodes.label: Tenant isolation tests
nodes.rationale: Run as the application role. The forgotten case is two sequential requests for different tenants on one pooled connection, which catches SET versus SET LOCAL.

nodes.label: Shared schema shards later
nodes.rationale: tenant_id is already the natural partition key. Keep it on every table and avoid cross-tenant foreign keys so splitting clusters later is routing.

nodes.label: Default to shared schema with RLS
nodes.rationale: Choose separation only when isolation is contractual or regulatory. Schema-per-tenant chosen for safety buys a permanent migration tax for a property FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY already provides.

nodes.label: SELECT alias visibility
nodes.rationale: WHERE runs before the select list exists so aliases raise 42703. ORDER BY runs after so the alias works. Repeat the expression in WHERE.

nodes.label: SELECT * is for psql not code
nodes.rationale: New columns silently widen payloads, defeat index-only scans, leak column order, and collapse duplicate join names to the last one.

nodes.label: pg returns bigint as a string
nodes.rationale: bigint and numeric exceed Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER so pg returns strings. count(*) is bigint; cast to int in SQL. Do not parseInt a real bigint.

nodes.label: Three-valued logic in WHERE
nodes.rationale: WHERE keeps only true. Unknown is discarded like false, silently. NULL != 5 is unknown so the NULL row is dropped.

nodes.label: IS DISTINCT FROM
nodes.rationale: Null-safe comparison: NULL differs from everything except another NULL. NULL = NULL is null; NULL IS NOT DISTINCT FROM NULL is true.

nodes.label: NOT IN with NULL returns nothing
nodes.rationale: x NOT IN (a, NULL) expands to x != a AND x != NULL, which can never be true. Usually arrives from a subquery with a nullable column.

nodes.label: NOT EXISTS over NOT IN
nodes.rationale: Null-safe anti-join and usually plans better. Prefer NOT EXISTS for subqueries always.

nodes.label: Half-open time ranges
nodes.rationale: BETWEEN is inclusive on both ends so monthly reports double-count midnight. Use >= start AND < end.

nodes.label: Predicates that defeat indexes
nodes.rationale: An index on col serves a predicate on bare col. date(created_at), lower(email), or col + 1 require a rewrite or a matching expression index.

nodes.label: LIKE ILIKE and POSIX regex
nodes.rationale: Btree serves only anchored LIKE prefix. ILIKE and leading-wildcard LIKE need lower() plus expression index or pg_trgm. Escape user wildcards.

nodes.label: OFFSET cost grows with depth
nodes.rationale: OFFSET is defined as produce then discard. Measured 1.22 ms at 0 vs 105.85 ms at 499980 on 500000 rows; EXPLAIN showed rows=500000 feeding Limit of 20.

nodes.label: Keyset pagination
nodes.rationale: WHERE id > $1 ORDER BY id LIMIT 20 seeks the index. Same depth: 0.93 ms and 4 buffers versus 105.85 ms and 5045. Costs random access.

nodes.label: OFFSET pages drift under writes
nodes.rationale: A count, not a position. An insert between requests serves the boundary row twice; a delete hides a row. Keyset uses a value cursor.

nodes.label: Unique ORDER BY tiebreaker
nodes.rationale: Ties have undefined order. Paging 100 rows by 5 without a unique column: 54 distinct ids and 46 repeats. Append the primary key.

nodes.label: LIMIT n+1 next-page flag
nodes.rationale: count(*) on 500000 rows was 25.69 ms; reltuples 0.49 ms. Asking for one extra row answers has-next at no extra scan. Clamp user LIMIT.

nodes.label: Always name INSERT target columns
nodes.rationale: Positional VALUES binds to current column order so a schema change silently rewires inserts. Omit vs DEFAULT apply the default; explicit NULL overrides it.

nodes.label: Bulk insert speed ladder
nodes.rationale: 10000 rows: autocommit 19551 ms, one transaction 2262 ms, multi-row VALUES 148 ms, unnest 81 ms, COPY 243 ms. WAL flush plus round trips dominate.

nodes.label: 65535 parameter ceiling
nodes.rationale: Protocol stores the count in 16 bits. 21845 rows times 3 columns succeeded; one more failed with 08P01 about parameter formats. Chunk or unnest one array per column.

nodes.label: Identity consumed before conflict
nodes.rationale: Sequences are non-transactional. Three runs of a two-row idempotent seed left last_value at 6. Gaps are expected.

nodes.label: RETURNING on every write
nodes.rationale: INSERT and UPDATE return the row after the change; DELETE returns it just before disappearing. Same statement, no READ COMMITTED race, one round trip.

nodes.label: RETURNING old and new (PostgreSQL 18)
nodes.rationale: New in 18: RETURNING old.qty AS was, new.qty AS now. Pre-18 needs a self-join. INSERT old is null; DELETE new is null.

nodes.label: ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING trap
nodes.rationale: A skipped row is not returned. Retry path reading rows[0].id crashes. Force a row with a no-op DO UPDATE; xmax = 0 distinguishes insert from update.

nodes.label: RETURNING feeding a CTE
nodes.rationale: DELETE RETURNING into INSERT archive is one atomic statement. Sub-statements share a snapshot and can only see another CTE via its RETURNING output. No ORDER BY on RETURNING itself.

nodes.label: Atomic upsert
nodes.rationale: Only correct insert-if-absent. Check-then-insert raced: 20 workers produced 20 duplicates and zero errors. MERGE can still raise unique_violation under concurrent inserts.

nodes.label: EXCLUDED proposed row
nodes.rationale: EXCLUDED is the row that would have been inserted. table.qty + EXCLUDED.qty accumulates; SET qty = EXCLUDED.qty overwrites. WHERE on DO UPDATE skips no-op writes.

nodes.label: xmax = 0 as was_insert
nodes.rationale: xmax is 0 for a freshly inserted tuple. Implementation detail; prefer created_at versus updated_at if the distinction is load-bearing.

nodes.label: Conflict target needs a unique index
nodes.rationale: 42P10 without a matching unique or exclusion constraint. Partial indexes need a matching WHERE. Deferrable unique constraints cannot be the arbiter.

nodes.label: UPDATE FROM join update
nodes.rationale: FROM supplies rows, WHERE joins, SET reads source columns. Unmatched targets stay untouched. Duplicate sources pick one row arbitrarily with no error.

nodes.label: UPDATE FROM duplicate-source trap
nodes.rationale: Three candidate prices, rowCount 1, one value chosen arbitrarily. MERGE rejects the same input with 21000. Deduplicate with DISTINCT ON if staying on UPDATE FROM.

nodes.label: Lost update from read-modify-write
nodes.rationale: 20 concurrent SELECT-then-UPDATE increments produced 2 with no errors. SET qty = qty + 1 produced 20 under a row lock.

nodes.label: In-place increment SET qty = qty + 1
nodes.rationale: When the new value is a function of the old one, compute it in SQL. Otherwise FOR UPDATE, optimistic version, or SERIALIZABLE plus 40001 retry.

nodes.label: COALESCE PATCH semantics
nodes.rationale: SET col = COALESCE($n, col) leaves omitted fields alone but cannot set a column to null. For that, build SET from present keys over an allowlist.

nodes.label: UPDATE writes a new tuple version
nodes.rationale: Never in-place. Dead versions await VACUUM. Non-HOT updates also add index entries. SET x = x is not free.

nodes.label: Extended query protocol
nodes.rationale: Not escaping. Statement is parsed then values are bound. Multi-statement text with parameters fails 42601. Concatenated payload executed two statements and dropped a table.

nodes.label: Parameters cannot be identifiers
nodes.rationale: ORDER BY $1 sorts by a constant string. name and price produced identical order with no error. Allowlist columns or format %I.

nodes.label: Identifier allowlist
nodes.rationale: User input selects a key in a map of hard-coded identifiers. Interpolated text never comes from the request. Injection payload rejected 400 before SQL.

nodes.label: format %I for dynamic identifiers
nodes.rationale: Quotes as an identifier so a DROP payload becomes a nonexistent column name. %L quotes literals; %s quotes nothing. Values in app code still use $1.

nodes.label: Empty params array stays simple protocol
nodes.rationale: [] still uses the simple query protocol and runs multiple statements. Safety comes from bound values, not from the argument being present.

nodes.label: FROM WHERE GROUP BY HAVING SELECT DISTINCT ORDER BY LIMIT
nodes.rationale: SELECT is seventh so aliases do not exist in WHERE. DISTINCT applies after the select list. LIMIT without ORDER BY is arbitrary.

nodes.label: Logical order is not execution order
nodes.rationale: Defines semantics. Planner may push predicates, use top-N heapsort, reorder joins. Putting the most selective WHERE first has no effect.

nodes.label: WHERE versus HAVING
nodes.rationale: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after. Aggregates in WHERE raise 42803. Non-aggregates in WHERE reduce work.

nodes.label: No default row order
nodes.rationale: Not insertion order. Can change after VACUUM, a plan switch, or an UPDATE that relocates a heap tuple. If order matters, state it.

nodes.label: NULLS LAST and NULLS FIRST
nodes.rationale: Default NULLS LAST for ASC and NULLS FIRST for DESC. Reversing a UI sort moves empty rows from bottom to top. Indexes record null ordering too.

nodes.label: musl versus glibc collation split
nodes.rationale: Identical PostgreSQL 18.4, both reporting datcollate en_US.utf8. Alpine musl sorts by byte value; Debian glibc uses dictionary order. Range queries change too.

nodes.label: Pin an ICU collation
nodes.rationale: ICU ships with PostgreSQL and is identical across images. builtin C.UTF-8 is fast and stable for identifiers. Nondeterministic ICU can do case-insensitive equality but forbids LIKE.

nodes.label: libc upgrade can corrupt text btrees
nodes.rationale: Index is physically ordered by the old collation. New rules miss present rows. Remedy REINDEX; prevention is ICU or C/builtin.

nodes.label: ON DELETE RESTRICT NO ACTION CASCADE SET NULL
nodes.rationale: RESTRICT raises 23001 immediately and cannot defer. NO ACTION raises 23503 and can be DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED. CASCADE is transitive. Unindexed FKs scan the child table.

nodes.label: ctid batched DELETE
nodes.rationale: DELETE takes no LIMIT (42601). Batch via ctid IN (SELECT ctid ... LIMIT n). 100000 rows: one shot 115 ms, 10 batches 484 ms, but locks release, VACUUM is not held back, job is interruptible.

nodes.label: DELETE does not shrink the table
nodes.rationale: 47 MB before and after deleting half the rows, still 47 MB after VACUUM, 24 MB after VACUUM FULL. VACUUM truncates only trailing empty pages.

nodes.label: Soft delete is an UPDATE
nodes.rationale: Setting deleted_at fires no cascade, unique constraints still see the row, every query needs WHERE deleted_at IS NULL. Orphaned orders stayed visible.

nodes.label: DISTINCT ON
nodes.rationale: Keeps the first row per group as ORDER BY produced them, whole row included. PostgreSQL-specific. Index (group, sort) removes the Sort.

nodes.label: DISTINCT ON ORDER BY rule
nodes.rationale: DISTINCT ON expressions must be the leading ORDER BY expressions or 42P10. Omitting ORDER BY is legal and returns an arbitrary row per group.

nodes.label: DISTINCT ON versus row_number versus LATERAL
nodes.rationale: DISTINCT ON for top-1 over a whole table. row_number for top-N or the rank. LATERAL when the outer set is small and indexed, and to keep groups with no match.

nodes.label: TRUNCATE
nodes.rationale: Near O(1) new empty files. 4.4 ms versus DELETE 12.7 ms on 10000 rows. No WHERE, no RETURNING, ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, own privilege, blocked by inbound FKs.

nodes.label: TRUNCATE is transactional in PostgreSQL
nodes.rationale: 100 rows, TRUNCATE inside a transaction, ROLLBACK, all 100 back. Unlike MySQL and Oracle where TRUNCATE commits implicitly.

nodes.label: TRUNCATE RESTART IDENTITY
nodes.rationale: Plain TRUNCATE left next id at 10001. Sequences are separate objects. Tests asserting id === 1 fail on the second run without RESTART IDENTITY.

nodes.label: TRUNCATE CASCADE versus DROP CASCADE
nodes.rationale: TRUNCATE CASCADE empties referencing tables transitively. DROP CASCADE removes dependent objects and leaves child data. Prefer naming every table.

nodes.label: TRUNCATE fires no row triggers
nodes.rationale: AFTER DELETE FOR EACH ROW logged 2 for DELETE and nothing more for TRUNCATE. Audit and counters silently skip. Use AFTER TRUNCATE FOR EACH STATEMENT.

nodes.label: COALESCE
nodes.rationale: First non-null argument; short-circuits. NULLIF(a, b) returns NULL when equal, used as x / NULLIF(y, 0) to avoid 22012.

nodes.label: GREATEST and LEAST skip nulls
nodes.rationale: GREATEST(NULL, 2) returned 2. Opposite of almost every other operator. Row-wise, not aggregates.

nodes.label: CASE expression
nodes.rationale: First match wins; implicit ELSE NULL. Short form uses = so WHEN NULL never matches. Put IS NULL first in the long form.

nodes.label: || versus concat versus concat_ws
nodes.rationale: 'x' || NULL is NULL; concat('x', NULL) is x. concat_ws skips null values including their separator; a null separator voids the call.

nodes.label: SQL strings are 1-indexed
nodes.rationale: substring('abcdef' FROM 2 FOR 3) is bcd; FOR is a length not an end. split_part field 2 is the second field. Unlike JavaScript.

nodes.label: length versus octet_length
nodes.rationale: 'héllo' is length 5 and octet_length 6. varchar(n) counts characters. Btree index entries have a byte limit.

nodes.label: format placeholders
nodes.rationale: %I identifier, %L literal, %s unquoted. Injection payload became a quoted column name rather than executed SQL.

nodes.label: now() is transaction start
nodes.rationale: Alias for transaction_timestamp(). Two inserts 150 ms apart shared a timestamp. statement_timestamp is per statement; clock_timestamp advances mid-statement.

nodes.label: date maps to JS Date at local midnight
nodes.rationale: date 2026-01-01 printed as 2025-12-31T18:30:00Z at UTC+5:30. Return to_char YYYY-MM-DD or setTypeParser on OID 1082. timestamptz is lossless.

nodes.label: date_trunc bucketing
nodes.rationale: Returns a timestamp so it sorts and indexes. Pass a timezone or a Berlin 00:30 order lands in the previous UTC day. Prefer over to_char grouping.

nodes.label: age() versus timestamp subtraction
nodes.rationale: age returns a symbolic interval where 1 mon is 28 to 31 days. Subtraction is elapsed days and hours. pg returns PostgresInterval objects.

nodes.label: interval 1 day versus 24 hours
nodes.rationale: 1 day keeps wall-clock time across DST (23 or 25 hours). 24 hours is elapsed. Same time tomorrow versus expires in 24 hours.

nodes.label: timestamptz for instants
nodes.rationale: Stores UTC, renders in session TimeZone. timestamp without zone is a wall-clock reading with no recoverable instant. SET TIME ZONE on a pool leaks.

nodes.label: generate_series
nodes.rationale: Set-returning function. Both endpoints inclusive so one day hourly is 25 rows. Descending needs a negative step or silently no rows. Step 0 raises 22023.

nodes.label: Gap filling with generate_series
nodes.rationale: LEFT JOIN from the series so empty days survive. count(e.id) not count(*) or every gap reads 1. Planner assumes 1000 SRF rows.

nodes.label: WITH ORDINALITY
nodes.rationale: Adds a position column to any set-returning function so client array order survives a join.

nodes.label: VALUES as a table expression
nodes.rationale: Needs AS t(cols). Types inferred from the first row. Join a client list without a temp table. Each batch size is a different statement for the plan cache.

nodes.label: unnest parallel arrays
nodes.rationale: Column-wise not a cross join. Mismatched lengths pad the short array with NULL, no error. Always cast $1::text[]. Prefer FROM unnest over select-list SRFs.

nodes.label: unnest N rows through one parameter per column
nodes.rationale: 5000 rows through 3 parameters. Multi-row VALUES would need 15000 and hit 65535 at 21845 rows. One statement shape so the plan cache stays warm. 81 ms versus COPY 243 ms at 10000 rows.

nodes.label: = ANY($1) for IN lists
nodes.rationale: One array parameter, no generated $1..$n, no ceiling, avoids the NOT IN null trap.

nodes.label: Lexicographic row comparison
nodes.rationale: (a, b) > ($1, $2) is left-to-right like words. Equivalent to an OR chain the planner handles worse. Tuple, ORDER BY and index must match columns and direction.

nodes.label: NULL in a row constructor
nodes.rationale: (1, NULL) < (1, 2) is null so WHERE discards it and pagination silently stops. Only paginate on NOT NULL columns.

nodes.label: Opaque keyset cursor
nodes.rationale: Encode the sort-key pair server-side. Meaning is tied to sort order. Base64 is not encryption; validate decoded types before binding.

nodes.label: Phase 4 gate: INSERT RETURNING, UPDATE WHERE, parameterize
MERGE SQL-standard table sync
nodes.rationale: MERGE inserts, updates and deletes in one pass. It is not a drop-in replacement for ON CONFLICT and is the wrong tool for concurrent upsert.

nodes.label: WHEN first matching branch wins
nodes.rationale: Order decides the action. A bare WHEN MATCHED before a conditional DELETE swallows every matched row.

nodes.label: MERGE USING source
nodes.rationale: Source may be a table, subquery, or VALUES. Application rows usually arrive via unnest of array parameters.

nodes.label: WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE
nodes.rationale: PostgreSQL 17 delete half of a reconcile: target rows the source no longer has. Before 17 this was DELETE WHERE NOT EXISTS.

nodes.label: MERGE rowCount is total across branches
nodes.rationale: command is MERGE and rowCount is 3 with no insert/update/delete split. Breakdown needs RETURNING merge_action().

nodes.label: MERGE RETURNING since PostgreSQL 17
nodes.rationale: Widely-repeated advice said MERGE has no RETURNING. Support arrived in 17; this page repeated the false claim until measured.

nodes.label: merge_action()
nodes.rationale: Returns INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE per row. Legal only in a MERGE RETURNING list; elsewhere raises 42601.

nodes.label: old. and new. in MERGE RETURNING
nodes.rationale: PostgreSQL 18 aliases. old.qty is null on INSERT, but a stored NULL looks the same — use merge_action() for the branch.

nodes.label: ON CONFLICT is index-arbitrated
nodes.rationale: A unique index is the arbiter so concurrent upserts resolve. MERGE evaluates ON against its snapshot and is not index-arbitrated.

nodes.label: MERGE concurrent 23505 or silent duplicate
nodes.rationale: Two transactions can both take NOT MATCHED. Isolation below SERIALIZABLE does not fix it; no unique constraint yields a silent duplicate.

nodes.label: ON CONFLICT in request handlers, MERGE in batch jobs
nodes.rationale: Concurrency is the dividing line, not RETURNING. MERGE wins for controlled ETL, DELETE-in-pass, complex WHEN, or portability.

nodes.label: 21000 MERGE cannot affect row a second time
nodes.rationale: Two source rows match one target. Deduplicate the source first, typically DISTINCT ON (key).

nodes.label: MERGE availability 15 / 17 / 18
nodes.rationale: MERGE arrived in 15. 17 added RETURNING, merge_action() and WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE. 18 added old./new. aliases.

nodes.label: Phase 5 gate: LEFT JOIN WHERE bug, NOT IN trap, join plus sum()
Phase 5 join fixture j_customers j_orders j_order_items
nodes.rationale: Dee has no orders; order 13 has no items. From topic 03 onward order 14 is an orphan with NULL customer_id.

nodes.label: INNER JOIN matching pairs
nodes.rationale: Output is pairs that satisfy ON. Unmatched left rows vanish; N matches repeat the left row N times. Dee gone, Ann twice.

nodes.label: JOIN is INNER JOIN
nodes.rationale: INNER is optional. Comma form is also inner but a missing condition is a silent cross join.

nodes.label: Nested Loop Hash Join Merge Join
nodes.rationale: Equijoin unlocks all three. Non-equality leaves only nested loop. Planner picks by cost from statistics and indexes.

nodes.label: NOT NULL FK makes child-to-parent count knowable
nodes.rationale: Child JOIN parent via NOT NULL FK yields one row per child. Parent JOIN child drops parents with no children.

nodes.label: Join fan-out
nodes.rationale: Duplicated parent rows make sum(o.total) 450 against a true 350. The join changes grain; the aggregate is then applied at the wrong grain.

nodes.label: Result grain
nodes.rationale: A join sets grain to the finest side. Aggregates are correct only on columns at that grain.

nodes.label: Pre-aggregate the child then join
nodes.rationale: Reduce the child to one row per parent before joining so no multiplication happens.

nodes.label: count(DISTINCT) rescues counts only
nodes.rationale: sum(DISTINCT o.total) collapses different orders that share a total. DISTINCT on the query removes rows, not contributions.

nodes.label: LEFT JOIN at-least-once guarantee
nodes.rationale: Every left row appears at least once, not exactly once. Fan-out still applies. Unmatched left rows are NULL-extended.

nodes.label: Manufactured NULLs indistinguishable from stored
nodes.rationale: Test a NOT NULL right-hand column, normally the primary key, to detect unmatched rows.

nodes.label: count(*) vs count(col) after LEFT JOIN
nodes.rationale: count(*) counts the NULL-extended row (5 vs 4). Per group it turns no orders into a count of 1.

nodes.label: LEFT JOIN IS NULL anti-join
nodes.rationale: Works if the tested column is NOT NULL. Prefer NOT EXISTS in new code for a dedicated Hash Anti Join.

nodes.label: WHERE on right table cancels LEFT JOIN
nodes.rationale: ON is the match rule; WHERE runs after NULL extension. NULL = 'paid' is unknown and discarded. Measured 4 rows vs 2.

nodes.label: Outer-join predicate classification
nodes.rationale: Right-table predicates belong in ON; left-table predicates in WHERE; the join key in ON. A left filter in ON does not filter.

nodes.label: Joins chain left to right
nodes.rationale: Each ON may reference any table already introduced. Referencing a later table is 42P01.

nodes.label: Inner joins reorder, outer joins do not
Downstream INNER JOIN cancels LEFT JOIN
nodes.rationale: NULL-extended rows fail the later equijoin. Continue LEFT, or parenthesise the inner pair — those are different queries.

nodes.label: join_collapse_limit default 8
nodes.rationale: Past the limit the planner stops exploring and textual order starts to matter. Split wide joins rather than raising it.

nodes.label: Fan-out compounds across independent branches
nodes.rationale: 2 tags × 3 comments = 6 rows. Pre-aggregate each child. Diagnose with count(*) vs count(DISTINCT parent.id).

nodes.label: Junction table composite primary key
nodes.rationale: Composite PK identifies the pair, forbids duplicates, and indexes the first column. Add a separate index on the second FK.

nodes.label: array_agg FILTER plus coalesce
nodes.rationale: FILTER drops the manufactured NULL row; coalesce turns empty-group NULL into {}. They fix two different NULLs.

nodes.label: Has ALL tags relational division
nodes.rationale: IN is has-any. GROUP BY parent HAVING count(DISTINCT tag_id) = cardinality($1) is has-all.

nodes.label: Two-query parent then children is not N+1
nodes.rationale: Two round trips regardless of page size. Prefer when parents are paginated or child sets are large.

nodes.label: RIGHT JOIN is LEFT JOIN with operands swapped
nodes.rationale: Prefer LEFT so the preserved table is read first. RIGHT earns its keep when FROM order is not yours to choose.

nodes.label: FULL OUTER JOIN
nodes.rationale: Keeps unmatched rows from both sides. The reconciliation, migration-verify, and snapshot-diff tool.

nodes.label: FULL JOIN only merge or hash joinable
nodes.rationale: Must track unmatched rows on both sides. Nested loop has no cheap bookkeeping, so inequality FULL JOIN is rejected.

nodes.label: Emulate FULL OUTER with LEFT plus anti-join UNION ALL
USING on FULL JOIN coalesces the key
nodes.rationale: Merged column is coalesce(left, right), never NULL for a row present on either side.

nodes.label: IS DISTINCT FROM for snapshot diffs
nodes.rationale: <> yields NULL when either side is NULL and silently drops the differing row.

nodes.label: Accidental comma join
nodes.rationale: FROM a, b with a missing WHERE is legal and silent: 4×5=20 with no error. Explicit JOIN ON makes the omission a syntax error.

nodes.label: Calendar spine gap fill
nodes.rationale: CROSS JOIN generate_series then LEFT JOIN facts with the date filter in ON. count(fact.id) not count(*); coalesce(sum, 0); to_char the date.

nodes.label: date parsed as local midnight then UTC-shifted
nodes.rationale: TZ=Asia/Calcutta makes 2026-01-01 come back as 2025-12-31T18:30:00.000Z. Format with to_char or setTypeParser(1082).

nodes.label: USING merged join column
nodes.rationale: Requires identical names. SELECT * emits one merged column. On outer joins that column is coalesced.

nodes.label: NATURAL JOIN infers from schema
nodes.rationale: A shared created_at silently cut two rows to one. No shared names degenerates to a cross join. Do not write NATURAL JOIN.

nodes.label: pg SELECT * duplicate names last-wins
nodes.rationale: Server sent six columns; JS object had four keys. Alias columns or use rowMode array.

nodes.label: Self join via aliases
nodes.rationale: FROM j_emp JOIN j_emp is 42712. Aliases give two roles. LEFT JOIN keeps the NULL-parent root.

nodes.label: Adjacency-list hierarchy
nodes.rationale: Cheapest hierarchy to write; reads need N joins or WITH RECURSIVE. Opposite trade to materialised path or closure table.

nodes.label: WITH RECURSIVE hierarchy walk
nodes.rationale: Anchor plus recursive term until empty. UNION ALL. A cycle loops forever; CYCLE (PG14+) or a path array stops it.

nodes.label: lag() beats self join for previous row
nodes.rationale: Joining on id - 1 assumes contiguous ids and breaks after deletes.

nodes.label: LATERAL correlated FROM subquery
nodes.rationale: Lets a FROM subquery see tables to its left and run once per driving row, returning many columns and many rows.

nodes.label: LEFT JOIN LATERAL ON true
nodes.rationale: CROSS JOIN LATERAL drops empty driving rows. ON true is required syntax; matching already happened in the subquery WHERE.

nodes.label: LATERAL top-N per group
nodes.rationale: With a real dimension table and an index, 9.3 ms vs 51.8 ms for row_number() on 200k rows — 5.6×. Probe ~1500 rows instead of numbering all 200000.

nodes.label: UNION deduplicates and blocks
nodes.rationale: HashAggregate 491 ms vs Append 142 ms over 600k rows — 3.5×. UNION cannot stop early under LIMIT.

nodes.label: Default to UNION ALL
nodes.rationale: Use UNION only when duplicates are possible and wrong. Disjoint sources cannot produce them.

nodes.label: EXCEPT
nodes.rationale: Compares whole rows, not a key. Prefer anti-join when the question is which entities are missing.

nodes.label: Union column names come from the first branch
Alias replaces the table name
nodes.rationale: Referring to the original name after aliasing is 42P01. That replacement is what makes self joins possible.

nodes.label: 42702 ambiguous column
nodes.rationale: PostgreSQL refuses rather than guessing. The dangerous case is an unambiguous column rebound after a later migration.

nodes.label: Output alias usable in ORDER BY and GROUP BY not WHERE
nodes.rationale: WHERE and HAVING run before SELECT so the alias does not exist (42703). GROUP BY accepting it is a PostgreSQL extension.

nodes.label: Alias every table and qualify every column
count(*) arrives as a string from pg
nodes.rationale: bigint exceeds JS safe integers. Cast ::int or register a type parser.

nodes.label: Range join with tstzrange @>
nodes.rationale: Price at time of sale. Default [) makes the 2026-06-01 changeover unambiguous. Index the range with GiST.

nodes.label: EXCLUDE USING gist no-overlap
nodes.rationale: Overlapping validity periods become a silent fan-out on only the affected SKUs.

nodes.label: Expression index pays only when selective
nodes.rationale: 200k×200k lower() join 211.5 then 212.6 ms — no change. Same index 59× faster with a 50-row driving side (65.2 → 1.1 ms).

nodes.label: Non-equality ON leaves nested loop only
Semi and anti joins
nodes.rationale: Split at the positive/negative seam: EXISTS/IN are interchangeable, while one anti-join spelling silently loses data.

nodes.label: Semi joins: EXISTS and IN
nodes.rationale: A semi join filters the left side by existence, emits the left row at most once, and exposes no right-hand columns — so it cannot fan out.

nodes.label: Semi join
nodes.rationale: Short-circuits after the first match. Written as EXISTS or IN. Use EXISTS when correlated, IN/= ANY for independent lists.

nodes.label: Parallel Hash Semi Join
nodes.rationale: EXISTS and IN both plan to Parallel Hash Semi Join. The millisecond gap is noise; choosing between them is readability, not performance.

nodes.label: JOIN plus DISTINCT costs 2.5x
nodes.rationale: HashAggregate at 189.98 ms vs Hash Semi Join at ~73–91 ms. The join materialises duplicates the semi join never produces. Gap grows with children per parent.

nodes.label: EXISTS must be correlated
nodes.rationale: Uncorrelated EXISTS is true whenever the inner table has any row. Extra conditions belong inside the subquery. SELECT 1 is convention; the select list is never evaluated.

nodes.label: = ANY($1::int[]) for IN lists
nodes.rationale: One array parameter instead of N placeholders. Avoids string assembly and the 65535-parameter protocol ceiling.

nodes.label: LATERAL LIMIT 1 when columns are needed
nodes.rationale: A semi join exposes no right-hand columns. Need the matched row? Rewrite as LEFT JOIN LATERAL … LIMIT 1, not by adding columns to EXISTS.

nodes.label: Anti joins and the NOT IN trap
nodes.rationale: NOT EXISTS implements the anti join correctly. NOT IN returns the empty set the moment the subquery contains one NULL.

nodes.label: Anti join
nodes.rationale: Keeps left rows with no match. Default spelling is NOT EXISTS. Must prove absence, so it cannot short-circuit the way a semi join does.

nodes.label: NOT IN NULL trap
nodes.rationale: x NOT IN (a,b,NULL) expands to AND of inequalities including x <> NULL, which is NULL for any x. WHERE keeps only true, so every row vanishes. Measured: Dee became [].

nodes.label: Hash Anti Join
nodes.rationale: NOT EXISTS gets Parallel Hash Anti Join. NOT IN gets Seq Scan plus subplan because the planner cannot assume the column is NULL-free.

nodes.label: LEFT JOIN … WHERE pk IS NULL
nodes.rationale: Older idiom that plans as Hash Anti Join. Correctness depends on the tested column being NOT NULL — test the primary key, not a nullable column.

nodes.label: EXCEPT is not an anti join
nodes.rationale: EXCEPT compares whole rows, de-duplicates the left side, and plans as HashSetOp. It answers set difference, not 'which left rows have no related row'.

nodes.label: Anti join needs the child FK index more
nodes.rationale: Absence must be proven for every unmatched left row. Without an index on the correlated child column that is a scan per left row.

nodes.label: GROUP BY and aggregates
nodes.rationale: GROUP BY emits one row per group. Every select-list column must be a grouping key or an aggregate. Most bugs satisfy that rule in letter and violate it in spirit.

nodes.label: Aggregation fixture
nodes.rationale: Six orders, five customers, five items. Eve has no orders; order 15 has NULL total; coupon is NULL on three orders; cancelled total is 0 not NULL.

nodes.label: agg_events 500000-row table
nodes.rationale: 5000 users, 4 kinds, 40 MB / 3783 heap pages, 71428 NULL amounts. Used for every timing in chunk 05 and later performance pages.

nodes.label: Independent fixture columns
nodes.rationale: kind from g/5000 not g%4. With user_id = g%5000, g%4 is determined by user_id when 4 divides 5000, so every user has one kind. Two moduli that share a factor are not independent.

nodes.label: Collapsing rows
nodes.rationale: An aggregate takes many values and returns one. GROUP BY decides which values go into each many. Every aggregate except count(*) skips NULL inputs.

nodes.label: NULL-skipping aggregate rule
nodes.rationale: count(*) counts rows; count(expr) counts non-NULL expr. sum/avg/min/max skip NULLs. Open group: two rows, avg 50.00 over one priced value.

nodes.label: avg(x) is sum(x)/count(x)
nodes.rationale: Not sum(x)/count(*). Measured 50.00 vs avg(coalesce(total,0))=25.00 on the open group. Which is correct is a product question.

nodes.label: Aggregate return types
nodes.rationale: count and sum(int) return bigint; sum(bigint) and avg return numeric; min/max keep the input type. avg is numeric so money does not drift.

nodes.label: bigint and numeric arrive as strings
nodes.rationale: pg will not guess a JS number that cannot represent the range. rows[0].n + 1 is '61'. Cast ::int for bounded counts or setTypeParser OID 20.

nodes.label: sum()::int overflow 22003
nodes.rationale: The ::int that makes JS convenient reintroduces the overflow bigint exists to prevent. (sum(amount)*20)::int raised 22003; left as bigint returned 3936859560.

nodes.label: Empty groups and grouping keys
nodes.rationale: Two things decide result shape: one row vs zero over an empty selection, and what the grouping key does with NULLs and expressions.

nodes.label: No GROUP BY always returns one row
nodes.rationale: Implicit group over everything. With GROUP BY, empty selection emits zero rows. Check rows[0].n without GROUP BY; check rows.length with it.

nodes.label: sum over nothing is NULL
nodes.rationale: count over nothing is 0. NULL propagates: sum(total)+shipping is NULL. coalesce(sum(x),0) in SQL before any arithmetic.

nodes.label: NULL as a grouping key
nodes.rationale: Three NULL coupons form one group. Grouping, DISTINCT, UNION and PARTITION BY use IS NOT DISTINCT FROM. Predicates use three-valued =.

nodes.label: GROUP BY omits missing combinations
nodes.rationale: No (IN, paid) row showing 0. A grid UI goes ragged. Manufacture the spine with a cross join of the dimensions and LEFT JOIN the aggregate.

nodes.label: date_trunc uses session time zone
nodes.rationale: UTC server groups by UTC days. An 18:00+00 order is already tomorrow in Delhi. Name AT TIME ZONE explicitly. Bug only appears for rows past local midnight.

nodes.label: pg parses date as local midnight
nodes.rationale: TZ=Asia/Calcutta turns 2026-03-01 into 2026-02-28T18:30:00.000Z. Return the day as to_char text so the driver cannot reinterpret it.

nodes.label: What you are allowed to select
nodes.rationale: Every expression must reduce to one value per group. PostgreSQL refuses to guess; the error is 42803, the most-seen SQL error in this phase.

nodes.label: 42803 grouping error
nodes.rationale: MySQL loose mode picks an arbitrary row. ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY restores strictness; PostgreSQL never had the loose mode.

nodes.label: Four ways out of 42803
nodes.rationale: Add to GROUP BY (changes grouping), take min/max/array_agg[1], collect all values, or take one whole row via DISTINCT ON / row_number. Do not add to GROUP BY reflexively.

nodes.label: DISTINCT ON one whole row per group
nodes.rationale: Every column comes from the same row. min(id), max(total) can invent a pair that never existed. ORDER BY must start with the DISTINCT ON keys; add NULLS LAST.

nodes.label: Functional dependency on primary key
nodes.rationale: GROUP BY o.id licenses o.status. Per table only; grouping by the other side's key is 42803. Lost inside UNION/DISTINCT/SRF views.

nodes.label: UNIQUE does not grant functional dependency
nodes.rationale: A unique column can be NULL and NULLs group together, so uniqueness alone does not guarantee one row per group. Requires a declared PRIMARY KEY.

nodes.label: Ordinals, aliases and DISTINCT
nodes.rationale: Where 1 and an output alias are legal, and why GROUP BY x with no aggregate is SELECT DISTINCT x, all fall out of evaluation order.

nodes.label: SQL evaluation order
nodes.rationale: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT (aliases born) → windows → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT. WHERE cannot see aliases (42703); ORDER BY can.

nodes.label: GROUP BY ordinals
nodes.rationale: GROUP BY 1,2 breaks silently when a column is inserted in the select list. Reserve ordinals for long expressions; name columns in anything that ships.

nodes.label: GROUP BY output alias is a PG extension
nodes.rationale: GROUP BY runs before SELECT, yet PostgreSQL permits output names including computed expressions. Standard SQL does not; it will not port.

nodes.label: GROUP BY without aggregate is DISTINCT
nodes.rationale: 54.49 ms vs 55.74 ms on 500000 rows, both HashAggregate. DISTINCT cannot HAVING-filter. Combining DISTINCT + GROUP BY is almost always undiagnosed fan-out.

nodes.label: GROUP BY does not order
nodes.rationale: HashAggregate emits hash order. GroupAggregate happens to emit sorted. A report that ships without ORDER BY reshuffles when the planner switches.

nodes.label: 42703 vs 42803
nodes.rationale: 42703 is no such column (alias too early or typo). 42803 is grouping error (column exists but is not one-per-group). Aggregate in GROUP BY is 42803 because it is circular.

nodes.label: How GROUP BY executes
nodes.rationale: Two strategies: hash table or sort-and-walk. Same query over 500000 rows was 59 ms or 118 ms depending on work_mem.

nodes.label: HashAggregate
nodes.rationale: Hash table, one entry per group. Memory scales with group count, not row count. Output is hash order. Chosen when groups fit in work_mem.

nodes.label: GroupAggregate
nodes.rationale: Sort by the key, then one pass. Needs sorted input. Output is grouped-key order. Over an ordered index scan it uses O(1) memory.

nodes.label: work_mem is per node per worker
nodes.rationale: A plan with three hashes and three sorts peaks at a multiple of the setting. Raise with SET LOCAL inside a transaction, never globally.

nodes.label: Partial and Finalize aggregation
nodes.rationale: Workers produce combinable partials; leader merges. count/sum/min/max/avg combine. count(DISTINCT x) cannot. actual rows=166666.67 is average per loop.

nodes.label: HashAggregate Batches spill
nodes.rationale: Batches: 1 fits. Batches: 5 with Disk Usage 3696kB spilled (PG 13+ partitions instead of exceeding work_mem). 59.57 ms → 117.68 ms at work_mem=64kB.

nodes.label: Compare Buffers before milliseconds
nodes.rationale: Identical plans, shared hit=3783, 59.57 ms vs 83.22 ms. Clock said 40% worse; buffers said identical work. Scan dominates: 4 groups 58.59 ms vs 5000 groups 59.57 ms.

nodes.label: GroupAggregate over ordered index scan
nodes.rationale: At 64kB work_mem the index dropped 117.68 ms to 85.19 ms and buffers 3801 to 577. At default work_mem the index changed nothing. Heap Fetches: 0 is a true index-only scan.

nodes.label: count variants
nodes.rationale: count(*), count(col) and count(DISTINCT col) return 6, 5 and 2 over the same six rows. The wrong one is never a syntax error.

nodes.label: Three different questions
nodes.rationale: How many orders, how many have a total, how many different coupons — spelled almost identically.

nodes.label: Three count forms
nodes.rationale: count(*) counts rows. count(expr) counts non-NULL. DISTINCT then de-duplicates survivors and does not bring NULLs back. count(DISTINCT coupon)=2, not 3.

nodes.label: count(1) is not faster than count(*)
nodes.rationale: 26.73 vs 28.35 ms, identical plans, buffers=3783. count(*) is 'no argument'; the executor counts tuples. Scan is the cost.

nodes.label: count(DISTINCT (a, b)) row constructor
nodes.rationale: count(DISTINCT a, b) parses as two-argument count and fails 42883. Wrap columns in a row constructor.

nodes.label: A row containing NULL is not NULL
nodes.rationale: count(DISTINCT (status, coupon)) is 4 including (open,NULL) and (cancelled,NULL). Composite comparison uses IS NOT DISTINCT FROM per field.

nodes.label: The LEFT JOIN trap and fan-out
nodes.rationale: LEFT JOIN invents a row for every unmatched left row. count(*) counts it. Eve is reported as having one order.

nodes.label: LEFT JOIN count(*) trap
nodes.rationale: Never count(*) inside a LEFT JOIN. Count a NOT NULL column of the right table — its PK. count(o.total) under-counts real orders that are unpriced. HAVING count(*) > 0 matches everyone.

nodes.label: Join fan-out inflates sum
nodes.rationale: Order 10 has two items, so its 100 is added twice. Measured 650 against true 550. Two child joins multiply.

nodes.label: sum(DISTINCT) is not a fan-out fix
nodes.rationale: It de-duplicates values, not rows. Two different 200s collapse. Measured 350 — a third wrong answer. There is no DISTINCT-shaped fix for sum.

nodes.label: LATERAL pre-aggregation
nodes.rationale: Aggregate the child before joining so no duplication reaches parent columns. Measured 6 orders, 550 revenue, 5 item rows. LEFT JOIN LATERAL … ON true keeps childless parents.

nodes.label: count(DISTINCT) survives fan-out
nodes.rationale: De-duplicating ids is idempotent under row duplication; addition is not. Diagnose fan-out by comparing count(*) to count(DISTINCT parent pk).

nodes.label: What counting costs
nodes.rationale: Over the same 500000 rows, counting cost 27 ms to 209 ms. The expensive form is count(DISTINCT) because it cannot be parallelised.

nodes.label: count(DISTINCT) is not combinable
nodes.rationale: Two workers both seeing user 7 cannot combine partial counts without the values. Falls back to a single-threaded external merge sort. 208.87 ms, Disk 5880kB.

nodes.label: DISTINCT-subquery rewrite
nodes.rationale: count(*) FROM (SELECT DISTINCT user_id …) is a parallel HashAggregate. 208.87 ms → 57.61 ms, 3.6×, no spill.

nodes.label: Index flips the rewrite ranking
nodes.rationale: With a btree leading on the counted column, count(DISTINCT) becomes an index-only scan at 63.53 ms / 575 buffers and beats the rewrite's 76.21 ms sequential scan.

nodes.label: MVCC prevents a stored row count
nodes.rationale: The correct count depends on the asking transaction's snapshot. A stored counter would also serialise every insert and delete.

nodes.label: HAVING vs WHERE
nodes.rationale: WHERE filters rows into groups; HAVING filters groups out. Test: can the predicate be decided by looking at one row?

nodes.label: Filtering groups, not rows
nodes.rationale: HAVING can see aggregates; WHERE cannot, because when WHERE runs no aggregate has been computed yet.

nodes.label: WHERE vs HAVING
nodes.rationale: WHERE status='paid' is a row predicate. HAVING count(*)>1 is a group predicate. HAVING may use an aggregate not in the select list. HAVING a non-key column is 42803.

nodes.label: HAVING without GROUP BY
nodes.rationale: Filters the single implicit group. HAVING count(*)>99 on six rows returns zero rows, not a row containing 6. The only way an ungrouped aggregate returns nothing.

nodes.label: HAVING cannot see output aliases
nodes.rationale: Both WHERE and HAVING run before SELECT materialises. Error is 42703. Repeat the expression, or wrap and filter outside — the only way to filter a window result.

nodes.label: HAVING count(*) > 0 after LEFT JOIN
nodes.rationale: The NULL-extended row makes count(*) at least 1. Use count(o.id) or EXISTS. 'Customers who have ordered' is a semi-join.

nodes.label: What HAVING costs
nodes.rationale: HAVING on a grouping column is rewritten into WHERE and costs nothing. HAVING on an aggregate cannot be, and every discarded group was still built.

nodes.label: HAVING on grouping columns is rewritten
nodes.rationale: GROUP BY user_id, kind HAVING kind='purchase' becomes Group Key: user_id and Filter on the seq scan. Plans identical to WHERE. Rewrite requires a non-volatile grouping-column predicate.

nodes.label: HAVING on an aggregate cannot be pushed
nodes.rationale: Filter sits on Finalize HashAggregate. Selectivity does not reduce work: keeping 0 of 5000 groups was no cheaper than keeping all. Same buffers=3783.

nodes.label: EXISTS instead of HAVING count > 0
nodes.rationale: count(…)>0 forces a full count of every group. EXISTS stops at the first match and can use an index. Does not apply when the threshold is genuinely >1.

nodes.label: 42P20 window functions not allowed in HAVING
nodes.rationale: Windows run after HAVING. Filter a window in an outer WHERE. rank() OVER (ORDER BY count(*) DESC) is legal because windows run after aggregation.

nodes.label: FILTER (WHERE ...)
nodes.rationale: Restricts one aggregate without restricting the query. Not pure CASE sugar: the two disagree about the empty set.

nodes.label: Conditional aggregation
nodes.rationale: FILTER attaches a predicate to a single aggregate. Other aggregates in the same select list still see all rows. Standard SQL since PG 9.4.

nodes.label: FILTER (WHERE …)
nodes.rationale: Goes after the aggregate's closing parenthesis and before OVER. Takes a full WHERE-style predicate. MySQL and SQL Server do not have it.

nodes.label: FILTER vs CASE on empty match
nodes.rationale: Rows exist but none match: sum FILTER is NULL, sum(CASE ELSE 0) is 0. No rows at all: both sums are NULL. count FILTER is 0 in every case.

nodes.label: count(CASE … ELSE 0) counts every row
nodes.rationale: count counts non-NULL and 0 is not NULL. Working CASE omits ELSE so non-matches are NULL. FILTER has no ELSE to get wrong.

nodes.label: FILTER pivot
nodes.rationale: GROUP BY dimension with one FILTER count per category. Counts come back 0 for empty cells; sums come back NULL and need coalesce. Columns are fixed at query-writing time.

nodes.label: When FILTER pays
nodes.rationale: FILTER is not faster than CASE. It is faster than one subquery per number: 4× the buffers and 2.5× the time.

nodes.label: FILTER vs four scalar subqueries
nodes.rationale: FILTER 65.45 ms / 3783 buffers; CASE 65.14 ms / 3783; four subqueries 161.21 ms / 15132. Buffer ratio is exactly the number of scans.

nodes.label: FILTER is not a scan filter
nodes.rationale: No index can serve a FILTER predicate. One aggregate should use WHERE. FILTER pays from the second aggregate onwards.

nodes.label: FILTER vs GROUP BY shape
nodes.rationale: Neither is faster (65 vs 72 ms). FILTER: one row, N columns, zeros for absent categories, frozen set. GROUP BY: N rows, omits empty categories, discovers new ones.

nodes.label: FILTER on aggregate window functions
nodes.rationale: Clause order is aggregate(...) FILTER (WHERE …) OVER (…). row_number/rank/lag are not aggregates and reject FILTER.

nodes.label: 42809 FILTER on a non-aggregate
nodes.rationale: wrong_object_type. Also what you get from a misspelled aggregate name rather than 'does not exist'.

nodes.label: Arrays and strings
nodes.rationale: array_agg and string_agg collect a group into one value and disagree about NULL handling, empty groups, and what arrives in JavaScript.

nodes.label: string_agg
nodes.rationale: Drops NULLs and emits no delimiter for them. Empty group is NULL not ''. text-only; integer needs ::text or 42883. coalesce before concatenation.

nodes.label: array_agg
nodes.rationale: Keeps NULLs as elements. Prefer FILTER (WHERE x IS NOT NULL) over array_remove: if every value is NULL, remove gives {} and FILTER gives NULL. Arrives as a real JS array.

nodes.label: ORDER BY inside the collection aggregate
nodes.rationale: An unordered array_agg changed order when a sibling aggregate with its own ORDER BY was added, because the executor sorted the shared input. Outer ORDER BY orders result rows, not aggregate input.

nodes.label: 42P10 DISTINCT ORDER BY must match arguments
nodes.rationale: array_agg(DISTINCT status ORDER BY id) is incoherent: after de-duplicating by status there is no single id. De-duplicate in a subquery if you need min(id).

nodes.label: JSON shapes
nodes.rationale: jsonb_build_object, to_jsonb, jsonb_agg and jsonb_object_agg cover naming fields, converting a row, collecting an array, and building a keyed map.

nodes.label: jsonb_build_object
nodes.rationale: Alternating key, value. Verbose on purpose: the API contract is written in the query, so adding a table column cannot change the response.

nodes.label: to_jsonb
nodes.rationale: Emits every column. Never point it at a table you do not control. Safe form names columns in a subquery. numeric becomes a JSON number; cast money to text first.

nodes.label: jsonb_object_agg
nodes.rationale: Rows into a keyed map. NULL key raises 22023 at runtime. Duplicate keys silently keep the last value — aggregate over already-grouped input.

nodes.label: json versus jsonb
nodes.rationale: json stores verbatim text; jsonb stores parsed binary, collapses duplicates, drops whitespace, reorders keys. jsonb is 60 vs 23 bytes here, GIN-indexable. Difference is invisible from Node because JSON.parse collapses duplicates too.

nodes.label: jsonb_agg
nodes.rationale: Collects rows into a JSON array. Arrives as a JS array; JSON.parse throws. Put ORDER BY inside, same sibling-sort inheritance as array_agg.

nodes.label: 22023 field name must not be null
nodes.rationale: jsonb_object_agg rejects a NULL key only when such a row exists, so a query that works for months breaks on the first NULL grouping value.

nodes.label: The empty-array trap
nodes.rationale: A parent with no children should return []. The naked aggregate returns [null]; FILTER alone returns null. Getting [] takes FILTER plus coalesce.

nodes.label: LEFT JOIN NULL row kept by array_agg
nodes.rationale: LEFT JOIN invents a childless parent row with NULL child columns. array_agg and jsonb_agg keep NULLs, so the client sees [null] and length 1.

nodes.label: FILTER empty group is NULL
nodes.rationale: FILTER (WHERE child.id IS NOT NULL) removes the fake row, leaving an empty group. Every aggregate over an empty input is NULL — same rule as sum over no rows.

nodes.label: Canonical child-collection idiom
nodes.rationale: coalesce(jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object(...) ORDER BY k) FILTER (WHERE id IS NOT NULL), '[]'::jsonb). Four parts: build_object, ORDER BY, FILTER, coalesce. '{}' is the empty PostgreSQL array, not a JSON array.

nodes.label: Two-level LATERAL nested payload
nodes.rationale: LEFT JOIN LATERAL … ON true nests inner GROUP BY so each order aggregates its items before the outer aggregate collects orders. Flat dual joins multiply fan-out.

nodes.label: Shape in SQL versus stitch in JS
nodes.rationale: Shape in SQL when nesting is fixed and child sets are small — one round trip, atomic, untyped. Stitch in JS when pieces are needed separately or children need pagination. Either beats N+1. Measured 292 vs 580 bytes.

nodes.label: string_agg, array_agg, jsonb_agg
nodes.rationale: These aggregates fold a group into a collection, enabling a one-query nested API payload. Every one returns NULL where empty was expected, and [null] where [] was expected.

nodes.label: string_agg
nodes.rationale: Returns text and skips NULL inputs. Opposite of array_agg and jsonb_agg on NULLs.

nodes.label: array_agg
nodes.rationale: Returns an array of the input type and keeps NULLs as elements.

nodes.label: json_agg / jsonb_agg
nodes.rationale: Returns a JSON array and keeps NULL inputs as null. jsonb_agg(child.*) also leaks every child column.

nodes.label: jsonb_object_agg
nodes.rationale: Returns a jsonb object. Key must not be NULL (error 22023).

nodes.label: OVER keeps the rows
nodes.rationale: Same aggregate, same numbers, different row count. GROUP BY collapses; OVER (PARTITION BY) attaches the group value to every original row.

nodes.label: PARTITION BY is GROUP BY that does not collapse
nodes.rationale: For each row PostgreSQL finds rows sharing the partition key, computes the aggregate, and attaches it to that row. OVER () is one partition of the whole result.

nodes.label: Running total via ORDER BY in OVER
nodes.rationale: ORDER BY inside OVER implies RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, turning the aggregate cumulative. Inner ORDER BY changes values; outer ORDER BY only presentation.

nodes.label: FILTER before OVER
nodes.rationale: count(*) FILTER (WHERE …) OVER (…). Reverse order is a syntax error. FILTER attaches only to aggregates, not row_number or rank.

nodes.label: Where windows run
nodes.rationale: Windows run after GROUP BY and HAVING, before DISTINCT and ORDER BY. Cannot filter a window in the same query level; can window over an aggregate.

nodes.label: 42P20 windowing_error
nodes.rationale: WHERE or HAVING on a window is circular: WHERE decides which rows exist and the window value depends on those rows. Compute the window in a subquery or CTE and filter outside.

nodes.label: sum(count(*)) OVER ()
nodes.rationale: count(*) is computed per GROUP BY group; then the window sums those group rows. Standard percentage-of-total on a grouped report without a self-join.

nodes.label: Named WINDOW clause
nodes.rationale: Naming convenience between HAVING and ORDER BY. Planner already merges identical definitions. Can extend with ORDER BY and a frame; cannot change PARTITION BY or override an existing ORDER BY.

nodes.label: DISTINCT runs after windows
nodes.rationale: A window value such as row_number makes every row unique, so SELECT DISTINCT stops de-duplicating. De-duplicate at an inner level first.

nodes.label: What windows cost
nodes.rationale: Every window needs input sorted by PARTITION BY then ORDER BY. One window over 500000 rows took 530 ms; two sharing a sort 999 ms; two that cannot 1518 ms.

nodes.label: WindowAgg is not parallel-aware
nodes.rationale: No Gather in the plan. Extra cores do not help. Reduce input, share partitions, or provide an ordered index.

nodes.label: Compatible windows share one sort
nodes.rationale: If one partition/order spec is a prefix of the other, one Sort serves both WindowAgg nodes. Different partitions re-sort the whole intermediate (temp blocks 1070 → 3671).

nodes.label: Index matching PARTITION BY then ORDER BY
nodes.rationale: (user_id, amount DESC) turned 530 ms external merge into 283 ms index-only scan, 3783 → 575 buffers. Incremental Sort appears when the index supplies only a prefix.

nodes.label: Window functions
nodes.rationale: A window computes an aggregate without collapsing rows. That difference from GROUP BY makes running totals, percentages of total, and rank-within-group expressible.

nodes.label: The four ranking functions
nodes.rationale: row_number, rank, dense_rank and percent_rank take no arguments and differ only in tie behaviour.

nodes.label: row_number
nodes.rationale: Consecutive integers; ties broken arbitrarily. Non-deterministic unless ORDER BY is unique. Always add a unique tiebreaker before WHERE rn = 1.

nodes.label: rank
nodes.rationale: Ties share a place; next value skips the gap (1, 1, 3). max(rank) equals row count, not distinct values. Ranking functions ignore the frame clause.

nodes.label: dense_rank
nodes.rationale: Ties share a place with no gap (1, 1, 2). Use for distinct score levels rather than sporting position.

nodes.label: percent_rank
nodes.rationale: (rank - 1) / (rows - 1), always 0 to 1. Sibling cume_dist is the proportion of rows at or before this one.

nodes.label: ntile
nodes.rationale: Divides into n buckets; remainder goes to earliest buckets (7 into 3 → 3,2,2). Splits ties across boundaries, so unsuitable for grading. Prefer percentile_cont thresholds.

nodes.label: Top-N per group
nodes.rationale: Three shapes: row_number + filter, DISTINCT ON (top-1), LATERAL LIMIT. Winner depends on group count versus table size.

nodes.label: Run Condition
nodes.rationale: PostgreSQL 15+ pushes outer WHERE rn <= N into WindowAgg for monotonic functions (row_number, rank, dense_rank, count). Emitted 15000 instead of 500000; the Sort still processes all rows.

nodes.label: DISTINCT ON top-1
nodes.rationale: Shortest PostgreSQL-only top-1 per key. Cannot return N > 1. Measured 546.62 ms without index on this table.

nodes.label: LATERAL top-N per group
nodes.rationale: Wins when the driving set is small and each probe is indexed. Timed out at 30s without an index (5000 full scans); 906.59 ms with one. Only form that takes OFFSET per group.

nodes.label: Non-covering window index made top-N slower
nodes.rationale: Index Scan (not Index Only Scan) because id was not in the index: 434.74 ms / 3783 buffers → 533.67 ms / 500574 buffers. INCLUDE selected columns, or keep the sequential scan. Compare Buffers, not just milliseconds.

nodes.label: Ranking functions
nodes.rationale: row_number, rank and dense_rank differ only in ties. ntile has an uneven-division rule that breaks equal-sized quartile claims.

nodes.label: lag and lead
nodes.rationale: Fetch a value a fixed number of rows away. Makes change-since-last-time a column. Counts rows, not days.

nodes.label: lag
nodes.rationale: lag(expr, offset=1, default=NULL) from a preceding row. Does not cross PARTITION BY. Without ORDER BY, previous means scan order. Non-constant offset is accepted and can yield all NULLs.

nodes.label: lead
nodes.rationale: Same arguments as lag, looking forward. Last row of each partition is NULL unless a default is supplied.

nodes.label: generate_series date spine before lag
nodes.rationale: lag returns the previous row. A missing day silently compares across the gap. Build a dense spine, LEFT JOIN, count(o.id) not count(*). Use nullif(lag(n), 0) for percent change.

nodes.label: last_value default-frame trap
nodes.rationale: ORDER BY implies RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, so last_value is the current row. Fix with ROWS … UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING, or first_value over the reverse order.

nodes.label: first_value
nodes.rationale: Returns expr from the first row of the frame. Correct under the default frame only because the frame starts at UNBOUNDED PRECEDING. Prefer it over last_value with reversed ORDER BY.

nodes.label: nth_value
nodes.rationale: 1-based index into the frame. With the default frame, nth_value(x, 2) is NULL until the frame contains two rows. No negative form — reverse the order.

nodes.label: lag, lead, first_value, last_value
nodes.rationale: lag/lead count rows relative to the current row and ignore the frame. first_value/last_value/nth_value index the frame — which is why last_value famously returns the current row.

nodes.label: Naming a subquery
nodes.rationale: A CTE binds a name to a subquery for one statement. It is not a temp table. One WITH, comma-separated list; lives only while the statement runs.

nodes.label: CTE (WITH)
nodes.rationale: Readability feature, not a performance feature. Referenced like a table anywhere a table can appear. WITH attaches to SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and MERGE.

nodes.label: CTE forward reference 42P01
nodes.rationale: A CTE sees only earlier declarations. Forward reference is 42P01 relation does not exist. WITH RECURSIVE lifts the restriction for the whole list. Duplicate names are 42712.

nodes.label: CTE name shadows a real table
nodes.rationale: No warning. Inside the statement the CTE wins and the table is unreachable by that name. Give CTEs names that cannot collide.

nodes.label: The inlining rule
nodes.rationale: Before PG12 every CTE was an optimization fence. Since 12 a qualifying CTE is folded in. Same query 28.42 ms inlined vs 174.49 ms MATERIALIZED — 6.1×.

nodes.label: CTE inlining conditions
nodes.rationale: Inlined when referenced once, not MATERIALIZED, not recursive, does not write, and has no volatile function. Inlined CTE leaves no CTE node; filter can reach the scan and parallelise.

nodes.label: MATERIALIZED fence
nodes.rationale: Forces a CTE Scan after materialising every row (500000 into Disk 21344kB, no parallelism). Use only when the query depends on the fence.

nodes.label: LIMIT does not fence a CTE
nodes.rationale: The CTE is still inlined. Limit stays below the outer filter so 10 rows then filter to 5, not first 10 matching the filter. Protects semantics, not cost.

nodes.label: Volatility classes and CTE inlining
nodes.rationale: IMMUTABLE and STABLE (now()) inline. VOLATILE (random(), clock_timestamp()) fences because re-evaluation could change the answer. Same classification as indexability.

nodes.label: References, hints and the plan
nodes.rationale: Referenced twice, a CTE is computed once. NOT MATERIALIZED is a request the planner may ignore. No CTE node is not the same as the filter reaching the scan.

nodes.label: Multiply-referenced CTE computed once
nodes.rationale: Automatic materialization: Buffers 3803, 56.5 ms. NOT MATERIALIZED doubled work (7606 buffers, 124.1 ms). This is the one execution guarantee a CTE gives that a repeated subquery does not.

nodes.label: NOT MATERIALIZED is advisory
nodes.rationale: Ignored when inlining would change the answer — volatile, recursive, or data-modifying CTEs stay fenced. A random() CTE still planned as CTE Scan despite the hint.

nodes.label: OFFSET 0 subquery fence
nodes.rationale: Classic pre-12 fence. Still blocks subquery pull-up in PG18: no CTE node, but filter stuck above Subquery Scan and no parallelism. Removing a pointless OFFSET 0 can change the plan.

nodes.label: CTEs (WITH)
nodes.rationale: WITH binds a name for one statement so a four-step report reads as four named steps. The non-obvious part is the plan: qualifying CTEs fold in; MATERIALIZED costs 6× here.

nodes.label: One statement, several writes
nodes.rationale: A CTE may contain INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE or MERGE. With RETURNING feeding the next step, a move-then-record is one atomic statement and one round trip.

nodes.label: Archive pattern
nodes.rationale: WITH moved AS (DELETE … RETURNING *) INSERT INTO archive SELECT * FROM moved. No moment the row exists in neither table or both. Also upsert-plus-audit via xmax = 0.

nodes.label: Unreferenced write CTE still runs
nodes.rationale: A SELECT CTE nobody references can be discarded; a write is a promised side effect and executes exactly once. Delete the CTE, not just the reference.

nodes.label: Data-modifying CTE always fenced
nodes.rationale: One of the five inlining exclusions. NOT MATERIALIZED cannot override it, because inlining would execute the write once per reference.

nodes.label: The snapshot rule
nodes.rationale: Every part of one statement sees the same pre-statement snapshot. Sibling writes are invisible except via RETURNING. Makes the result independent of unspecified CTE order.

nodes.label: Sibling SELECT cannot see the write
nodes.rationale: Measured visible_to_sibling 0, visible_via_returning 1, and 1 row present afterwards. Re-read the table and you get the world before the statement started.

nodes.label: Two CTEs writing the same row
nodes.rationale: No error: a reported 1, b reported 0, final value 1. SERIALIZABLE does not help — one transaction. Merge into one UPDATE, disjoint WHERE, or separate statements. MERGE would raise 21000 for the analogous mistake.

nodes.label: When a transaction beats one multi-CTE write
nodes.rationale: Use BEGIN when a later step must read an earlier write, the branch is in application code, the same rows are written twice, or the work should be batched. Constraints still fail the whole statement.

nodes.label: Data-modifying CTEs
nodes.rationale: Three rules: a write CTE always runs; its effect is visible only through RETURNING; execution order is unspecified so two writes on one row are a silent bug.

nodes.label: Scalar and row subqueries
nodes.rationale: A subquery in an expression position must produce one row and one column. Enforced at runtime, so today's one-row table is tomorrow's 21000.

nodes.label: Scalar subquery
nodes.rationale: Uncorrelated form is evaluated once and attached to every row. More than one row is 21000; zero rows is NULL, not an error. Prefer an aggregate or unique key over LIMIT 1.

nodes.label: 21000 more than one row returned
nodes.rationale: Planner cannot know the row count, so the query is accepted and the executor discovers the problem. LIMIT 1 without ORDER BY converts a loud error into a plan-dependent answer.

nodes.label: Row constructor comparison
nodes.rationale: (a, b) > (1, 5) is lexicographic: a > 1 or (a = 1 and b > 5). Correct spelling for keyset pagination. Any NULL component yields NULL, same three-valued logic as NOT IN.

nodes.label: Correlated subquery
nodes.rationale: References an outer column, so it cannot be computed once. An N+1 written inside one statement: no round trips, same shape of work.

nodes.label: SubPlan loops per outer row
nodes.rationale: SubPlan plus loops=5000 is the diagnosis. Rewrite as GROUP BY plus LEFT JOIN unless the outer set is small by construction or the planner already un-correlated it.

nodes.label: count() is 0, sum() is NULL over empty
nodes.rationale: No rows, a zero total, and a NULL total collapse into two outputs. coalesce when the API wants a number. LEFT JOIN rewrite of count() needs coalesce(o.n, 0) to keep zeros.

nodes.label: Correlated cost coupled to visibility map
nodes.rationale: Best case 145 ms vs GROUP BY 65 ms (2.2×). After stale visibility map 414 ms vs 90 ms (4.6×); Heap Fetches 0 → 133359. Do not benchmark on a freshly vacuumed table.

nodes.label: IN, EXISTS and the NOT IN trap
nodes.rationale: IN, = ANY and EXISTS agree. Their negations do not: NOT IN against one NULL returns no rows. The most expensive NULL behaviour in SQL.

nodes.label: IN / = ANY / EXISTS as semi join
nodes.rationale: IN is defined as = ANY. All three plan as a semi join that stops at the first match. Choice is readability, not speed. EXISTS SELECT 1 vs SELECT * is identical.

nodes.label: NOT IN NULL trap
nodes.rationale: x NOT IN (a, NULL) is x <> a AND x <> NULL. Comparison to NULL is unknown; WHERE unknown drops every row. Measured 1 → 0 after one NULL elsewhere. NOT EXISTS still returned 1.

nodes.label: NOT EXISTS anti join
nodes.rationale: Never compares a value to NULL; a NULL join key simply does not match. Default for every subquery negation. LEFT JOIN … WHERE right.id IS NULL is the older null-safe spelling.

nodes.label: = ANY($1::int[]) list parameter
nodes.rationale: One parameter regardless of list length; empty array matches nothing. Empty IN () is a syntax error. Never interpolate a NOT IN list — a null turns the predicate into no rows.

nodes.label: Subqueries
nodes.rationale: A subquery is a query used as a value, a set, or a table. Which of those three it is decides row cardinality, how often it runs, and whether a NULL in a negated set form empties the result.

nodes.label: Scalar subquery
nodes.rationale: Returns exactly 1 row × 1 column. Runs once if uncorrelated. Error 21000 if more than one row, often only in production.

nodes.label: Set subquery
nodes.rationale: Used with IN / ANY / EXISTS. Any number of rows. Runs once as a semi join when uncorrelated.

nodes.label: Table subquery
